The excerpt provides qualitative context for comparing powder-flowability tests in metal additive manufacturing, but it does not report the Marchetti and Hulme-Smith (2021) regression analysis or identify a statistically best-correlated metric for spreadability. It characterizes FT4 powder rheometry as especially relevant because it measures dynamic shear resistance, which resembles the forces acting during powder-bed spreading. FT4 reports metrics including basic flowability energy (BFE) for confined downward blade motion and specific energy (SE) for unconfined upward motion. The text cautions that FT4 results are generally more reliable for comparative assessment than for design data. The Revolution avalanche tester is also described as simulating dynamic spreading behavior, whereas conventional gravity-based methods such as the Hall flowmeter and angle of repose may be less representative of spreading. The excerpt discusses flowability as an indicator of spreading behavior and links better flowability with improved layer homogeneity, packing, density, and final-part quality. However, it contains no direct comparison among Hall flow, Hausner ratio, FT4 rheometry, shear-cell measurements, and angle of repose, and no correlation coefficients, regression results, or conclusion about which metric best predicts spreadability.

From text 'balbaa2021roleofpowder pages 4-8'.

M.A. Balbaa, A. Ghasemi, E. Fereiduni, M.A. Elbestawi, S.D. Jadhav, and J.-P. Kruth. Role of powder particle size on laser powder bed fusion processability of alsi10mg alloy. Additive Manufacturing, 37:101630, Jan 2021. URL: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.addma.2020.101630, doi:10.1016/j.addma.2020.101630. This article has 249 citations and is from a highest quality peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt introduces the flowability characterization methods used for gas-atomized AlSi10Mg powders but does not provide the requested numerical Hausner ratios, Hall flow times, angles of repose, or detailed FT4 measurement results. Flowability was evaluated using Hall and Carney flowmeters in accordance with ASTM B213-17, together with the FT4 Freeman powder rheometer. The text notes that Hall flow testing is relatively close to additive-manufacturing conditions, particularly powder-fed processes, but has major limitations for cohesive powders that may nevertheless remain suitable for powder bed fusion. FT4 is recommended because the precision blade–powder interaction more closely resembles the recoater–powder interaction in laser powder bed fusion. The fine AlSi10Mg powder had a mean particle size of approximately 9 µm, while the coarse powder was approximately 40 µm. Morphologically, the fine powder was highly spherical and satellite-free but exhibited a strong tendency for interparticle attachment and agglomeration; the coarse powder showed no clear agglomeration. These observations indicate potentially greater cohesion and poorer flow for the fine powder. The excerpt contains no comparisons with steel or titanium powders, and it does not discuss low-density effects, granular Bond numbers, or aluminium-alloy cohesion quantitatively.

## pqac-00000053

From text 'haydari2021thespreadingbehavioura pages 27-31'.

Z Haydari. The spreading behaviour of stainless steel powders for additive manufacturing. Unknown journal, 2021.

The excerpt provides general methods and concepts relevant to evaluating LPBF powder flowability, but it does not report specific AlSi10Mg Hausner ratio values, Hall flow times, angle-of-repose values, FT4 measurements, or comparisons with steel and titanium powders. It defines flowability as the ability of a powder to flow in a desired manner in specific equipment and emphasizes that it is a multidimensional property influenced by powder characteristics and handling or measurement conditions. Angle of repose is measured from a powder heap formed through a funnel; steeper angles indicate greater cohesion. ## pqac-00000058

From text 'bhattachar2004evaluationofthe pages 1-3'.

Shobha N. Bhattachar, David B. Hedden, Angela M. Olsofsky, Xianggui Qu, Wen-Yaw Hsieh, and Kelly G. Canter. Evaluation of the vibratory feeder method for assessment of powder flow properties. International journal of pharmaceutics, 269 2:385-92, Jan 2004. URL: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ijpharm.2003.09.024, doi:10.1016/j.ijpharm.2003.09.024. This article has 38 citations and is from a domain leading peer-reviewed journal.

Bhattachar et al. (2004) evaluated a vibratory feeder as a rapid, material-sparing method for characterizing pharmaceutical powder flow. The method measures avalanche flow dynamically by recording powder flow-rate profiles and using fractal-dimension analysis; its output is a powder flow index (PFI). Seventeen pharmaceutical powders were tested, and the PFI trends correlated well with flow properties reported in the literature. Results were also compared with the Aero-Flow instrument’s mean time to avalanche (MTA), with the two methods showing excellent agreement using nonparametric analysis of ranked data. The excerpt does not provide information on tapping tests, tilting tubes or boxes, onset-angle measurements, or discharge-mass fluctuation as a cohesion index. It does mention that other researchers calculated a Flowability Index from the standard deviation of MTA values across increasing rotational speeds, and a Cohesion Index from MTA. Thus, within this excerpt, the Bhattachar study primarily supports vibratory-feeder avalanche testing and the PFI as a flowability measure; it does not establish that discharge-mass fluctuations, tapping, or tilting-angle methods were used in the study.

## pqac-00000059

From text 'bodhmage2006correlationbetweenphysicala pages 23-27'.

AK Bodhmage. Correlation between physical properties and flowability indicators for fine powders. Unknown journal, 2006.

The excerpt supports tapping-based density indices and tilting-box angle-of-repose testing as flowability measurements, but it does not specifically describe a vibratory feeder method, discharge-mass fluctuations, or the Bhattachar (2004) method. Tapping is used to obtain tapped density, which is compared with loose-packed bulk density through the Hausner ratio (HR = TD/BD). The related Carr Index is calculated from the difference between tapped and bulk density relative to tapped density; cohesive powders generally have HR greater than 1.4, while Carr Index values above 20–25% indicate non-free-flowing material. For angle-of-repose testing, the excerpt identifies both tilting-box and fixed-cone methods. Static angle of repose is the angle formed by a powder pile with the horizontal, while dynamic angle of repose is measured on the inclined powder surface in a rotating drum. The excerpt cautions that cohesive powders may be difficult to measure directly and that boundary friction at rotating-drum end caps can produce faulty results. It also describes avalanche testing: powder in a slowly rotating disk builds to an unstable condition and slides down; the avalanche is detected photoelectrically, with shorter avalanche times corresponding to better flowability. No evidence is provided here that discharge-mass fluctuations serve as a cohesion index or that vibration-induced discharge is the specific flowability metric requested.

## pqac-00000060

From text 'talebi2021characterisationofspreadability pages 28-33'.

FAA Talebi. Characterisation of spreadability behaviour of ti6al4v powders for additive manufacturing. Unknown journal, 2021.

The excerpt provides partial support for using tapping or vibration-related density changes as a flowability indicator, but it does not specifically describe a vibratory feeder method, discharge-mass fluctuations as a cohesion index, a tilting tube or tilting box onset-angle test, vibration-induced discharge, or the Bhattachar (2004) method. It states that tapping simulates vibrations arising during powder processing and handling. For finer powders, tapping allows particles to rearrange as interparticle forces are overcome, increasing the compacted or tapped bulk density. The difference between tapped density and aerated/apparent bulk density can indicate sensitivity to vibration. The excerpt also presents Hausner Ratio (HR) and Carr’s Compressibility Index (CI), calculated from tapped and apparent densities, as simple indicators of powder flowability. Lower HR and CI correspond generally to better flow, while higher values indicate increasingly cohesive or poorly flowing powders. However, the text cautions that HR and CI are insufficient as standalone measures, particularly because additive-manufacturing powder deposition does not involve tapping or compression. It additionally describes the Hall flowmeter as measuring mass flow through a funnel, while noting limited sensitivity, operator dependence, and problems with cohesive powders. No onset-angle or feeder-discharge data are reported here.

## pqac-00000061

From text 'bodhmage2006correlationbetweenphysical pages 23-27'.

AK Bodhmage. Correlation between physical properties and flowability indicators for fine powders. Unknown journal, 2006.

The excerpt provides partial background relevant to tilting-box-based flowability testing, but it does not discuss the specific Bhattachar (2004) vibratory-feeder method, vibration-induced discharge, discharge-mass fluctuations as a cohesion index, or tapping as a feeder-based flowability measure. It identifies the angle of repose as a method for quantifying granular-material cohesiveness and notes that static and dynamic angles of repose are distinct measurements. The static angle is formed by a powder pile with the horizontal, while the dynamic angle is formed by the inclined powder surface in a rotating drum. Riley et al. (1978) used both tilting-box and fixed-cone methods, and the excerpt emphasizes that angle-of-repose measurements are faster than the Jenike procedure. For cohesive powders, direct angle measurement may be difficult; one reported approach used mixtures with a free-flowing material and extrapolated angle-versus-composition data to estimate a theoretical angle. The excerpt also mentions avalanching as a separate flowability technique: free-flowing powders have shorter avalanche times, while less-flowable powders take longer to avalanche. However, no evidence is provided here linking discharge fluctuations or vibratory-feeder output directly to cohesion.

## pqac-00000062

From text 'haydari2021thespreadingbehavioura pages 27-31'.

Z Haydari. The spreading behaviour of stainless steel powders for additive manufacturing. Unknown journal, 2021.

The excerpt provides general context for evaluating powder flowability but does not specifically describe the Bhattachar (2004) vibratory feeder method, tapping as a flowability index, discharge-mass fluctuations as a cohesion index, tilting-tube or tilting-box onset angles, or vibration-induced discharge testing. It emphasizes that powder flowability is multidimensional and depends on powder properties as well as handling, storage, and measurement conditions. Several conventional methods are identified: flow function, internal and wall friction, angle of repose, Hall flowmeter testing, and FT4 powder rheometry. Angle of repose is measured from the heap formed when powder is deposited through a funnel; a steeper angle generally indicates greater cohesion. The Hall flowmeter measures the time required for powder to discharge through an orifice, but it is mainly suitable for free-flowing powders and provides a comparative rather than fully consistent flow-rate measure. The FT4 rheometer measures dynamic flow resistance and is relevant to powder-bed fusion because shear is an important force during spreading. These principles support interpreting discharge behavior and cohesion-related fluctuations, but the requested vibratory feeder and tilting-angle procedures would require additional source material.

## pqac-00000063

From text 'fernander2026powdercharacterizationfor pages 11-11'.

D. Scott Fernander, Rakeshkumar Karunakaran, Paul R. Mort, and Michael P. Sealy. Powder characterization for in-space additive manufacturing. npj Advanced Manufacturing, Mar 2026. URL: https://doi.org/10.1038/s44334-026-00071-2, doi:10.1038/s44334-026-00071-2. This article has 1 citations.

The excerpt provides general context for evaluating powder flowability but does not specifically describe the requested vibratory feeder, tapping, tilting tube, tilting box, or vibration-induced discharge methods, nor does it mention Bhattachar (2004). It explains that flowability tests are commonly used as a go/no-go criterion for whether a powder will function in a printer, while noting that such tests provide limited information about the particle attributes responsible for poor flow. Additional characterization methods are therefore needed to diagnose performance issues and identify appropriate adjustments. The excerpt also cautions that greater flowability is not universally desirable: highly flowable multicomponent powders may segregate rapidly, whereas some cohesion can help maintain uniformity and reduce segregation. For in-space additive manufacturing, powder flow is especially challenging because it does not occur naturally in zero gravity without externally applied forces, such as drawing powder through a tube. info.name: open_targets_search
info.description:
Search for disease-target associations from OpenTargets database.

Adds new disease-target association data to the state and returns top search results.

disease_names.description:
List of disease names to search for.
Usage:
disease_names = ["Alzheimer's"] ->
    Returns top targets for Alzheimer's
disease_names = ["Alzheimer's", "Diabetes"], target_names = ["PSEN1"] ->
    Filters for only PSEN1-Alzheimer's/Diabetes evidence
disease_names = ["Alzheimer's"], drug_names = ["Aducanumab"] ->
    Filters for Alzheimer's disease-target pairs treated by Aducanumab
disease_names.title: Disease Names

target_names.description:
List of target names to search for.
Usage:
target_names = ["BACE1"] ->
    Returns top diseases associated with BACE1
target_names = ["BACE1", "APP"], disease_names = ["Alzheimer's"] ->
    Filters for only these target-Alzheimer's pairs
target_names = ["BACE1"], drug_names = ["Aducanumab"] ->
    Filters for BACE1 disease pairs treated by Aducanumab
target_names.title: Target Names

drug_names.description:
List of drug names to generate or filter results.
Usage:
drug_names = ["Aducanumab"] ->
    Returns all disease-target pairs treated by Aducanumab
drug_names = ["Aducanumab"], disease_names = ["Alzheimer's"] ->
    Filters for Alzheimer's pairs treated by Aducanumab
drug_names = ["Aducanumab"], target_names = ["BACE1"] ->
    Filters for BACE1 disease pairs treated by Aducanumab
drug_names.title: Drug Names

info.name: create_artifact
info.description:
Create an artifact that can be used in the final answer, based on information
you have collected so far.

How it works: the full message history thus far is passed to another LLM,
along with the question and your description. The LLM is tasked to create
an artifact that matches your specifications, including a title, caption,
and markdown content. You drive the process by specifying the type and
describing what you want.

Only use this tool *after* you have gathered sufficient evidence or
information to create a new artifact. Do not call this tool in parallel
with tools that are searching for information or evidence that would be
necessary to create this artifact.

It is very helpful after calls to several search tools,
after calls to the `gather_evidence` tool, but it is not required.
However, it should be called before the `answer` tool at
least one time, but more may be given if specifically helpful for
the task, so that the `answer` tool can use the artifacts for the answer.

An artifact can be any string representable fact or list of facts,
formatted using markdown syntax. The artifact will be generated as one of
the following types:
- table: Markdown tables with rows and columns (e.g., findings, methods, molecules)
- code_block: Code snippets in fenced code blocks
- blockquote: Quoted text or important facts (using > prefix)
- image: AI-generated image (chart, diagram, or visualization)

Each artifact consists of:
- A short title (3-8 words) that names what the artifact contains
- A caption (1-2 sentences) describing what the artifact shows and why it's useful
- Markdown content in a single element type (validated automatically with retries if needed)
  For image type, content is a markdown image embed ``![title](data:image/png;base64,...)``,
  embedding the PNG directly as a base64 data URL.

artifact_type.description:
Artifact type to create. Must be one of: table,
code_block, blockquote, image.
artifact_type.title: Artifact Type

description.description:
Description of what you want in the artifact. Be specific
about what information should be included, how it should be organized,
and what columns/sections/content you want. This guides the summary LLM.
For image type, describe the visual you want generated in detail.
description.title: Description

info.name: clinical_trials_search
info.description:
Search for clinical trials, with support for repeated calls and concurrent execution.

Will add new clinical trials to the state, and return metadata about the number of trials found.

query.description:
The search query string. Supports complex boolean expressions, field-specific
searches, and query modifiers through operators. All configuration is done through
operators in the query string.
Query Syntax:
    Basic Search:
        Simple text automatically uses default EXPANSION[Relaxation] and COVERAGE[Contains]
        >>> "heart attack"

    Modified Search:
        Use operators to modify search behavior:
        >>> 'EXPANSION[None]COVERAGE[FullMatch]"exact phrase"'
        >>> 'EXPANSION[Concept]heart attack'

    Field Search:
        Specify fields using AREA operator:
        >>> 'AREA[InterventionName]aspirin'
        >>> 'AREA[Phase]PHASE3'

    Location Search:
        Use SEARCH operator for compound location queries:
        >>> 'cancer AND SEARCH[Location](AREA[LocationCity]Boston AND AREA[LocationState]Massachusetts)'

    Complex Boolean:
        Combine terms with AND, OR, NOT and parentheses:
        >>> '(cancer OR tumor) AND NOT (EXPANSION[None]pediatric OR AREA[StdAge]CHILD)'

    Date Ranges:
        Use RANGE to specify date ranges with formats like "yyyy-MM" or "yyyy-MM-dd".
        Note that MIN and MAX can be used for open-ended ranges:
        >>> AREA[ResultsFirstPostDate]RANGE[2015-01-01, MAX]

Operators:
    EXPANSION[type]: Controls term expansion
        - None: Exact match only, case and accent sensitive
        - Term: Includes lexical variants (plurals, spellings)

info.name: patent_search
info.description:
Search for patents to increase the patent count.

Repeat previous calls with the same query to continue a search.
Only repeat a maximum of three times.
This tool can be called concurrently.
This tool introduces novel patents, so invoke it when just beginning
or when unsatisfied with the current evidence.

query.description:
A search query for patents (using Google Patents). Never include temporal
filters here (e.g. specific years or dates); instead use the `after` and `before`
arguments. Never include author filters here; instead use the `inventor` argument.
Supports the following syntax, but they can be brittle and are not preferred; try
simple queries where possible:
- Boolean operators: AND (default), OR, and - (NOT)
- Exact phrases: "quoted text"
- Proximity: NEAR/x, ADJ/x (ordered), WITH (20 words), SAME (200 words)
- Field search: TI=(title), AB=(abstract), CL=(claims)
- CPC codes: cpc:A01B or CPC=B60R22/low (includes children)
- Wildcards: ? (0-1 char), * (0+ chars), # (exactly 1 char)
- Chemistry: exact molecule names, SSS=molecule (substructure),
  ~molecule (similar), SMILES strings, SMARTS=pattern, InChI keys,
  CL=~molecule (chemistry in claims)

info.name: view_images
info.description:
Retrieve images from a document.

Use this tool when you need to see figures, tables, or other visual content.
The tool works by asking a weaker LLM agent to scan through the document, looking for
visual content matching the query you provide. When the agent finds matches, it will
crop the page to the relevant region. It can be tasked to return multiple images,
if desired. Note that the weaker LLM may be worse at *understanding* images than
you, so double-check its conclusions about the returned images. It is also stateless,
i.e. it will not remember what you have asked it to find in the past.

Use this tool carefully. It is difficult to retrieve images, and the images
themselves will fill up your context window quickly. Here are some guidelines:
1. ALWAYS use this tool if the question explicitly mentions 'Table X' or 'Figure Y'.
   These questions require visual content and cannot be answered with text alone.
2. Use this tool as a fallback when gather_evidence fails repeatedly (2+ times
   returning 'No relevant evidence'). This suggests the answer may be in visual content.
3. When gather_evidence returns text mentioning 'see Figure X' or 'shown in Table Y',
   you should call this tool to examine that specific visual reference.
4. Only call this tool after directly inspecting relevant text with read_text
   to confirm the document likely contains the visual you need.
5. Don't use this tool in a broad-spectrum way (don't call on many documents
   just to see what might be relevant).
6. Never call this tool in parallel with itself.
7. Users like visual evidence, so call this tool at least once before answering so you
   can provide some image citations in the answer. Add this to your plan so you do not forget.
   For images to be presented to the user, they must be cited in the final answer after retrieval
   by this tool. You may ignore this instruction if the request is for the question is asking
   for a specific piece of information and is not an open-ended research question.
8. NEVER cite full-page images in your final answer, unless they are full-page panels figures or
   tables. Cite relevant cropped regions if available, otherwise consider calling this tool again
   to find a smaller region that answers the query.

query.description:
Query to search for visual content in the document. If you know the specific
figure/table/formula you are looking for, you can specify it here (e.g. "find me
Figure 3" or "extract the table on page 10"). You can also request based on content
(e.g. "find me all volcano plots of gene X" or "I need the formula for the growth rate").
You can even include explicit instructions for the LLM agent to follow (if helpful, not
necessarily required). The more specific and clear your query is here, the higher the
chance of success.
query.title: Query

text_name.description: Name of a text chunk (e.g., 'smith2023example pages 1-5').
text_name.title: Text Name

info.name: create_plan
info.description:
Create a plan for to construct a thorough and accurate answer.

Decompose the input task into a set of sub-objectives that need to
be met in order to form the answer. Subsequently, when working on solving
the query, you can focus on these objectives one by one. Note that the
`update_plan` tool allows you to change the objectives if needed.

In addition to the objectives you deem necessary, add one final objective
to call the `answer` tool with your final answer, so that you do not
forget to submit your answer.

plan_json.description:
A JSON string representing the plan. It should be a dictionary
with top-level key "objectives", whose value is a list of objectives.
Each objective should be a dictionary with the following keys:
- "id": (int) an integer id for the plan objective
- "objective": (str) a human readable description of the objective's goal
- "rationale": (str) a human readable rationale
    describing why this objective is necessary and appropriate for the query.
- "status": (str) updated task status, default to pending,
    one of: pending, in-progress, or completed.
    "pending" is yet to be started,
    "in-progress" is the current objective being solved,
    "completed" is successfully completed with acceptance criteria met.
- "result": (str|None) The result of the objective, default to None.
- "evaluation": (str|None) Description of why the objective result
    meets the criteria for being complete. Default to None.
plan_json.title: Plan Json

The updated_json should be a JSON string representing a single plan objective object.

strategy if the current plan is not working. Only change strategy significantly
as a last resort, after trying very hard to make the current plan work.

Only mark an objective as completed if you are absolutely sure that it has been fully
met. If it is only partially met, you may add additional objectives to the plan for

info.name: read_text
info.description:
Given a list of text names, read their contents.

This tool is valuable to read the full contents of specific parts of documents,
complementing the `gather_evidence` tool's indirect approach.
This can be an especially useful tool if `gather_evidence` does not find evidence,
but you think it is very likely that specific documents are still relevant to the question.

text_name_list.description:
A list of up to 10 text names to read.
These text names can be any valid text names retrieved by other tools.
text_name_list.title: Text Name List

info.name: gather_evidence
info.description:
Given a specific question, gather evidence from full-text of documents that have been retrieved by
previous tool calls.

Here is how the tool works: the provided question is posed to all texts retrieved thus far
by other tools. An LLM sees each text independently and is prompted to find information relevant
to the question.

That is, we sample evidence `e \sim LLM(prompt, text, q)` for each text. We only return pieces of
evidence `e` that are sufficiently relevant to the question; if the text is irrelevant, then `e`
is not included in the final response of this tool. Note that this LLM does not see the conversation
history thus far, only the question and each text. Note that it only sees text, no images or other
media from the contents (though tables and formulae may be parseable in some cases).

Think of this tool as an efficient way to deeply scan all retrieved documents for evidence. It
is complementary to the `read_text` tool, which can be used to directly inspect a subset of the
retrieved documents.

A valuable time to invoke this tool is after another tool finds potentially relevant documents.
Feel free to invoke this tool in parallel with other tools, but do not call this tool in parallel with itself.
Only invoke this tool when the document count is above zero, or this tool will be useless.

If you call this tool 2+ times and repeatedly get 'No relevant evidence found',
consider whether the answer might be in visual content (figures/tables) rather than text,
and use appropriate tools if available to access that content.

Once you receive evidence from this tool:

1. Read Carefully: Don't skim. The evidence may contain multiple similar terms
   or values—make sure you identify the RIGHT one.

2. For Comparative Questions: If the question asks "which X has greatest Y",
   check that the evidence includes information about ALL relevant X options, not
   just one or two. If you only see partial information, gather more evidence.

3. Check for Noise: Verify that numbers or terms aren't just metadata
   (page numbers, reference IDs, dates). Look for the value in meaningful
   scientific context.

4. Context Matters: A term appearing 71 times doesn't mean it's always the answer.
   Verify which occurrence actually answers the question asked.

If the evidence doesn't clearly answer the question, gather more evidence before
concluding. Don't guess based on partial information.

question.description: Specific question to gather evidence for.
question.title: Question

text_name_focus_list.description:
if there are known text names that are relevant to the question,
you can specify them here. This will ensure that the tool will look at these text names
first, and then look at the rest of the evidence. If left as `None`, an embedding
search will be performed on underlying content to find most relevant texts.
text_name_focus_list.title: Text Name Focus List

info.name: answer
info.description:
Submit your final answer to the user. You MUST call this tool on your final answer.
If you mark all objectives as completed but have not yet called this tool, then
the answer will not be submitted. Note that this tool should only be called once, as it
immediately terminates the run and submits the answer.

Write an answer based on the evidence from gather_evidence results in message history.
If the context provides insufficient information, provide a partial answer and explain
why it is partial (e.g. the question is currently an open question in the field,
you were unable to obtain certain papers, etc.).

For each part of your answer, indicate which sources most support it via citation IDs at
the end of sentences, like (pqac-0000ABCD).
You are only allowed to cite available context IDs, indicated in previous messages by "Context IDs that may be cited:".
## Valid citation examples, only use comma/space delimited parentheticals:

- (pqac-0000ABCD, pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000IJKL)

## Invalid citation examples:

- (pqac-0000ABCD and pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000ABCD;pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000ABCD-pqac-0000EFGH)
- pqac-0000ABCD and pqac-0000EFGH
- Example's work pqac-0000ABCD
- (pages pqac-0000ABCD)
- ![description](pqac-0000ABCD)
- ()

Do not concatenate citation ids, just use them as-is.

When writing your answer, embed artifacts if relevant artifacts have been previously
created by the `create_artifact` tool. To embed an artifact, simply include this in your
answer, on its own line and without any additional formatting (i.e. no backticks, code fences,
quotes, additional tags, etc.).
Always provide at least some introductory sentence or paragraph before referring to an artifact,
so that the artifact is properly contextualized.
Here is an example reference to an artifact with ID "artifact-XY":
<artifact id="artifact-XY"/>

Valid artifact IDs are indicated in previous messages by 'Artifact IDs that may be injected into the answer:'.


Double-check your answer:

1. Evidence Match: Re-read the specific evidence snippets you're citing. Does your
   answer actually match what they say? Don't rely on memory from 20+ messages ago.

2. For Comparative Questions ("which X has greatest/maximum/highest Y"):
   - Did you examine ALL options mentioned in the evidence?
   - Did you explicitly compare their values?
   - Example: If evidence mentions "Pancreatic: 0.92, Liver: 0.85, Lung: 0.78",
     verify you compared all three, not just two.

3. For Specific Value Questions ("How many", "What is the", specific terms):
   - Does the exact value you're stating appear in the evidence?
   - Are you extracting from the right context (not noise like page numbers)?

4. Sanity Check: Read your answer. Does it directly address what was asked?

Don't use Markdown image syntax like ![...](...) to reference media in your answer,
because media get automatically linked by the system based on your answer's citations.

Write in the style of a scientific article, with concise sentences and
coherent paragraphs. This answer will be used directly,
so do not add any extraneous information.

answer.description: valid answer, cited with citation IDs.
answer.title: Answer

messages.content:
Use the tools to answer the question: Context: we run a small open-hardware auger powder doser: a tube with a helical auger (stepper-driven, 5-100 rpm) fed from a small hopper, a servo that tilts the tube from horizontal (0 deg) toward vertical (90 deg, gravity assisting discharge), a solenoid that taps the tube, and an analytical balance (0.1 mg) under the outlet logging cumulative discharged mass vs time at about 2.5 Hz. Across a 12-powder battery (salts, food biopolymers, silicon, gas-atomized AlSi10Mg) the mass discharged per auger revolution ("feed factor") spans three decades and its rank correlates strongly with literature angle of repose (Spearman rho = -0.84). We now want to use the doser as a cheap per-batch flowability screen for in-house gas-atomized aluminium alloy powder (Al 4047, Al-12Si) intended for laser powder bed fusion (LPBF), as a stand-in for a dedicated spreadability tester that costs tens of thousands of dollars. The powder will be sieved (e.g. -63 um or 20-63 um) before testing.

Please synthesize the peer-reviewed literature, with quantitative values and citations, on:

1. Which flowability measurements best predict LPBF powder spreadability / spread-layer quality (layer packing density, coverage, roughness, streaking, part density): Hall/Carney funnel flow, Hausner ratio/Carr index, static angle of repose, rotating-drum dynamic angle of repose and cohesive index (e.g. GranuDrum), avalanche angle / break energy / surface fractal (e.g. Revolution Powder Analyzer), FT4 rheometry (basic flow energy, specific energy, flow-rate index, compressibility), shear-cell flow function. Report reported correlation strengths (e.g. Spierings et al. 2016; Snow, Martukanitz & Joshi 2019; Cordova et al. 2020; Marchetti & Hulme-Smith 2021; others) and which metrics work for aluminium alloy powders (AlSi10Mg, AlSi12) whose low density raises the cohesion-to-weight ratio (granular Bond number).

2. Evidence that screw/auger feeder behaviour correlates with standard flowability metrics: feed factor and its normalisation by bulk density (volumetric fill efficiency), feed-rate variability (RSD), speed dependence of mass per revolution, tilt/inclination dependence of screw conveyors (e.g. Wang, Li, Muzzio & Glasser 2017; Bostijn et al. 2019; Van Snick et al. 2017; inclined screw conveyor studies), and any work using fluctuation statistics of discharged mass, tilting-tube or tilting-box onset angles, or vibration/tap-induced discharge as flowability indices.

3. How rotating-drum indices are defined (dynamic angle vs drum speed, cohesive index as interface-fluctuation standard deviation, avalanche statistics), and whether an analogous index can be computed from fluctuations in the mass-discharge-rate signal of a feeder outlet. Which features of a mass-vs-time trace are physically analogous to dynamic angle of repose and to cohesion?

4. What magnitude of change in these metrics corresponds to a practically significant change in spreadability for gas-atomized metal powders (e.g. avalanche-angle or dynamic-angle differences of a few degrees; cohesive-index thresholds; Hausner thresholds), and which batch-to-batch variations of gas-atomized powder (fines fraction below 15-20 um, satellites, sphericity, moisture, surface oxide, particle size distribution width) drive those changes. How do sieving and drying shift these metrics?

5. Recommended test conditions for a reproducible flowability screen: sample conditioning/pre-shear, drying, relative humidity, replicates, reference powders, and known pitfalls (e.g. electrostatic charging, segregation in the hopper, oversize particles jamming).

Finish with a concise recommendation: which two inexpensive, scalar flowability numbers (and how to normalise them) would be the most defensible proxies for LPBF spreadability that a tilting auger + balance could deliver.


Start by making a plan, and update the plan as you go. Your answer will be returned to the user when all plan objectives are completed. Be thorough and ensure your evidence matches the user's question.
I'll create a comprehensive plan to address this multi-faceted question about powder flowability measurements for LPBF spreadability prediction using an auger-based system.

Abstract:
Metal additive manufacturing technologies, such as Laser Powder-Bed Fusion, often rate as sustainable due to their high material efficiency. However, there are several drawbacks that reduce the overall sustainability and offer potential for improvement. One such drawback is waste emerging from the process. These smoulder particles form when the laser hits the powder-bed surface, are blown away from the part by the shielding gas stream and accumulate on the edge of the build chamber. Usually, smoulder does not contribute to the circular reuse of powder that was part of the powder-bed but was not integrated into a part. Instead, it marks an end-of-life state of powder. Significant amounts of smoulder accumulate depending on the irradiated area or the build volume in one job, respectively. This results in the waste of powder that was produced with low energy efficiency. This study investigates the question of whether smoulder can transform from waste to resource via common powder characterization methods and first build jobs using processed smoulder. The investigation of process-relevant powder properties like apparent density and flowability showed no significant difference between virgin powder and smoulder. Sample characterization indicated that neither porosity, surface quality nor mechanical properties deteriorate when samples contain about 50% smoulder. This allows for the reuse of smoulder in terms of powder characterization and part quality.

Abstract:
The particle shape influences the part properties in laser powder bed fusion, and powder flowability and powder layer density (PLD) are considered the link between the powder and part properties. Therefore, this study investigates the relationship between these properties and their influence on final part density for six 1.4404 (316L) powders and eight AlSi10Mg powders. The results show a correlation of the powder properties with a Pearson correlation coefficient (PCC) of −0.89 for the PLD and the Hausner ratio, a PCC of −0.67 for the Hausner ratio and circularity, and a PCC of 0.72 for circularity and PLD. Furthermore, the results show that beyond a threshold, improvement of circularity, PLD, or Hausner ratio have no positive influence on the final part density. While the water-atomized, least-spherical powder yielded parts with high porosity, no improvement of part density was achieved by feedstock with higher circularities than gas-atomized powder.

## 11. A Comprehensive Approach to Powder Feedstock Characterization for Powder Bed Fusion Additive Manufacturing: A Case Study on AlSi7Mg

    title = "A Comprehensive Approach to Powder Feedstock Characterization for Powder Bed Fusion Additive Manufacturing: A Case Study on AlSi7Mg",

Abstract:
In powder bed fusion additive manufacturing, the powder feedstock quality is of paramount importance; as the process relies on thin layers of powder being spread and selectively melted to manufacture 3D metallic components. Conventional powder quality assessments for additive manufacturing are limited to particle morphology, particle size distribution, apparent density and flowability. However, recent studies are highlighting that these techniques may not be the most appropriate. The problem is exacerbated when studying aluminium powders as their complex cohesive behaviors dictate their flowability. The current study compares the properties of three different AlSi7Mg powders, and aims to obtain insights about the minimum required properties for acceptable powder feedstock. In addition to conventional powder characterization assessments, the powder spread density, moisture sorption, surface energy, work of cohesion, and powder rheology, were studied. This work has shown that the presence of fine particles intensifies the pick-up of moisture increasing the total particle surface energy as well as the inter-particle cohesion. This effect hinders powder flow and hence, the spreading of uniform layers needed for optimum printing. When spherical particles larger than 48 µm with a narrow particle distribution are present, the moisture sorption as well as the surface energy and cohesion characteristics are decreased enhancing powder spreadability. This result suggest that by manipulating particle distribution, size and morphology, challenging powder feedstock such as Al, can be optimized for powder bed fusion additive manufacturing.

Abstract:
Powder bed fusion (PBF) is the most commonly adopted additive manufacturing process for fabricating complex metal parts via the layer-wise melting of a powder bed using a laser beam. However, the qualification of PBF-manufactured parts remains challenging and expensive, thereby limiting the broader industrialization of the technology. Powder characteristics significantly influence part properties, and understanding the influencing factors contributes to effective quality standards for PBF. In this study, the influence of the particle size distribution (PSD) median and width on powder flowability and part properties is investigated. Seven gas-atomized SS316L powders with monomodal PSDs, a median particle size ranging from 10 μm to 60 μm, and a distribution width of 15 μm and 30 μm were analyzed and subsequently processed. The PBF-manufactured parts were analyzed in terms of density and melt pool dimensions. Although powder flowability was inversely related to the median particle size, it was unrelated to the distribution width. An inverse relationship between the median particle size and the part density was observed; however, no link was found to the distribution width. Likely, the melt pool depth and width fluctuation significantly influence the part density. The melt pool depth decreases and the width fluctuation increases with an increasing median particle size.

The final part density in laser powder bed fusion is influenced by the powder particle size distribution. Too fine powders are not spreadable, and too coarse powders cause porosity. Powder blends, especially bimodal ones, can exhibit higher packing densities and changes in flowability compared to their monomodal constituents. These properties can influence final part density. Therefore, the influence of bimodal powder on final part density was investigated. Two gas atomized 316L (1.4404) powders with a D50 of 20.3 µm and 60.3 µm were blended at weight ratios of 3:1, 1:1, and 1:3, and the original and blended powders were processed. The results show that the final part porosity increases almost linearly with an increasing volume fraction of coarse powder. Furthermore, the final part density is independent of powder bulk density and flowability. Measurements of the top surface show that an increase of part porosity by coarse powder is caused by an increase in melt pool fluctuation, which in turn causes irregular solidified scan tracks. Additionally, the results show that the powder segregation during coating is stronger for the bimodal powder; however, no influence of the segregation on the part density could be found.

Therefore, six monomodal powders with different particle size distributions, from coarse to fine, are spread in an 84.5 µm deep cavity to determine their powder layer densities for a single layer. These findings suggest the existence of a particle size distribution that is sufficiently small to minimize the wall effect in a thin layer while still being sufficiently large to guarantee a good flowability of the powder.

Abstract:
Powder bed fusion additive manufacturing (PBFAM) of metals has the potential to enable new paradigms of product design, manufacturing and supply chains while accelerating the realization of new technologies in the medical, aerospace, and other industries. Currently, wider adoption of PBFAM is held back by difficulty in part qualification, high production costs and low production rates, as extensive process tuning, post‐processing, and inspection are required before a final part can be produced and deployed. Physics‐based modeling and predictive simulation of PBFAM offers the potential to advance fundamental understanding of physical mechanisms that initiate process instabilities and cause defects. In turn, these insights can help link process and feedstock parameters with resulting part and material properties, thereby predicting optimal processing conditions and inspiring the development of improved processing hardware, strategies and materials. This work presents recent developments of our research team in the modeling of metal PBFAM processes spanning length scales, namely mesoscale powder modeling, mesoscale melt pool modeling, macroscale thermo‐solid‐mechanical modeling and microstructure modeling. Ongoing work in experimental validation of these models is also summarized. In conclusion, we discuss the interplay of these individual submodels within an integrated overall modeling approach, along with future research directions.

Metal powders are key to metal additive manufacturing technologies such as powder bed fusion. These powder feedstocks experience a range of forces and physical phenomena both during the powder bed fusion process and additional post-processing stages that can alter their composition and material properties. To evaluate such effects, these powders need to be characterized, tested, and analyzed at critical stages of their lifecycles. This paper provides a review of the current state of the art for powder evaluation methods and their applicability for powder bed fusion production. Methods are categorized by the properties they evaluate, either particulate or bulk properties. Effects of these properties on the flowability and spreadability of powders are synthesized and practical management guidelines are defined. This paper aims at providing an overview of powder evaluation for powder bed fusion, practical considerations for the development of powder test and evaluation programs, and provide insights for future research undertakings in the field.

Abstract:
Purpose Predicting powder blend flowability is necessary for pharmaceutical manufacturing but challenging and resource-intensive. The purpose was to develop machine learning (ML) models to help predict flowability across multiple flow categories, identify key predictive features, and arrive at formulations with improved flow properties. Methods A dataset of 410 blends, composed of 9 active pharmaceutical ingredients (APIs) and 18 excipients with varying silica dry-coating parameters, was analyzed. Supervised ML models were trained to predict various flowability categories (very cohesive, cohesive, semi-cohesive, well-flowing, and free-flowing). Particle size, morphology, surface properties, and coating parameters were used as features. Classification algorithms, including Random Forest (RF) and Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost), were evaluated. Unsupervised clustering identified natural groupings within flowability data. Results The best-performing models achieved up to 85% accuracy for predicting flowability regimes of individual components and 87% for blends. Individual components generally showed higher accuracy than blends, except in the uncoated scenario with 2 flow regimes, where blends outperformed with 94.67%. SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) and Feature Importance analysis indicated dry coating parameters as the most influential factors, followed by particle size and morphology. ML models effectively identified category transitions between flow regimes, offering insights into blend optimization. Conclusion Integrating ML with mechanistic approaches effectively predicted powder blend flowability across diverse categories and elucidated feature-property relationships. These outcomes can facilitate the rational design of blends having enhanced flow properties at reduced experimental effort through judiciously selected dry coating of a blend constituent; making this approach promising for advancing pharmaceutical process and product development.

Abstract:
In continuous powder handling processes, precise and consistent feeding is crucial for ensuring the quality of the final product. The intermixing effect caused by agitators, which alters the powder’s bulk density, flow rate, and flow patterns, plays a significant role in this process, yet it is often overlooked. This study combines discrete element method (DEM) modeling and experiments using a commercial-scale feeder to propose a Digital Twin (DT) framework. The DEM model accurately captures key flow features, such as bypass trajectories, stagnant zones, and preferential flow patterns, while providing quantitative predictions for the feed factor and zones prone to material accumulation. Scenario analysis is performed to identify the most favorable operating ranges of the screw-agitator ratio and screw speed, considering the cohesive properties of the powder. The study demonstrates that powders with poor flow characteristics require tighter operational constraints, as the screw-agitator ratio is susceptible to variations in mass feed rate. This contribution highlights the importance of selecting an appropriate screw-agitator ratio instead of maintaining a fixed value. Properly choosing this ratio helps determine an optimal operation window, which aims to achieve a minimum agitation level needed to induce unhindered flow and reduce variability in the mass flow rate.

Abstract:
Abstract Screw feeder performance is a critical aspect in continuous manufacturing processes. Pharmaceutical excipients, such as mannitol, microcrystalline cellulose, lactose monohydrate, and anhydrous dibasic calcium phosphate can present problems in ensuring a continuous stable feed rate due to their sub-optimal flow properties. In alignment with Quality by Design (QbD) goals, the aim of this work was to identify and explain critical sources of variability of some powder excipients delivery by screw feeding, in particular to continuous processing lines. Pharmaceutical excipients with a wide range of material properties were selected, and the impact of their flow and density properties on screw feeder performance was investigated. The analysis of the powder conveying by the screws was performed at different hopper fills and different screw speeds. A multivariable model involving bulk density (CBD) and parameters from FT4 dynamic downwards testing (SI) and dynamic upwards testing (SE) explained 95.7% of excipients feed rates (p < .001). The study gathers valuable information about the screw feeder performance and input materials properties that can help process understanding and QbD-based development of solid dosage forms in continuous processing lines.

Abstract:
The most widely used metal additive manufacturing processes utilize powder that is spread or fed onto a building platform. Although there are reviews of the literature on some aspects of the powder, many aspects have been un-der-reviewed or unreviewed. The present work is a review of the literature on these aspects. Articles published in the open literature through the end of February 2022 were collected by consulting highly regarded relevant biblio-graphic databases, such as Google Scholar and Science Direct. The aspects reviewed were emerging methods of powder production, methods used to improve the quality of a powder after production by a well-established method, influence of variables of well-established powder production methods on powder properties, influence of powder production method on powder properties, and influence of powder reuse on properties of powders of a wide collection of alloys. One key finding was that with regard to powder reuse, the only consistent finding is that it leads to increase in the oxygen content of the powder. Another key finding was that the literature on the aspects of the literature reviewed herein contains many shortcomings and gaps, which suggest potential areas for future research, such as techniques for optimization of process variables for a given combination of metal powder and powder production method and development of methods for production of powders of new/emerging metallic materials.

Abstract:
<jats:p>In this paper, the qualities of aluminum powder made from industrial aluminum scrap through water atomization for use in Additive Manufacturing were examined. This investigation aims at determining what factors the water atomization process have on the quality of the powder, and if it can be utilized as a sustainable method of manufacturing. Aluminum powder was created under controlled conditions by altering some of the primary aspects of the process; specifically, water pressure and the molten metal's temperature. We used two types of spectroscopic analysis, Energy Dispersive X-ray Spectroscopy (EDX), and X-ray Fluorescence (XRF) to measure the chemical makeup of the aluminum powder, as well as particle size distribution, particle morphology, and compatibility with additive manufacturing processes. The results indicate that water atomization creates aluminum powder with particles that are generally in the size range of 20–100 μm. The EDX and XRF showed that the aluminum powder contained approximately 80.63% aluminum, and there were variances in elemental composition and relatively large amounts of oxygen content that averaged approximately 43.5%. Small amounts of other minor elements, including silicon, copper, and iron were also observed, which may be due to the alloying elements within the scrap material. Additionally, the powders demonstrated irregular shapes to their particles, which is representative of the inherent properties of the water-atomized powders produced from recycled aluminum feedstocks. Overall, this research has shown the viability of producing powder from aluminum scrap as an alternate source of raw material for powder production, and will help to increase sustainability of the supply chain for Additive Manufacturing, by reducing dependence on virgin material, decreasing energy requirements and minimizing environmental impacts of traditional powder production methods.</jats:p>

## pqac-00000000

From text 'haydari2021thespreadingbehavioura pages 31-34'.

Z Haydari. The spreading behaviour of stainless steel powders for additive manufacturing. Unknown journal, 2021.

The excerpt provides qualitative evidence rather than correlation coefficients, R-squared values, or a direct ranking of Hall funnel, Hausner ratio, angle of repose, rotating-drum dynamic angle, cohesive index, FT4 rheometry, and shear-cell measurements. It identifies FT4 rheometry as especially relevant to LPBF because it measures dynamic shear-related powder resistance, approximating interactions during spreading. FT4 specific energy is associated with interparticle friction: a higher value indicates lower flowability, and the cited stainless-steel comparison found that the high-specific-energy sample had poor deposition and lower final-part quality. However, FT4 results are described as reliable mainly for comparative rather than design data, and its stress distribution is not fully understood. The Revolution Powder Analyser (rotating drum/avalanche testing) is also presented as more representative of dynamic spreading than gravity-based tests such as Hall flow and angle of repose, while providing dynamic-flow and packing analyses. Across the excerpt, better flowability is qualitatively linked to more homogeneous layers, higher packing efficiency and powder-layer density, improved sinterability, lower porosity, better surface quality, and improved final-part density and mechanical properties. Hausner ratio, avalanche angle, and Revolution analysis were used together in one cited study, but no individual predictive strength is reported. Shear-cell testing may miss flowability changes detected by FT4. No quantitative evidence is supplied for cohesive index or Hall funnel performance.

## pqac-00000001

From text 'haydari2021thespreadingbehaviour pages 31-34'.

Z Haydari. The spreading behaviour of stainless steel powders for additive manufacturing. Unknown journal, 2021.

The excerpt provides qualitative rather than statistical evidence and reports no correlation coefficients, R-squared values, or formal ranking among Hall funnel, Hausner ratio, angle of repose, rotating-drum dynamic angle, cohesive index, FT4 rheometry, and shear-cell measurements. It identifies flowability as an indicator of powder spreading and links improved flowability with more homogeneous layers, higher packing efficiency, better surface quality, and increased final-part density; poor flowability produces poor deposition, voids or empty patches, greater porosity, and reduced part quality. Among the methods discussed, FT4 rheometry is presented as particularly relevant to LPBF because it measures dynamic shear-related flow resistance under conditions intended to resemble AM powder behaviour. Its specific energy (SE) is useful comparatively: higher SE indicates greater particle-particle friction and lower flowability, while lower-SE stainless-steel powders showed acceptable AM behaviour. However, FT4 results are described as comparative rather than design data because stress distribution in the powder bed is not fully understood. The Revolution rotating-drum analyser is also intended to imitate dynamic spreading and supports dynamic-flow and packing analysis. Hausner ratio, avalanche angle, Revolution analysis, and rheometry were used together in one cited study, where higher flowability corresponded to better packing and improved part properties, but the excerpt does not establish which individual test best predicts spreadability, layer density, or part density. Shear-cell testing may not fully detect flowability changes that FT4 can reveal.

It provides qualitative comparisons among three powders. Powder B, consisting of coarser and more spherical particles, had the lowest static angle of repose (26 ± 3°), followed by powder A (30 ± 4°), while powder C, containing the most fine and irregular particles, had the highest value (39 ± 4°). The same qualitative ranking was observed for low-speed dynamic angle of repose: powders A and B flowed better than powder C. Powder B also had the lowest cohesive index, whereas powder C had the highest, indicating that dynamic angle and cohesive index distinguish powders with apparently better flow and lower cohesion. Carney flow was stable for A and B (approximately 6 s), but C varied from 16 to 22 s before decreasing to 14 s. The discussion states that flow and apparent density influence printed-part porosity and that equivalent-chemistry powders produced relative part densities from 94.4 ± 2.3% to 99.4 ± 0.3% under identical conditions, but it does not identify which flowability test best predicts those outcomes. Thus, this excerpt supports a qualitative ranking—B best, A intermediate, C worst—but supplies no predictive validation or direct spreadability measurements.

The excerpt emphasizes that no single flowability measurement directly represents LPBF spreadability or final part density. Flowability is an application-dependent umbrella term, and spreadability additionally incorporates layer homogeneity, packing or bulk density, and cohesion. The passage identifies angle of repose (AoR), Carr index (CI), Hausner ratio (HR), and flow function (ffc) as comparative flowability metrics, with Table 3 providing classification ranges: excellent flow corresponds to AoR 25–30°, CI ≤10%, HR 1.00–1.11, and ffc ≥10; very poor flow corresponds to AoR 56–65°, CI 32–37%, HR 1.46–1.59, and ffc ≤2. HR is described as a useful measure of cohesion, while FT4 rheometry is noted for quality control and confirming processing performance. Shear-cell testing yields MPS, UYS, ffc, friction angles, cohesion, and wall friction, but the excerpt cautions that conventional compressive shear testing may not represent PBF recoating conditions. The excerpt discusses qualitative effects—sphericity, particle size, PSD, surface roughness, and fines—but does not report direct correlation coefficients, R-squared values, or a ranking comparing Hall funnel, HR, AoR, rotating-drum dynamic angle, CI, FT4, and shear-cell measurements against spread-layer quality or part density.

It also lists shear-cell testing, powder rheometry, revolution powder analysis, and modified film-applicator methods as characterization approaches. ## pqac-00000012

From text 'bostijn2019amultivariateapproach pages 10-14'.

N. Bostijn, J. Dhondt, A. Ryckaert, E. Szabó, W. Dhondt, B. Van Snick, V. Vanhoorne, C. Vervaet, and T. De Beer. A multivariate approach to predict the volumetric and gravimetric feeding behavior of a low feed rate feeder based on raw material properties. International Journal of Pharmaceutics, 557:342-353, Feb 2019. URL: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ijpharm.2018.12.066, doi:10.1016/j.ijpharm.2018.12.066. This article has 90 citations and is from a domain leading peer-reviewed journal.

This excerpt establishes how Bostijn et al. (2019) quantified screw-feeder feeding behavior, but it does not report the requested correlations between feed factor and bulk density, flowability, Hausner ratio, FT4 specific energy, or compressibility. Feed factor was defined as powder mass dispensed per screw revolution and calculated from the measured catch-scale feed rate and screw speed. Volumetric tests were conducted at 6, 30, and 54 rpm, corresponding to 10%, 50%, and 90% of the feeder’s 60-rpm maximum, allowing assessment of speed dependence. For each material and speed, the study extracted FFmax—the highest observed feed factor and an indicator of maximum feeding capacity—and FFdecay, the hopper fill level at which feed factor declined to 90% of FFmax. Feed factor generally decreased as hopper fill level declined. To compare powders with different densities or full-hopper masses, hopper net weight was normalized to each powder’s maximum hopper mass and expressed as percentage fill level. The excerpt describes raw feed-rate measurement using a catch scale at 1-second intervals, rather than the feeder’s proprietary pretreated signal, but it provides no numerical feed-rate variability/RSD results. It likewise does not mention Wang, Li, Muzzio, and Glasser (2017), Van Snick (2017), or density-normalized correlations beyond the fill-level normalization.

## pqac-00000013

From text 'bostijn2019amultivariateapproach pages 1-6'.

N. Bostijn, J. Dhondt, A. Ryckaert, E. Szabó, W. Dhondt, B. Van Snick, V. Vanhoorne, C. Vervaet, and T. De Beer. A multivariate approach to predict the volumetric and gravimetric feeding behavior of a low feed rate feeder based on raw material properties. International Journal of Pharmaceutics, 557:342-353, Feb 2019. URL: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ijpharm.2018.12.066, doi:10.1016/j.ijpharm.2018.12.066. This article has 90 citations and is from a domain leading peer-reviewed journal.

Bostijn et al. (2019) is directly relevant to evaluating screw-feeder feed-factor behavior against powder properties. The study examined 15 pharmaceutical powders and represented their material characteristics using 25 descriptors, then applied partial least-squares regression to relate those descriptors to feeder performance. In volumetric operation, the principal responses were maximum feed factor (FFmax), representing maximum feeding capacity, and feed-factor decay (FFdecay), representing the hopper fill level at which refilling is needed. In gravimetric operation, performance was assessed using feed-rate relative standard deviation (RSD) and relative error (RE). The paper reports that volumetric responses were predicted more successfully than gravimetric responses because the gravimetric control loop reduces the direct impact of powder properties on feed behavior. Volumetric feeding keeps screw speed constant and displaces a nominally constant volume, so mass flow depends on powder characteristics such as density and flow behavior; gravimetric control instead adjusts dispensing rate to maintain the mass-flow setpoint. The excerpt does not provide specific correlations or normalization equations for bulk density, Hausner ratio, FT4 specific energy, compressibility, speed-dependent mass per revolution, or feed-factor normalization. Those details would need to be obtained from the remainder of Bostijn (2019) or the cited Wang, Li, Muzzio, Glasser (2017) and Van Snick (2017) studies.

B. V. Snick, J. Holman, Christopher W. Cunningham, Ashish Kumar, J. Vercruysse, T. D. Beer, J. Remon, and C. Vervaet. Continuous direct compression as manufacturing platform for sustained release tablets. International journal of pharmaceutics, 519 1-2:390-407, Mar 2017. URL: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ijpharm.2017.01.010, doi:10.1016/j.ijpharm.2017.01.010. This article has 172 citations and is from a domain leading peer-reviewed journal.

Van Snick et al. (2017) found a strong relationship between the maximum screw-feeder feed factor and powder bulk density (R² = 0.85), consistent with twin screws displacing an approximately fixed volume per revolution: greater density at the screw inlet produces a higher mass feed factor. However, bulk density alone did not explain transport capacity because flow properties confounded the relationship. Abstract:
Preparation and formulation of amorphous solid dispersions (ASDs) are becoming more and more popular in the pharmaceutical field because the dissolution of poorly water-soluble drugs can be effectively improved this way, which can lead to increased bioavailability in many cases. During downstream processing of ASDs, technologists need to keep in mind both traditional challenges and the newest trends. In the last decade, the pharmaceutical industry began to display considerable interest in continuous processing, which can be explained with their potential advantages such as smaller footprint, easier scale-up, and more consistent product, better quality and quality assurance. Continuous downstream processing of drug-loaded ASDs opens new ways for automatic operation. Therefore, the formulation of poorly water-soluble drugs may be more effective and safe. However, developments can be challenging due to the poor flowability and feeding properties of ASDs. Consequently, this review pays special attention to these characteristics since the feeding of the components greatly influences the content uniformity in the final dosage form. The main purpose of this paper is to summarize the most important steps of the possible ASD-based continuous downstream processes in order to give a clear overview of current course lines and future perspectives.

Abstract:
With the rise of additive technologies, the characterization of metal powders is increasingly required. There is a need to precisely match the properties of metal powders to a specific machine and to ensure highly consistent production. Therefore, the study aims at a detailed characterization of ten metal powders (Metal powder 316 L, Zn, Sn, Al, Cu, Mn, Fe, Bronze, Ti and Mo powder), for which the particle size distribution, morphology, static and dynamic angle of repose and the effective internal friction angle (AIFE) were determined. The AIFE parameter and flow index were determined from three commonly used rotary shear devices: The computer-controlled Ring Shear Tester RST-01. pc, the Brookfield PFT Powder Flow Tester and the FT4 Powder rheometer. The results showed that the values for the device of one manufacturer did not fully correspond to the values of another one. The flow characteristics of the metal powders were quantified from the particle size distribution data, static angle of repose, and AIFE data. According to the particle size distribution and angle of repose (AOR), 50% of the tested metal powders fell into the free-flowing mode. According to the evaluation of AIFE, 20% of the samples fell into the lower area. Based on the flow indexes calculated from the measurements of the shear devices used, 100% (RST-01.pc), 70% (PFT) and 50% (FT4) of the samples were included in the free-flowing category. When comparing the results, attention should be paid not only to the nature of the material, but also to the methodology and equipment used. A comparison of methodologies revealed similarities in the changing behavior of the different metal powders. A comparison of effective angles of AIFE and static AOR was shown, and a hypothesis of the conversion relation was derived.

The excerpt reports that Cordova et al. evaluated the effect of moisture on the spreadability of several metal powders, including AlSi10Mg, using open and funnel tools intended to approximate powder-layer spreading in powder-bed fusion. Moisture reduced flowability and the relative density of the spread layer for all tested powders. AlSi10Mg was particularly sensitive because its greater surface roughness and more irregular particle shape promoted moisture adsorption; air drying improved the relative density of AlSi10Mg layers. The excerpt also notes that surface satellites and roughness can increase water adsorption, while humidity harms spreading repeatability. These findings support measuring both powder flowability and deposited-layer density when assessing pre-treatment and drying.

For Snow et al., spreadability is characterized through measurable relationships between powder properties and spreading performance. The proposed metrics include build-plate coverage percentage, powder deposition rate, and the rate of change of the avalanche angle. Input variables include layer thickness, recoating speed, spreader material, and powder quality, while angle of repose is treated as an indicator of spreadability. Increasing recoating speed increased deposition rate and the rate of change of avalanche angle, but did not directly affect build-plate coverage. Blade material had a notable effect on coverage. The work did not provide in-depth quantification of packing fraction or a direct spread-layer-density correlation.

## pqac-00000044

From text 'haydari2021thespreadingbehaviour pages 27-31'.

Z Haydari. The spreading behaviour of stainless steel powders for additive manufacturing. Unknown journal, 2021.

The excerpt provides background for comparing flowability metrics, but it does not report the Marchetti and Hulme-Smith (2021) regression analysis or identify which metric best correlated with spreadability. It emphasizes that powder flowability is multidimensional and depends not only on powder properties but also on handling, storage, measurement conditions, and equipment. The relevant methods include Hall flowmeter testing, Hausner ratio or density-based measures (although the Hausner ratio itself is not discussed in this excerpt), FT4 powder rheometry, shear-cell measurements, and angle of repose. Shear-cell characterization measures flow function, internal friction, and wall friction; flow function is calculated from consolidation stress and unconfined yield strength, while particle angularity, size distribution, voids, loading, and surface properties affect internal friction. Angle of repose is a gravity-based indicator in which steeper heaps generally indicate greater cohesion. Hall flow measures the time required for powder to pass through an orifice, but is primarily suitable for free-flowing powders and may not represent additive-manufacturing stress states. In contrast, FT4 rheometry measures dynamic shear resistance, and the excerpt specifically notes that shear is indicative of powder-bed-fusion spreading. Thus, the passage supports interpreting FT4 and shear-related metrics as physically relevant to spreadability, while warning that conventional tests may have limited applicability or comparability.

## pqac-00000045

From text 'haydari2021thespreadingbehavioura pages 27-31'.

Z Haydari. The spreading behaviour of stainless steel powders for additive manufacturing. Unknown journal, 2021.

The excerpt provides background for comparing powder-flowability tests, but it does not report the Marchetti and Hulme-Smith (2021) regression analysis or identify which metric best correlated with spreadability. It emphasizes that flowability is multidimensional and depends on powder properties as well as handling, storage, measurement conditions, and equipment. The described metrics include Jenike flow function, internal and wall friction from shear testing, angle of repose, Hall flow time, density measurements, and FT4 powder rheometry. Flow function is classified using the ratio of major consolidation stress to unconfined yield strength, with higher values indicating easier flow. Angle of repose is interpreted such that steeper heaps indicate greater cohesiveness. Hall flow is a comparative gravity-flow test mainly appropriate for free-flowing powders and may not represent additive-manufacturing conditions because the laboratory stress state differs from real processing; it is also affected by arching, bridging, clinging, and other effects. FT4 rheometry measures dynamic flow resistance and shear-related properties, making it particularly relevant to powder-bed spreading because shear is an important force in that process. Thus, the excerpt supports methodological distinctions and limitations but contains no comparative regression outcomes for Hall flow, Hausner ratio, FT4, shear cell, or angle of repose.

## pqac-00000046

From text 'marchetti2021flowabilityofsteel pages 10-11'.

Lorenzo Marchetti and Christopher Hulme-Smith. Flowability of steel and tool steel powders: a comparison between testing methods. Powder Technology, 384:402-413, May 2021. URL: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.powtec.2021.01.074, doi:10.1016/j.powtec.2021.01.074. This article has 73 citations and is from a domain leading peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt reports regression relationships among flowability measurements but does not directly identify which metric best correlates with spreadability. It states that major principal stress (MPS), a shear-cell metric, correlates more strongly with Hausner ratio, FT4-type specific energy, and angle of repose. It also states that shear-cell cohesion and ultimate yield strength correlate more strongly with compressibility and angle of repose. Thus, angle of repose appears repeatedly as a strong cross-method correlate, while Hausner ratio and specific energy are specifically associated with MPS. Hall flow is only listed in the references through ASTM standards in this excerpt, and no direct regression result involving spreadability or a ranking of Hall flow, Hausner ratio, FT4 rheometry, shear cell, and angle of repose is provided. The supplied pages therefore support identifying angle of repose as an important correlated metric, but are insufficient to establish the single best predictor of spreadability.

## pqac-00000047

From text 'haydari2021thespreadingbehaviour pages 31-34'.

Z Haydari. The spreading behaviour of stainless steel powders for additive manufacturing. Unknown journal, 2021.

The excerpt provides qualitative context for comparing powder-flowability tests in metal additive manufacturing, but it does not report the Marchetti and Hulme-Smith (2021) regression analysis or identify a statistically best-correlated metric for spreadability. It characterizes FT4 powder rheometry as especially relevant because it measures dynamic shear resistance, which resembles the forces acting during powder-bed spreading. FT4 reports metrics including basic flowability energy (BFE) for confined downward blade motion and specific energy (SE) for unconfined upward motion. The text cautions that FT4 results are generally more reliable for comparative assessment than for design data. The Revolution avalanche tester is also described as simulating dynamic spreading behavior, whereas conventional gravity-based methods such as the Hall flowmeter and angle of repose may be less representative of spreading. The excerpt discusses flowability as an indicator of spreading behavior and links better flowability with improved layer homogeneity, packing, density, and final-part quality. However, it contains no direct comparison among Hall flow, Hausner ratio, FT4 rheometry, shear-cell measurements, and angle of repose, and no correlation coefficients, regression results, or conclusion about which metric best predicts spreadability.
