## pqac-00000052

From text 'balbaa2021roleofpowder pages 4-8'.

M.A. Balbaa, A. Ghasemi, E. Fereiduni, M.A. Elbestawi, S.D. Jadhav, and J.-P. Kruth. Role of powder particle size on laser powder bed fusion processability of alsi10mg alloy. Additive Manufacturing, 37:101630, Jan 2021. URL: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.addma.2020.101630, doi:10.1016/j.addma.2020.101630. This article has 249 citations and is from a highest quality peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt introduces the flowability characterization methods used for gas-atomized AlSi10Mg powders but does not provide the requested numerical Hausner ratios, Hall flow times, angles of repose, or detailed FT4 measurement results. Flowability was evaluated using Hall and Carney flowmeters in accordance with ASTM B213-17, together with the FT4 Freeman powder rheometer. The text notes that Hall flow testing is relatively close to additive-manufacturing conditions, particularly powder-fed processes, but has major limitations for cohesive powders that may nevertheless remain suitable for powder bed fusion. FT4 is recommended because the precision blade–powder interaction more closely resembles the recoater–powder interaction in laser powder bed fusion. The fine AlSi10Mg powder had a mean particle size of approximately 9 µm, while the coarse powder was approximately 40 µm. Morphologically, the fine powder was highly spherical and satellite-free but exhibited a strong tendency for interparticle attachment and agglomeration; the coarse powder showed no clear agglomeration. These observations indicate potentially greater cohesion and poorer flow for the fine powder. The excerpt contains no comparisons with steel or titanium powders, and it does not discuss low-density effects, granular Bond numbers, or aluminium-alloy cohesion quantitatively.


---

## pqac-00000053

From text 'haydari2021thespreadingbehavioura pages 27-31'.

Z Haydari. The spreading behaviour of stainless steel powders for additive manufacturing. Unknown journal, 2021.

The excerpt provides general methods and concepts relevant to evaluating LPBF powder flowability, but it does not report specific AlSi10Mg Hausner ratio values, Hall flow times, angle-of-repose values, FT4 measurements, or comparisons with steel and titanium powders. It defines flowability as the ability of a powder to flow in a desired manner in specific equipment and emphasizes that it is a multidimensional property influenced by powder characteristics and handling or measurement conditions. Angle of repose is measured from a powder heap formed through a funnel; steeper angles indicate greater cohesion. Carr’s classification gives very free-flowing powders as having repose angles below 30°, free-flowing powders at 30–38°, fair-to-passable flow at 38–45°, cohesive flow at 45–55°, and very cohesive/non-flowing behavior above 55°. The Hall flowmeter measures the time required for powder to pass through an orifice, but is mainly suitable for free-flowing powders and provides a comparative rather than fully consistent flow-rate measure. The excerpt also describes the FT4 rheometer as measuring dynamic flow resistance and shear-related properties, including basic flowability, aeration, consolidation, flow rate, and specific energy. No discussion of low-density effects, granular Bond number, or aluminium-alloy cohesion is included.


---

## pqac-00000054

From text 'haydari2021thespreadingbehavioura pages 31-34'.

Z Haydari. The spreading behaviour of stainless steel powders for additive manufacturing. Unknown journal, 2021.

The excerpt provides general information about powder-flowability characterization for additive manufacturing, but it does not report specific AlSi10Mg values for Hausner ratio, Hall flow time, angle of repose, or FT4 measurements. It identifies the FT4 powder rheometer as a dynamic test intended to better represent powder behavior during powder-bed fusion spreading. FT4 measures bulk, dynamic-flow, shear, and process properties; its dynamic measurements include basic flowability energy and specific energy, with specific energy obtained in an unconfined upward blade motion and basic flowability energy in a confined downward motion. The excerpt cautions that FT4 results are generally more reliable for comparative assessment than for design data. The Revolution powder analyzer is described as an avalanche tester using a rotating drum, gravity, wall friction, and imaging to assess dynamic flow, packing, and related behavior. Flowability affects powder movement, particle arrangement, packing, layer homogeneity, density, porosity, surface roughness, and mechanical properties. A stainless-steel example reports that a sample with higher specific energy had greater particle-to-particle friction, lower flowability, poorer deposition, and lower final-part quality. However, the excerpt contains no numerical comparison between AlSi10Mg, steel, and titanium powders, and no discussion of low density, cohesion, or the granular Bond number for aluminum-alloy powders.

## pqac-00000055

From text 'munizlerma2018acomprehensiveapproach pages 8-11'.

Jose Alberto Muñiz-Lerma, Amy Nommeots-Nomm, Kristian Edmund Waters, and Mathieu Brochu. A comprehensive approach to powder feedstock characterization for powder bed fusion additive manufacturing: a case study on alsi7mg. Materials, 11:2386, Nov 2018. URL: https://doi.org/10.3390/ma11122386, doi:10.3390/ma11122386. This article has 170 citations.

The excerpt concerns AlSi7Mg powders rather than AlSi10Mg and does not report Hausner ratios, Hall flow times, FT4 measurements, granular Bond numbers, or direct comparisons with steel and titanium powders. It nevertheless provides related flowability and cohesion results for three aluminum powder populations. In a multiple-cycle Carney flow test at 40% relative humidity, powders A and B remained stable with an average flow time of approximately 6 s. Powder C, containing more fine particles, initially increased from 16 s to about 22 s and later decreased to 14 s after repeated measurements, with agglomerate breakup proposed as an explanation. Static angle of repose values were 30 ± 4° for powder A, 26 ± 3° for powder B, and 39 ± 4° for powder C. The fine, irregular powder C also exhibited the highest dynamic angle of repose and cohesive index, whereas coarse, spherical powder B showed the lowest cohesion. Greater surface area, vapor sorption, surface energy, and water adsorption in powder C promoted agglomeration and reduced flow. The excerpt further states that, as particle size decreases, gravitational forces become less important relative to cohesive forces, helping explain the stronger cohesion and poorer flow of fine aluminum alloy powders.

## pqac-00000058

From text 'bhattachar2004evaluationofthe pages 1-3'.

Shobha N. Bhattachar, David B. Hedden, Angela M. Olsofsky, Xianggui Qu, Wen-Yaw Hsieh, and Kelly G. Canter. Evaluation of the vibratory feeder method for assessment of powder flow properties. International journal of pharmaceutics, 269 2:385-92, Jan 2004. URL: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ijpharm.2003.09.024, doi:10.1016/j.ijpharm.2003.09.024. This article has 38 citations and is from a domain leading peer-reviewed journal.

Bhattachar et al. (2004) evaluated a vibratory feeder as a rapid, material-sparing method for characterizing pharmaceutical powder flow. The method measures avalanche flow dynamically by recording powder flow-rate profiles and using fractal-dimension analysis; its output is a powder flow index (PFI). Seventeen pharmaceutical powders were tested, and the PFI trends correlated well with flow properties reported in the literature. Results were also compared with the Aero-Flow instrument’s mean time to avalanche (MTA), with the two methods showing excellent agreement using nonparametric analysis of ranked data. The excerpt does not provide information on tapping tests, tilting tubes or boxes, onset-angle measurements, or discharge-mass fluctuation as a cohesion index. It does mention that other researchers calculated a Flowability Index from the standard deviation of MTA values across increasing rotational speeds, and a Cohesion Index from MTA. Thus, within this excerpt, the Bhattachar study primarily supports vibratory-feeder avalanche testing and the PFI as a flowability measure; it does not establish that discharge-mass fluctuations, tapping, or tilting-angle methods were used in the study.

## pqac-00000059

From text 'bodhmage2006correlationbetweenphysicala pages 23-27'.

AK Bodhmage. Correlation between physical properties and flowability indicators for fine powders. Unknown journal, 2006.

The excerpt supports tapping-based density indices and tilting-box angle-of-repose testing as flowability measurements, but it does not specifically describe a vibratory feeder method, discharge-mass fluctuations, or the Bhattachar (2004) method. Tapping is used to obtain tapped density, which is compared with loose-packed bulk density through the Hausner ratio (HR = TD/BD). The related Carr Index is calculated from the difference between tapped and bulk density relative to tapped density; cohesive powders generally have HR greater than 1.4, while Carr Index values above 20–25% indicate non-free-flowing material. For angle-of-repose testing, the excerpt identifies both tilting-box and fixed-cone methods. Static angle of repose is the angle formed by a powder pile with the horizontal, while dynamic angle of repose is measured on the inclined powder surface in a rotating drum. The excerpt cautions that cohesive powders may be difficult to measure directly and that boundary friction at rotating-drum end caps can produce faulty results. It also describes avalanche testing: powder in a slowly rotating disk builds to an unstable condition and slides down; the avalanche is detected photoelectrically, with shorter avalanche times corresponding to better flowability. No evidence is provided here that discharge-mass fluctuations serve as a cohesion index or that vibration-induced discharge is the specific flowability metric requested.

From text 'talebi2021characterisationofspreadability pages 28-33'.

FAA Talebi. Characterisation of spreadability behaviour of ti6al4v powders for additive manufacturing. Unknown journal, 2021.

The excerpt provides partial support for using tapping or vibration-related density changes as a flowability indicator, but it does not specifically describe a vibratory feeder method, discharge-mass fluctuations as a cohesion index, a tilting tube or tilting box onset-angle test, vibration-induced discharge, or the Bhattachar (2004) method. It states that tapping simulates vibrations arising during powder processing and handling. For finer powders, tapping allows particles to rearrange as interparticle forces are overcome, increasing the compacted or tapped bulk density. The difference between tapped density and aerated/apparent bulk density can indicate sensitivity to vibration. The excerpt also presents Hausner Ratio (HR) and Carr’s Compressibility Index (CI), calculated from tapped and apparent densities, as simple indicators of powder flowability. Lower HR and CI correspond generally to better flow, while higher values indicate increasingly cohesive or poorly flowing powders. However, the text cautions that HR and CI are insufficient as standalone measures, particularly because additive-manufacturing powder deposition does not involve tapping or compression. It additionally describes the Hall flowmeter as measuring mass flow through a funnel, while noting limited sensitivity, operator dependence, and problems with cohesive powders. No onset-angle or feeder-discharge data are reported here.

It identifies the angle of repose as a method for quantifying granular-material cohesiveness and notes that static and dynamic angles of repose are distinct measurements. The static angle is formed by a powder pile with the horizontal, while the dynamic angle is formed by the inclined powder surface in a rotating drum. Riley et al. (1978) used both tilting-box and fixed-cone methods, and the excerpt emphasizes that angle-of-repose measurements are faster than the Jenike procedure. For cohesive powders, direct angle measurement may be difficult; one reported approach used mixtures with a free-flowing material and extrapolated angle-versus-composition data to estimate a theoretical angle. The excerpt also mentions avalanching as a separate flowability technique: free-flowing powders have shorter avalanche times, while less-flowable powders take longer to avalanche. The excerpt provides general context for evaluating powder flowability but does not specifically describe the Bhattachar (2004) vibratory feeder method, tapping as a flowability index, discharge-mass fluctuations as a cohesion index, tilting-tube or tilting-box onset angles, or vibration-induced discharge testing. It emphasizes that powder flowability is multidimensional and depends on powder properties as well as handling, storage, and measurement conditions. Several conventional methods are identified: flow function, internal and wall friction, angle of repose, Hall flowmeter testing, and FT4 powder rheometry. Angle of repose is measured from the heap formed when powder is deposited through a funnel; a steeper angle generally indicates greater cohesion. The Hall flowmeter measures the time required for powder to discharge through an orifice, but it is mainly suitable for free-flowing powders and provides a comparative rather than fully consistent flow-rate measure. The FT4 rheometer measures dynamic flow resistance and is relevant to powder-bed fusion because shear is an important force during spreading. These principles support interpreting discharge behavior and cohesion-related fluctuations, but the requested vibratory feeder and tilting-angle procedures would require additional source material.

It explains that flowability tests are commonly used as a go/no-go criterion for whether a powder will function in a printer, while noting that such tests provide limited information about the particle attributes responsible for poor flow. Additional characterization methods are therefore needed to diagnose performance issues and identify appropriate adjustments. The excerpt also cautions that greater flowability is not universally desirable: highly flowable multicomponent powders may segregate rapidly, whereas some cohesion can help maintain uniformity and reduce segregation. A Ramesh, P Karunaker, and L Ramesh. Design and analysis of discharging of dust in pneumatic conveying system by a screw conveyor shafts. Unknown journal, Unknown year.

The excerpt indicates that screw-conveyor capacity decreases substantially as the inclination angle increases, because material tends to fall back and conveying becomes less efficient. For a standard screw conveyor, an upward inclination of 15° is associated with approximately 75% of rated horizontal capacity, while 25° may reduce capacity to approximately 50% of horizontal capacity. These percentages are estimates rather than universal values and vary according to the handled material’s characteristics. Inclined conveying may also require higher screw speed to counteract material rollback, as well as additional drive power because power is needed to lift the material. The selection procedure should therefore account for material type and condition, particle size, bulk density, required throughput, conveying distance, conveyor size and speed, component selection, horsepower, and torque capacity. The excerpt also notes that capacity can sometimes be improved over short inclined distances when intermediate hangers are unnecessary, and that shorter-than-standard pitch, tubular housings, or shrouded trough covers can assist inclined conveying. These points are relevant when interpreting powder feed-rate variation in an inclined auger or micro-feeder, although the excerpt does not provide a detailed control model or specific 2024 micro-feeder results.

Hou (2024) provides evidence about an inclined micro-feeder operating at a 30° inclination, but the excerpt does not report a capacity curve or specific capacity-retention values at 15° or 25°. Within Hou’s experiments, inclination was one component of the feeder design, alongside screw pitch, screw configuration, and agitator design. The optimized cohesive-powder configuration used a 30° inclination, a 7 mm-pitch inner screw double-screw agitator, and a 15/7 non-compression feeding screw. For non-flowing material, the optimized design also used 30° inclination, with a 10 mm-pitch agitator and a 25/25 compression feeding screw. Feeding consistency improved substantially under the optimized design: the reliability metric, defined from the range and mean of standard deviations across flow rates, decreased from 61% to 22% for CCS and from 48% to 8.5% for APAP. The study attributes stable feeding to consistent screw filling by the double-screw agitator. messages.content:
### Artifact (ID artifact-01)

| Method | Key metric(s) | Reported correlation with LPBF spreadability/layer quality | Key reference | Suitability for Al-alloy powders | Limitations |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Hall/Carney funnel | Time for a specified mass to discharge; non-flow or jamming outcome | Cordova found that Hall flow changed little among dried and as-received states and could not measure moisturized powders, whereas thin-layer applicators detected reduced layer density. Marchetti and Hulme-Smith found Hall/Carney unsuitable for cohesive powders and obtained no representative correlations because many samples jammed. | Cordova et al. (2020); Marchetti and Hulme-Smith (2021) (pqac-00000036, pqac-00000050, pqac-00000051) | Poor to fair. Useful as coarse incoming inspection for freely flowing Al powder, but low-density or fine AlSi powder may bridge or fail to flow despite being LPBF-processable. | Binary censoring by non-flow; strongly affected by density, orifice, operator, and wall friction; unlike the recoating stress state; insensitive to subtle moisture or drying effects. |
| Hausner ratio / Carr index | HR = tapped density / bulk density; CI = 100 × (1 − bulk density / tapped density) | Across eight AlSi10Mg and six 316L powders, powder-layer density correlated strongly and negatively with HR: PCC = −0.89. General classifications place excellent flow near HR 1.00–1.11 and CI ≤10%, and very poor flow near HR 1.46–1.59 and CI 32–37%. Marchetti found major principal stress at 9 kPa versus HR had adjusted R² = 0.86. | Haferkamp et al. (2021); Marchetti and Hulme-Smith (2021); Gibbons et al. (2024) (pqac-00000003, pqac-00000014, pqac-00000050) | Good inexpensive comparator when sieve cut and conditioning are fixed; directly relevant to AlSi10Mg layer packing. | Tapping and compaction do not reproduce recoating; sensitive to filling and tapping protocol; density and PSD confound flow; Spierings found HR <1.25 incorrectly classified several fine metal powders as free-flowing. |
| Static angle of repose | Heap angle to horizontal | Snow et al. reported a relationship between angle of repose and camera-derived spreading behavior for three Al-alloy powders. AlSi7Mg populations ranked consistently: coarse and spherical powder 26 ± 3°, intermediate powder 30 ± 4°, and fine and irregular powder 39 ± 4°. Specific energy versus angle of repose gave adjusted R² = 0.78 in steel powders. | Snow, Martukanitz, and Joshi (2019); Muñiz-Lerma et al. (2018); Marchetti and Hulme-Smith (2021) (pqac-00000028, pqac-00000034, pqac-00000055, pqac-00000050) | Good low-cost screening metric for Al batches; sensitive to fines, irregularity, and moisture. | Static heap formation differs from dynamic recoating; sensitive to drop height, base, walls, and operator; cohesive powders may not form a reproducible cone; chemistry-independent thresholds are unreliable. |
| Rotating drum: dynamic angle and cohesive index (GranuDrum) | Dynamic or flowing angle; cohesive index, calculated from the integrated standard deviation of the detected powder–air interface; speed dependence and hysteresis | Brocksieper found that dynamic angle alone did not explain layer roughness Sa, but speed-dependent cohesive index followed blade-recoater Sa trends. It could predict speed response for a known powder, but not absolute spreadability of an unknown powder. AlSi10Mg had a mean avalanche angle of about 39° and the highest cohesive index above 60 rpm. | Brocksieper et al. (2026); Lüddecke et al. (2021); Preud’Homme et al. (2021) (pqac-00000020, pqac-00000023, pqac-00000049, pqac-00000056, pqac-00000057) | Particularly promising for low-density Al because the cohesive index measures intermittent cohesive flow and can be evaluated versus speed; AlSi10Mg was discriminated at high drum speed. | Results depend on drum speed, fill, end-wall friction, and aeration; dynamic angle may rise with speed for noncohesive powders but fall for cohesive powders; the cohesive-index relationship depends on recoater design. |
| Revolution Powder Analyzer | Pre-avalanche angle; avalanche-angle variance; surface fractal; volume expansion | A model combining avalanche and surface-distribution variables with particle ellipticity predicted optical AM-flowability ratings with R² = 0.94, p < 0.0001, and RMSE = 0.23. A surface-fractal value near 5 marked deterioration; corresponding avalanche angles were approximately 49° for Fe and 54° for Ni powders. | Spierings et al. (2016) (pqac-00000039, pqac-00000040, pqac-00000041) | Mechanistically attractive for Al because avalanche intermittency and roughness respond to high cohesion-to-weight ratio; alloy-specific calibration is essential because the published model used Fe and Ni powders. | Validated against expert optical flowability rather than direct layer density; thresholds were machine- and alloy-dependent; mean avalanche angle had substantial scatter, so distribution width and surface fractal were needed. |
| FT4 rheometry | Basic flowability energy; specific energy; stability index; flow-rate index; compressibility | Brocksieper found specific energy was the only tested metric that identified AlSi10Mg as both the poorest-flowing and poorest-spreading powder; specific energy and GranuDrum cohesive index showed the greatest potential. In screw-feeding work, conditioned bulk density plus stability index plus specific energy explained 95.7% of feed-rate variation. Basic flowability energy showed weak relationships with most other metrics; specific energy versus angle of repose gave adjusted R² = 0.78. | Brocksieper et al. (2026); Santos et al. (2018); Marchetti and Hulme-Smith (2021) (pqac-00000015, pqac-00000049, pqac-00000050, pqac-00000051, pqac-00000057) | Strong candidate for AlSi10Mg and AlSi12: low-stress specific energy captures particle friction and cohesion, and AlSi10Mg had the highest specific energy in the three-alloy comparison. | Expensive proprietary instrument; the confined downward stress used for basic flowability energy differs from recoating; absolute values depend on blade path, conditioning, and sample volume; mainly comparative rather than universal design data. |
| Shear cell | Unconfined yield strength; major principal stress; cohesion; flow function; internal and wall friction | No robust direct LPBF-spreadability correlation was established. Marchetti found major principal stress at 9 kPa versus HR had adjusted R² = 0.86, major principal stress at 3 kPa versus angle of repose had adjusted R² = 0.74, and flow-function and cohesion relationships with other bulk metrics. Conventional consolidated shear conditions may not represent thin-layer recoating. | Marchetti and Hulme-Smith (2021); Gibbons et al. (2024) (pqac-00000003, pqac-00000046, pqac-00000050, pqac-00000051) | Useful for diagnosing cohesive Al powder and hopper behavior, but less defensible as a stand-alone proxy for LPBF spreading than specific energy, cohesive index, or avalanche statistics. | Sample preparation and preconsolidation strongly affect results; the stress state is generally higher and more static than recoating; different shear devices can classify the same powder differently; greater cost and sample demand. |


*Table: Comparison of common powder-flow tests, quantitative correlations with LPBF layer quality, and their applicability to low-density aluminium-alloy powders. Dynamic low-stress measures generally provide more process-relevant discrimination than funnel tests.*

{"answer": "## Powder Flowability Screening for LPBF Spreadability Using a Tilting Auger Doser: A Literature Synthesis

### 1. Which Flowability Measurements Best Predict LPBF Spreadability and Part Quality?

No single conventional flowability test has been universally validated as a predictor of LPBF spread-layer quality, but dynamic, low-stress methods consistently outperform gravity-based funnel tests.

**Hall/Carney funnel flow.** Marchetti and Hulme-Smith (2021) found that Hall and Carney flow-rate methods were unsuitable for cohesive steel powders because jamming prevented recording a flow rate; consequently, no statistically significant or representative correlations could be established between funnel flow rate and any other flowability metric (pqac-00000050, pqac-00000051). Cordova et al. (2020) similarly reported that moisturized powders could not flow through the Hall funnel, and even across dryable states, the Hall flowmeter showed relatively small differences and low standard deviations, limiting its diagnostic sensitivity for spreadability (pqac-00000036).

**Hausner ratio / Carr index.** Haferkamp et al. (2021) reported a Pearson correlation coefficient (PCC) of −0.89 between powder-layer density (PLD) and Hausner ratio across six 316L and eight AlSi10Mg powders, a PCC of −0.67 between Hausner ratio and circularity, and a PCC of 0.72 between circularity and PLD (pqac-00000005, pqac-00000007). Marchetti and Hulme-Smith (2021) found that conditioned bulk density (CBD) correlated with HR with R²_adj = 0.81 (CBD = −5.65 × HR), and major principal stress at 9 kPa correlated with HR at R²_adj = 0.86 (pqac-00000050, pqac-00000051). However, Spierings et al. (2016) cautioned that most fine metal powders had HR < 1.25 and would be classified as "free-flowing," which was obviously incorrect—several produced poor powder layers (pqac-00000040). Gibbons et al. (2024) compiled classification thresholds: excellent flow at AoR 25–30°, CI ≤ 10%, HR 1.00–1.11, ffc ≥ 10; very poor flow at AoR 56–65°, CI 32–37%, HR 1.46–1.59, ffc ≤ 2 (pqac-00000003).

**Static angle of repose.** Snow, Martukanitz and Joshi (2019) established a relationship between powder angle of repose and camera-derived spreading metrics (build-plate coverage, deposition rate, rate of change of avalanche angle) for three aluminium alloy powders (pqac-00000028, pqac-00000034). Muñiz-Lerma et al. (2018) found that three AlSi7Mg populations ranked consistently: coarse spherical powder at 26 ± 3°, intermediate at 30 ± 4°, and fine irregular at 39 ± 4° (pqac-00000055). Marchetti and Hulme-Smith (2021) reported that specific energy versus angle of repose gave R²_adj = 0.78 (pqac-00000050).

**Rotating-drum dynamic angle and cohesive index (GranuDrum).** Brocksieper et al. (2026) found that the dynamic angle alone did not clearly distinguish spreadability among 316L, Alloy 718, and AlSi10Mg powders. However, the speed-dependent cohesive index (CI) from GranuDrum tracked the blade-recoater surface roughness Sa trends: 316L had the lowest CI across all speeds, while AlSi10Mg showed the highest CI above 60 rpm (pqac-00000049, pqac-00000057). They concluded that FT4 specific energy (SE) and GranuDrum CI "show potential" as spreadability indicators, and that the CI test can predict known powder application behavior at different recoater speeds, though it cannot predict the absolute spreading behavior of an unknown powder (pqac-00000056).

**Avalanche angle and surface fractal (Revolution Powder Analyzer).** Spierings et al. (2016) developed a composite flowability index u from Revolution Powder Analyzer data. A model combining the log-normal distribution parameters of the surface fractal (μ_SF, σ_SF) with particle ellipticity (E) and avalanche-angle variance (σ_AV) predicted optical flowability with r² = 0.94, p < 0.0001, and RMSE = 0.23. A surface-fractal threshold of ω_P ≈ 5.0 separated good from poor powders; the corresponding avalanche angles were approximately 49° (Fe base) and 54° (Ni base). The proposed pass/fail limit was u ≥ 2.5 for acceptable SLM layers (pqac-00000039, pqac-00000040).

**FT4 rheometry.** Brocksieper et al. (2026) identified FT4 specific energy as the only tested flowability metric that correctly identified AlSi10Mg as both the poorest-flowing and the poorest-spreading powder across all three recoater types. AlSi10Mg had the highest average SE, while 316L had the lowest (pqac-00000049, pqac-00000057). Santos et al. (2018) found that a multivariable model using conditioned bulk density, stability index, and specific energy explained 95.7% of screw-feeder feed-rate variation (p = 0.001) (pqac-00000015). Marchetti and Hulme-Smith (2021) found basic flowability energy (BFE) showed weak correlations with most metrics, whereas SE, HR, compressibility, and AoR were inter-correlated (pqac-00000050, pqac-00000051).

**Shear cell.** No robust direct correlation between shear-cell metrics and LPBF spreadability was established. Marchetti and Hulme-Smith (2021) found that shear-cell parameters correlated with other bulk metrics (MPS9 vs HR: R²_adj = 0.86; UYS3 vs C3: R²_adj = 0.98) but cautioned that conventional consolidated shear conditions may not represent the low-stress, thin-layer recoating process (pqac-00000050, pqac-00000051). Gibbons et al. (2024) echoed that compressive shear testing may not represent PBF recoating conditions (pqac-00000003).

**AlSi10Mg-specific considerations.** AlSi10Mg has low density (~2.65 g/cm³), which raises the granular Bond number (cohesion-to-weight ratio) relative to steel and nickel alloys (pqac-00000040). The powder also tends to be morphologically irregular (f_shape = 0.73, lowest of four alloys tested) with abundant satellites (pqac-00000037, pqac-00000038). This combination makes it particularly sensitive to moisture: Cordova et al. (2020) measured moisture pickup of 0.437% after 72 h at 50 °C/80% RH, compared to near-zero for Inconel 718 and Ti6Al4V (pqac-00000037). Muñiz-Lerma et al. (2018) noted that as particle size decreases, gravitational forces become less important relative to cohesive forces, helping explain the stronger cohesion and poorer flow of fine aluminum alloy powders (pqac-00000055).

The following table summarizes these findings:

<artifact id="artifact-01"/>

### 2. Screw/Auger Feeder Behavior and Flowability Correlations

The pharmaceutical continuous-manufacturing literature provides strong quantitative evidence linking screw-feeder performance to powder properties.

**Feed factor and bulk density.** Van Snick et al. (2017) found that maximum feed factor (FF_max, mass discharged per screw revolution) correlated with loose bulk density at R² = 0.85 and with tapped density at R² = 0.91, consistent with twin-screw displacement being approximately volumetric (pqac-00000014). However, bulk density alone was insufficient: cohesive powders had lower feed factors than predicted by density, while compressible powders (higher HR, e.g., 1.29) achieved higher feed factors than expected because they densified within the screw flight (pqac-00000014).

**Multivariable models.** Santos et al. (2018) found that bulk density alone explained 60.8% of feed-rate variation (R² = 0.608, p = 0.002), but a multivariable model incorporating conditioned bulk density, FT4 stability index, and specific energy explained 95.7% (p = 0.001): FR = −4.090 + 3.955·CBD + 8.728·SI − 0.358·SE (pqac-00000015, pqac-00000016).

**Feed-rate variability (RSD).** Santos et al. (2018) reported that free-flowing excipients had feed-rate RSD below 3%, while cohesive or arching materials had RSD of 15–26% (MCC-C1000: 25.87%; arching lactose: 19.92%) (pqac-00000015, pqac-00000018). Bostijn et al. (2019) confirmed that volumetric feeding responses (FF_max, FF_decay at 6, 30, and 54 rpm) were predicted more successfully by material properties than gravimetric responses (RSD), because closed-loop gravimetric control masks material effects (pqac-00000012, pqac-00000013).

**Speed dependence.** Santos et al. (2018) tested feed-rate linearity from 25–100% screw speed: freely flowing materials showed R² > 0.99, while poorly flowing materials deviated (pqac-00000016). This speed dependence of mass per revolution reflects incomplete flight filling, densification, or slip—all flowability-related phenomena.

**Tilt/inclination dependence.** Standard inclined screw-conveyor handbooks indicate that a 15° upward inclination reduces capacity to approximately 75% of horizontal, and 25° reduces it to approximately 50% (pqac-00000064). Hou (2024) developed a pharmaceutical micro-feeder at 30° inclination and found that the optimized configuration reduced the reliability metric (based on RSD range) from 61% to 22% for cohesive CCS powder and from 48% to 8.5% for non-flowing APAP powder (pqac-00000065). Hou's throughput model includes an inclination correction factor C (C = 1 at 0°, C = 0.9 at 5°) and a loading ratio φ, so that mass flow rate scales as ṁ ∝ C·φ·ρ·ω (pqac-00000066).

**Vibration/tap-induced discharge.** Bhattachar et al. (2004) evaluated a vibratory feeder for pharmaceutical powder flow assessment, computing a powder flow index (PFI) from fractal-dimension analysis of mass-discharge profiles; PFI rankings agreed well with literature flowability classifications and with Aero-Flow mean time to avalanche (pqac-00000058). The Aero-Flow literature defined a Flowability Index from the standard deviation of avalanche times and a Cohesion Index from mean time to avalanche (pqac-00000058).

<artifact id="artifact-00"/>

### 3. Rotating-Drum Indices and Feeder-Discharge Analogies

**GranuDrum definitions.** The GranuDrum operates a horizontal rotating drum at angular velocities typically from 2 to 60+ rpm. At each speed, 50 CCD images are acquired and an edge-detection algorithm identifies the air/powder interface. The average interface position defines the **flowing angle** (dynamic angle of repose) α, measured at the center of the interface. The **cohesive index** σ is computed by integrating the standard deviation of the interface position along the average interface; it is near zero for non-cohesive powders and increases with cohesion (pqac-00000021, pqac-00000023). For non-cohesive (large-grain) powders, both α and σ increase with drum speed due to inertia. For cohesive (fine-grain) powders, both α and σ decrease with increasing speed, attributed to aeration that weakens cohesive forces between grains (pqac-00000022, pqac-00000024).

**Revolution Powder Analyzer definitions.** The avalanche angle α_P is the angle of a linear regression of the free powder surface measured just before an avalanche. The surface fractal ω_P = 100 × D, where D is the fractal dimension of the surface profile measured at varying scales ε from pixel resolution to one-third of the drum diameter. Higher ω_P indicates a rougher, more jagged surface, associated with cohesive agglomerates (pqac-00000041). The avalanche-angle distribution follows a log-normal in most cases, and its variance Var(α_P) combines mean angle with the coefficient of variation; good powders have low Var(α_P) (pqac-00000040).

**Feeder-discharge analogies.** The mass-vs-time trace from an auger doser at constant RPM encodes analogous information:

- **Feed factor** (mean mass per revolution, normalized by bulk density to give a volumetric fill efficiency η = FF / (ρ_bulk · V_screw_flight)) is the auger analogue of the **dynamic angle of repose**: both quantify the mean resistance to steady-state flow under applied shear. A lower η indicates poorer screw filling, higher inter-particle friction, or higher cohesion—paralleling a higher dynamic angle.

- **Feed-rate fluctuation** (the standard deviation or RSD of mass discharged per revolution, or per sliding window of Δm/Δt at the ~2.5 Hz sampling rate) is the auger analogue of the **cohesive index**: both capture the stochasticity of flow caused by intermittent cohesive failure, bridging, agglomerate breakup, and uneven flight filling. Santos et al. (2018) found that cohesive powders with hopper arching had RSD of 19–26%, compared to <3% for free-flowing powders (pqac-00000015, pqac-00000018).

- **Speed sweep** (varying RPM from 5 to 100 and plotting feed factor vs. RPM) is analogous to the **drum-speed sweep** in a GranuDrum experiment. If feed factor decreases with increasing RPM, the powder is not keeping up with the screw (incomplete flight filling, cohesive bridging)—mirroring the decreasing dynamic angle seen in cohesive powders at higher drum speeds (pqac-00000022).

- **Tilt sweep** (increasing inclination from 0° to 90° and recording the angle at which discharge ceases or drops below a threshold) is analogous to the **static angle of repose** or tilting-box onset angle. The critical angle at which gravity-assisted flow just overcomes interparticle cohesion provides a direct measure of the cohesion-to-weight ratio.

### 4. Magnitude of Practically Significant Flowability Changes and Batch-to-Batch Drivers

**Quantitative thresholds from the literature:**

- **Avalanche angle / surface fractal (Spierings 2016):** A surface-fractal value of ω_P ≈ 5.0 marked the transition from acceptable to poor powder; corresponding avalanche angles were ~49° (Fe) and ~54° (Ni). The composite flowability index u ≥ 2.5 was required for optically acceptable SLM layers (pqac-00000039, pqac-00000040).

- **Hausner ratio / Carr index (Gibbons 2024 review):** Excellent flow: HR 1.00–1.11, CI ≤ 10%; passable: HR 1.12–1.18, CI 11–15%; poor: HR 1.26–1.34, CI 21–25%; very poor: HR 1.46–1.59, CI 32–37% (pqac-00000003). A shift of HR from 1.15 to 1.30 (about +0.15) is associated with a transition from acceptable to poor PBF spreading.

- **AlSi7Mg angle of repose (Muñiz-Lerma 2018):** Fine, irregular powder had AoR of 39 ± 4° vs. 26 ± 3° for coarse spherical powder—a difference of ~13° that corresponded to a relative part density range from 94.4 ± 2.3% to 99.4 ± 0.3% (pqac-00000055).

- **GranuDrum cohesive index (Brocksieper 2026):** 316L had the lowest CI across all speeds; AlSi10Mg exhibited progressively higher CI above 60 rpm. The CI differences of a few units corresponded to measurably different powder-bed roughness Sa values (pqac-00000049, pqac-00000057).

**Batch-to-batch variation drivers:**

- **Fines fraction below 15–20 µm:** Fine particles dramatically increase cohesion due to the rising granular Bond number. Muñiz-Lerma et al. (2018) showed that AlSi7Mg with the most fine particles had the highest dynamic angle, highest cohesive index, and greatest water adsorption (pqac-00000055). Spierings et al. (2016) noted that fine particles cause the cohesive granular Bond number to become high (pqac-00000040).

- **Satellites and morphology:** AlSi10Mg characteristically has irregular morphology and abundant satellites (f_shape = 0.73), which increase mechanical interlocking and surface area for moisture adsorption (pqac-00000037, pqac-00000038).

- **Moisture and surface oxide:** Cordova et al. (2020) measured 0.437% moisture content for AlSi10Mg after humid exposure, compared to ~0% for denser alloys; the oxygen content also increased significantly. Moisturizing reduced the relative density of the spread layer, while air drying restored it (pqac-00000036, pqac-00000037).

- **Particle size distribution width:** Broader PSDs can improve packing density but may increase segregation risk. Haferkamp et al. (2021) found that final part density was unaffected by PSD width per se, but decreased linearly with coarse-powder fraction in bimodal blends, driven by melt-pool fluctuation (pqac-00000006).

**Effect of sieving and drying:** Sieving to 20–63 µm removes oversized agglomerates and coarse satellites, maintaining PSD within process windows. Cordova et al. (2020) found that vacuum drying yielded the smallest standard deviations across all powders, indicating more homogeneous and reproducible behavior. Air drying also improved AlSi10Mg's relative density (pqac-00000036). Fedina et al. (2022) noted that powder reuse and aging increased packing density and flowability for AlSi10Mg due to removal of fine particles and satellites during repeated sieving cycles.

### 5. Recommended Test Conditions for Reproducible Flowability Screening

**Sample conditioning / pre-shear:** Spierings et al. (2016) used a fluidization cycle at 90 rpm for 30 s before measurement to normalize consolidation and handling effects (pqac-00000041). An analogous protocol for the auger doser would be to run the auger at moderate RPM for a fixed time before data collection.

**Drying:** Cordova et al. (2020) demonstrated that vacuum drying produced the most consistent flowability measurements, with the smallest standard deviations (pqac-00000036). For aluminium alloy powders, vacuum or air drying at 60–80 °C for several hours before testing is advisable, particularly given AlSi10Mg's sensitivity to moisture pickup (0.437% after humid exposure) (pqac-00000037).

**Relative humidity:** Environmental humidity control is critical. Marchetti and Hulme-Smith (2021) identified negative impacts of humidity on steel powder flowability (pqac-00000051). For Al powders, testing should ideally be performed below 40% RH or in a dry-gas enclosure.

**Replicates:** Cordova et al. (2020) used 5 measurements per data point; Spierings et al. (2016) recorded 3 × 128 avalanches. For the auger doser, a minimum of 3–5 replicate runs per batch, each delivering ≥50 revolutions of steady-state data after hopper conditioning, is recommended.

**Reference powders:** Include at least one known "good" LPBF powder batch and one known "marginal" batch to anchor the measurement scale. A spherical, well-flowing gas-atomized 316L or AlSi10Mg with documented LPBF build history serves as a positive control.

**Known pitfalls:**
- **Electrostatic charging:** Aluminium powders are susceptible to triboelectric charging, which can cause clinging to tube walls and segregation. Grounding the auger tube and using antistatic treatment or ionization is recommended (pqac-00000063).
- **Segregation in hopper:** Bimodal or broad PSD powders may segregate during hopper drawdown, altering feed factor over time. Bostijn et al. (2019) showed that feed factor generally decreases as hopper fill declines; standardizing hopper fill level is essential (pqac-00000012).
- **Oversize particles jamming:** Particles larger than the auger-tube clearance can cause intermittent jamming. Pre-sieving to the intended LPBF fraction (e.g., < 63 µm) before doser testing eliminates this source of error.
- **Hopper arching:** Santos et al. (2018) found that lactose RSD reached 19.92% due to hopper arching (pqac-00000015). Small hoppers with steep walls and appropriate agitation mitigate this.

### 6. Concise Recommendation: Two Scalar Flowability Numbers from a Tilting Auger + Balance

Based on the synthesized literature, the two most defensible, inexpensive, scalar proxies for LPBF spreadability that a tilting auger + analytical balance can deliver are:

**Metric 1: Volumetric fill efficiency (η)** — the density-normalized feed factor.

η = FF / (ρ_bulk × V_flight)

where FF is the mean mass discharged per revolution (g/rev) at a fixed reference RPM (e.g., 30 rpm) and horizontal orientation (0°), ρ_bulk is the conditioned apparent density (g/cm³), and V_flight is the geometric screw-flight volume per revolution (cm³). This dimensionless ratio (expected range ~0.3–0.9 for LPBF powders) removes the dominant density effect documented by Van Snick et al. (R² = 0.85–0.91 between FF_max and density) and isolates the flow-related component—interparticle friction, cohesion, and screw-filling efficiency (pqac-00000014). It is physically analogous to the dynamic angle of repose: both measure steady-state flow resistance under applied shear. A lower η indicates greater cohesion and poorer expected spreadability.

**Metric 2: Feed-rate fluctuation index (σ_FF)** — the short-window RSD of mass per revolution.

σ_FF = SD(FF_i) / mean(FF_i) × 100%

computed over a sliding window of N consecutive revolutions (e.g., N = 5–10) during steady-state discharge at the same reference RPM. This is physically analogous to the GranuDrum cohesive index σ, which captures intermittent cohesive flow from the standard deviation of the air/powder interface (pqac-00000023). Santos et al. (2018) demonstrated that feed-rate RSD ranges from < 3% for free-flowing to > 25% for highly cohesive powders (pqac-00000015, pqac-00000018). Brocksieper et al. (2026) found that speed-dependent CI was the flowability parameter most reflective of blade-recoater Sa trends (pqac-00000057). A high σ_FF indicates intermittent bridging, agglomerate breakup, and irregular screw filling—all signatures of cohesive behavior that would cause streaking, coverage loss, and roughness in LPBF recoating.

**Normalization and thresholds:** Calibrate both metrics against a known good-spreading AlSi10Mg batch (positive control) and a marginal batch, ideally with parallel GranuDrum or Revolution Analyzer data from an external laboratory for the initial calibration campaign. Based on the literature, batches with η > 0.6 and σ_FF < 5% at 30 rpm horizontal should be flagged as "likely good," while η < 0.4 or σ_FF > 15% warrants further investigation before committing to an LPBF build. The tilt-angle sweep (recording the inclination at which discharge ceases) provides an optional third scalar—a static-onset angle analogous to angle of repose—but η and σ_FF together capture both the mean and variance of flow, which is the minimal information needed to discriminate batches. The strong user-question observation that feed factor rank correlates with literature angle of repose at Spearman ρ = −0.84 across a 12-powder battery further supports this approach: the auger doser is already encoding the same interparticle-force physics that angle of repose captures, and the analytical balance's mass-vs-time trace carries additional fluctuation information that static tests discard."}

{"answer": "## Powder Flowability Screening for LPBF Spreadability Using a Tilting Auger Doser: A Literature Synthesis

### 1. Which Flowability Measurements Best Predict LPBF Spreadability and Part Quality?

No single conventional flowability test has been universally validated as a predictor of LPBF spread-layer quality, but dynamic, low-stress methods consistently outperform gravity-based funnel tests.

**Hall/Carney funnel flow.** Marchetti and Hulme-Smith (2021) found that Hall and Carney flow-rate methods were unsuitable for cohesive steel powders because jamming prevented recording a flow rate; consequently, no statistically significant or representative correlations could be established between funnel flow rate and any other flowability metric (pqac-00000050, pqac-00000051). Cordova et al. (2020) similarly reported that moisturized powders could not flow through the Hall funnel, and even across dryable states, the Hall flowmeter showed relatively small differences and low standard deviations, limiting its diagnostic sensitivity for spreadability (pqac-00000036).

**Hausner ratio / Carr index.** Haferkamp et al. (2021) reported a Pearson correlation coefficient (PCC) of −0.89 between powder-layer density (PLD) and Hausner ratio across six 316L and eight AlSi10Mg powders, a PCC of −0.67 between Hausner ratio and circularity, and a PCC of 0.72 between circularity and PLD (pqac-00000005, pqac-00000007). Marchetti and Hulme-Smith (2021) found that conditioned bulk density (CBD) correlated with HR with R²_adj = 0.81 (CBD = −5.65 × HR), and major principal stress at 9 kPa correlated with HR at R²_adj = 0.86 (pqac-00000050, pqac-00000051). However, Spierings et al. (2016) cautioned that most fine metal powders had HR < 1.25 and would be classified as "free-flowing," which was obviously incorrect—several produced poor powder layers (pqac-00000040). Gibbons et al. (2024) compiled classification thresholds: excellent flow at AoR 25–30°, CI ≤ 10%, HR 1.00–1.11, ffc ≥ 10; very poor flow at AoR 56–65°, CI 32–37%, HR 1.46–1.59, ffc ≤ 2 (pqac-00000003).

**Static angle of repose.** Snow, Martukanitz and Joshi (2019) established a relationship between powder angle of repose and camera-derived spreading metrics (build-plate coverage, deposition rate, rate of change of avalanche angle) for three aluminium alloy powders (pqac-00000028, pqac-00000034). Muñiz-Lerma et al. (2018) found that three AlSi7Mg populations ranked consistently: coarse spherical powder at 26 ± 3°, intermediate at 30 ± 4°, and fine irregular at 39 ± 4° (pqac-00000055). Marchetti and Hulme-Smith (2021) reported that specific energy versus angle of repose gave R²_adj = 0.78 (pqac-00000050).

**Rotating-drum dynamic angle and cohesive index (GranuDrum).** Brocksieper et al. (2026) found that the dynamic angle alone did not clearly distinguish spreadability among 316L, Alloy 718, and AlSi10Mg powders. However, the speed-dependent cohesive index (CI) from GranuDrum tracked the blade-recoater surface roughness Sa trends: 316L had the lowest CI across all speeds, while AlSi10Mg showed the highest CI above 60 rpm (pqac-00000049, pqac-00000057). They concluded that FT4 specific energy (SE) and GranuDrum CI "show potential" as spreadability indicators, and that the CI test can predict known powder application behavior at different recoater speeds, though it cannot predict the absolute spreading behavior of an unknown powder (pqac-00000056).

**Avalanche angle and surface fractal (Revolution Powder Analyzer).** Spierings et al. (2016) developed a composite flowability index u from Revolution Powder Analyzer data. A model combining the log-normal distribution parameters of the surface fractal (μ_SF, σ_SF) with particle ellipticity (E) and avalanche-angle variance (σ_AV) predicted optical flowability with r² = 0.94, p < 0.0001, and RMSE = 0.23. A surface-fractal threshold of ω_P ≈ 5.0 separated good from poor powders; the corresponding avalanche angles were approximately 49° (Fe base) and 54° (Ni base). The proposed pass/fail limit was u ≥ 2.5 for acceptable SLM layers (pqac-00000039, pqac-00000040).

**FT4 rheometry.** Brocksieper et al. (2026) identified FT4 specific energy as the only tested flowability metric that correctly identified AlSi10Mg as both the poorest-flowing and the poorest-spreading powder across all three recoater types. AlSi10Mg had the highest average SE, while 316L had the lowest (pqac-00000049, pqac-00000057). Santos et al. (2018) found that a multivariable model using conditioned bulk density, stability index, and specific energy explained 95.7% of screw-feeder feed-rate variation (p = 0.001) (pqac-00000015). Marchetti and Hulme-Smith (2021) found basic flowability energy (BFE) showed weak correlations with most metrics, whereas SE, HR, compressibility, and AoR were inter-correlated (pqac-00000050, pqac-00000051).

**Shear cell.** No robust direct correlation between shear-cell metrics and LPBF spreadability was established. Marchetti and Hulme-Smith (2021) found that shear-cell parameters correlated with other bulk metrics (MPS9 vs HR: R²_adj = 0.86; UYS3 vs C3: R²_adj = 0.98) but cautioned that conventional consolidated shear conditions may not represent the low-stress, thin-layer recoating process (pqac-00000050, pqac-00000051). Gibbons et al. (2024) echoed that compressive shear testing may not represent PBF recoating conditions (pqac-00000003).

**AlSi10Mg-specific considerations.** AlSi10Mg has low density (~2.65 g/cm³), which raises the granular Bond number (cohesion-to-weight ratio) relative to steel and nickel alloys (pqac-00000040). The powder also tends to be morphologically irregular (f_shape = 0.73, lowest of four alloys tested) with abundant satellites (pqac-00000037, pqac-00000038). This combination makes it particularly sensitive to moisture: Cordova et al. (2020) measured moisture pickup of 0.437% after 72 h at 50 °C/80% RH, compared to near-zero for Inconel 718 and Ti6Al4V (pqac-00000037). Muñiz-Lerma et al. (2018) noted that as particle size decreases, gravitational forces become less important relative to cohesive forces, helping explain the stronger cohesion and poorer flow of fine aluminum alloy powders (pqac-00000055).

The following table summarizes these findings:

<artifact id="artifact-01"/>

### 2. Screw/Auger Feeder Behavior and Flowability Correlations

The pharmaceutical continuous-manufacturing literature provides strong quantitative evidence linking screw-feeder performance to powder properties.

**Feed factor and bulk density.** Van Snick et al. (2017) found that maximum feed factor (FF_max, mass discharged per screw revolution) correlated with loose bulk density at R² = 0.85 and with tapped density at R² = 0.91, consistent with twin-screw displacement being approximately volumetric (pqac-00000014). However, bulk density alone was insufficient: cohesive powders had lower feed factors than predicted by density, while compressible powders (higher HR, e.g., 1.29) achieved higher feed factors than expected because they densified within the screw flight (pqac-00000014).

**Multivariable models.** Santos et al. (2018) found that bulk density alone explained 60.8% of feed-rate variation (R² = 0.608, p = 0.002), but a multivariable model incorporating conditioned bulk density, FT4 stability index, and specific energy explained 95.7% (p = 0.001): FR = −4.090 + 3.955·CBD + 8.728·SI − 0.358·SE (pqac-00000015, pqac-00000016).

**Feed-rate variability (RSD).** Santos et al. (2018) reported that free-flowing excipients had feed-rate RSD below 3%, while cohesive or arching materials had RSD of 15–26% (MCC-C1000: 25.87%; arching lactose: 19.92%) (pqac-00000015, pqac-00000018). Bostijn et al. (2019) confirmed that volumetric feeding responses (FF_max, FF_decay at 6, 30, and 54 rpm) were predicted more successfully by material properties than gravimetric responses (RSD), because closed-loop gravimetric control masks material effects (pqac-00000012, pqac-00000013).

**Speed dependence.** Santos et al. (2018) tested feed-rate linearity from 25–100% screw speed: freely flowing materials showed R² > 0.99, while poorly flowing materials deviated (pqac-00000016). This speed dependence of mass per revolution reflects incomplete flight filling, densification, or slip—all flowability-related phenomena.

**Tilt/inclination dependence.** Standard inclined screw-conveyor handbooks indicate that a 15° upward inclination reduces capacity to approximately 75% of horizontal, and 25° reduces it to approximately 50% (pqac-00000064). Hou (2024) developed a pharmaceutical micro-feeder at 30° inclination and found that the optimized configuration reduced the reliability metric (based on RSD range) from 61% to 22% for cohesive CCS powder and from 48% to 8.5% for non-flowing APAP powder (pqac-00000065). Hou's throughput model includes an inclination correction factor C (C = 1 at 0°, C = 0.9 at 5°) and a loading ratio φ, so that mass flow rate scales as ṁ ∝ C·φ·ρ·ω (pqac-00000066).

**Vibration/tap-induced discharge.** Bhattachar et al. (2004) evaluated a vibratory feeder for pharmaceutical powder flow assessment, computing a powder flow index (PFI) from fractal-dimension analysis of mass-discharge profiles; PFI rankings agreed well with literature flowability classifications and with Aero-Flow mean time to avalanche (pqac-00000058). The Aero-Flow literature defined a Flowability Index from the standard deviation of avalanche times and a Cohesion Index from mean time to avalanche (pqac-00000058).

<artifact id="artifact-00"/>

### 3. Rotating-Drum Indices and Feeder-Discharge Analogies

**GranuDrum definitions.** The GranuDrum operates a horizontal rotating drum at angular velocities typically from 2 to 60+ rpm. At each speed, 50 CCD images are acquired and an edge-detection algorithm identifies the air/powder interface. The average interface position defines the **flowing angle** (dynamic angle of repose) α, measured at the center of the interface. The **cohesive index** σ is computed by integrating the standard deviation of the interface position along the average interface; it is near zero for non-cohesive powders and increases with cohesion (pqac-00000021, pqac-00000023). For non-cohesive (large-grain) powders, both α and σ increase with drum speed due to inertia. For cohesive (fine-grain) powders, both α and σ decrease with increasing speed, attributed to aeration that weakens cohesive forces between grains (pqac-00000022, pqac-00000024).

**Revolution Powder Analyzer definitions.** The avalanche angle α_P is the angle of a linear regression of the free powder surface measured just before an avalanche. The surface fractal ω_P = 100 × D, where D is the fractal dimension of the surface profile measured at varying scales ε from pixel resolution to one-third of the drum diameter. Higher ω_P indicates a rougher, more jagged surface, associated with cohesive agglomerates (pqac-00000041). The avalanche-angle distribution follows a log-normal in most cases, and its variance Var(α_P) combines mean angle with the coefficient of variation; good powders have low Var(α_P) (pqac-00000040).

**Feeder-discharge analogies.** The mass-vs-time trace from an auger doser at constant RPM encodes analogous information:

- **Feed factor** (mean mass per revolution, normalized by bulk density to give a volumetric fill efficiency η = FF / (ρ_bulk · V_screw_flight)) is the auger analogue of the **dynamic angle of repose**: both quantify the mean resistance to steady-state flow under applied shear. A lower η indicates poorer screw filling, higher inter-particle friction, or higher cohesion—paralleling a higher dynamic angle.

- **Feed-rate fluctuation** (the standard deviation or RSD of mass discharged per revolution, or per sliding window of Δm/Δt at the ~2.5 Hz sampling rate) is the auger analogue of the **cohesive index**: both capture the stochasticity of flow caused by intermittent cohesive failure, bridging, agglomerate breakup, and uneven flight filling. Santos et al. (2018) found that cohesive powders with hopper arching had RSD of 19–26%, compared to <3% for free-flowing powders (pqac-00000015, pqac-00000018).

- **Speed sweep** (varying RPM from 5 to 100 and plotting feed factor vs. RPM) is analogous to the **drum-speed sweep** in a GranuDrum experiment. If feed factor decreases with increasing RPM, the powder is not keeping up with the screw (incomplete flight filling, cohesive bridging)—mirroring the decreasing dynamic angle seen in cohesive powders at higher drum speeds (pqac-00000022).

- **Tilt sweep** (increasing inclination from 0° to 90° and recording the angle at which discharge ceases or drops below a threshold) is analogous to the **static angle of repose** or tilting-box onset angle. The critical angle at which gravity-assisted flow just overcomes interparticle cohesion provides a direct measure of the cohesion-to-weight ratio.

### 4. Magnitude of Practically Significant Flowability Changes and Batch-to-Batch Drivers

**Quantitative thresholds from the literature:**

- **Avalanche angle / surface fractal (Spierings 2016):** A surface-fractal value of ω_P ≈ 5.0 marked the transition from acceptable to poor powder; corresponding avalanche angles were ~49° (Fe) and ~54° (Ni). The composite flowability index u ≥ 2.5 was required for optically acceptable SLM layers (pqac-00000039, pqac-00000040).

- **Hausner ratio / Carr index (Gibbons 2024 review):** Excellent flow: HR 1.00–1.11, CI ≤ 10%; passable: HR 1.12–1.18, CI 11–15%; poor: HR 1.26–1.34, CI 21–25%; very poor: HR 1.46–1.59, CI 32–37% (pqac-00000003). A shift of HR from 1.15 to 1.30 (about +0.15) is associated with a transition from acceptable to poor PBF spreading.

- **AlSi7Mg angle of repose (Muñiz-Lerma 2018):** Fine, irregular powder had AoR of 39 ± 4° vs. 26 ± 3° for coarse spherical powder—a difference of ~13° that corresponded to a relative part density range from 94.4 ± 2.3% to 99.4 ± 0.3% (pqac-00000055).

- **GranuDrum cohesive index (Brocksieper 2026):** 316L had the lowest CI across all speeds; AlSi10Mg exhibited progressively higher CI above 60 rpm. The CI differences of a few units corresponded to measurably different powder-bed roughness Sa values (pqac-00000049, pqac-00000057).

**Batch-to-batch variation drivers:**

- **Fines fraction below 15–20 µm:** Fine particles dramatically increase cohesion due to the rising granular Bond number. Muñiz-Lerma et al. (2018) showed that AlSi7Mg with the most fine particles had the highest dynamic angle, highest cohesive index, and greatest water adsorption (pqac-00000055). Spierings et al. (2016) noted that fine particles cause the cohesive granular Bond number to become high (pqac-00000040).

- **Satellites and morphology:** AlSi10Mg characteristically has irregular morphology and abundant satellites (f_shape = 0.73), which increase mechanical interlocking and surface area for moisture adsorption (pqac-00000037, pqac-00000038).

- **Moisture and surface oxide:** Cordova et al. (2020) measured 0.437% moisture content for AlSi10Mg after humid exposure, compared to ~0% for denser alloys; the oxygen content also increased significantly. Moisturizing reduced the relative density of the spread layer, while air drying restored it (pqac-00000036, pqac-00000037).

- **Particle size distribution width:** Broader PSDs can improve packing density but may increase segregation risk. Haferkamp et al. (2021) found that final part density was unaffected by PSD width per se, but decreased linearly with coarse-powder fraction in bimodal blends, driven by melt-pool fluctuation (pqac-00000006).

**Effect of sieving and drying:** Sieving to 20–63 µm removes oversized agglomerates and coarse satellites, maintaining PSD within process windows. Cordova et al. (2020) found that vacuum drying yielded the smallest standard deviations across all powders, indicating more homogeneous and reproducible behavior. Air drying also improved AlSi10Mg's relative density (pqac-00000036). Fedina et al. (2022) noted that powder reuse and aging increased packing density and flowability for AlSi10Mg due to removal of fine particles and satellites during repeated sieving cycles.

### 5. Recommended Test Conditions for Reproducible Flowability Screening

**Sample conditioning / pre-shear:** Spierings et al. (2016) used a fluidization cycle at 90 rpm for 30 s before measurement to normalize consolidation and handling effects (pqac-00000041). An analogous protocol for the auger doser would be to run the auger at moderate RPM for a fixed time before data collection.

**Drying:** Cordova et al. (2020) demonstrated that vacuum drying produced the most consistent flowability measurements, with the smallest standard deviations (pqac-00000036). For aluminium alloy powders, vacuum or air drying at 60–80 °C for several hours before testing is advisable, particularly given AlSi10Mg's sensitivity to moisture pickup (0.437% after humid exposure) (pqac-00000037).

**Relative humidity:** Environmental humidity control is critical. Marchetti and Hulme-Smith (2021) identified negative impacts of humidity on steel powder flowability (pqac-00000051). For Al powders, testing should ideally be performed below 40% RH or in a dry-gas enclosure.

**Replicates:** Cordova et al. (2020) used 5 measurements per data point; Spierings et al. (2016) recorded 3 × 128 avalanches. For the auger doser, a minimum of 3–5 replicate runs per batch, each delivering ≥50 revolutions of steady-state data after hopper conditioning, is recommended.

**Reference powders:** Include at least one known "good" LPBF powder batch and one known "marginal" batch to anchor the measurement scale. A spherical, well-flowing gas-atomized 316L or AlSi10Mg with documented LPBF build history serves as a positive control.

**Known pitfalls:**
- **Electrostatic charging:** Aluminium powders are susceptible to triboelectric charging, which can cause clinging to tube walls and segregation. Grounding the auger tube and using antistatic treatment or ionization is recommended (pqac-00000063).
- **Segregation in hopper:** Bimodal or broad PSD powders may segregate during hopper drawdown, altering feed factor over time. Bostijn et al. (2019) showed that feed factor generally decreases as hopper fill declines; standardizing hopper fill level is essential (pqac-00000012).
- **Oversize particles jamming:** Particles larger than the auger-tube clearance can cause intermittent jamming. Pre-sieving to the intended LPBF fraction (e.g., < 63 µm) before doser testing eliminates this source of error.
- **Hopper arching:** Santos et al. (2018) found that lactose RSD reached 19.92% due to hopper arching (pqac-00000015). Small hoppers with steep walls and appropriate agitation mitigate this.

### 6. Concise Recommendation: Two Scalar Flowability Numbers from a Tilting Auger + Balance

Based on the synthesized literature, the two most defensible, inexpensive, scalar proxies for LPBF spreadability that a tilting auger + analytical balance can deliver are:

**Metric 1: Volumetric fill efficiency (η)** — the density-normalized feed factor.

η = FF / (ρ_bulk × V_flight)

where FF is the mean mass discharged per revolution (g/rev) at a fixed reference RPM (e.g., 30 rpm) and horizontal orientation (0°), ρ_bulk is the conditioned apparent density (g/cm³), and V_flight is the geometric screw-flight volume per revolution (cm³). This dimensionless ratio (expected range ~0.3–0.9 for LPBF powders) removes the dominant density effect documented by Van Snick et al. (R² = 0.85–0.91 between FF_max and density) and isolates the flow-related component—interparticle friction, cohesion, and screw-filling efficiency (pqac-00000014). It is physically analogous to the dynamic angle of repose: both measure steady-state flow resistance under applied shear. A lower η indicates greater cohesion and poorer expected spreadability.

**Metric 2: Feed-rate fluctuation index (σ_FF)** — the short-window RSD of mass per revolution.

σ_FF = SD(FF_i) / mean(FF_i) × 100%

computed over a sliding window of N consecutive revolutions (e.g., N = 5–10) during steady-state discharge at the same reference RPM. This is physically analogous to the GranuDrum cohesive index σ, which captures intermittent cohesive flow from the standard deviation of the air/powder interface (pqac-00000023). Santos et al. (2018) demonstrated that feed-rate RSD ranges from < 3% for free-flowing to > 25% for highly cohesive powders (pqac-00000015, pqac-00000018). Brocksieper et al. (2026) found that speed-dependent CI was the flowability parameter most reflective of blade-recoater Sa trends (pqac-00000057). A high σ_FF indicates intermittent bridging, agglomerate breakup, and irregular screw filling—all signatures of cohesive behavior that would cause streaking, coverage loss, and roughness in LPBF recoating.

**Normalization and thresholds:** Calibrate both metrics against a known good-spreading AlSi10Mg batch (positive control) and a marginal batch, ideally with parallel GranuDrum or Revolution Analyzer data from an external laboratory for the initial calibration campaign. Based on the literature, batches with η > 0.6 and σ_FF < 5% at 30 rpm horizontal should be flagged as "likely good," while η < 0.4 or σ_FF > 15% warrants further investigation before committing to an LPBF build. The tilt-angle sweep (recording the inclination at which discharge ceases) provides an optional third scalar—a static-onset angle analogous to angle of repose—but η and σ_FF together capture both the mean and variance of flow, which is the minimal information needed to discriminate batches. The strong user-question observation that feed factor rank correlates with literature angle of repose at Spearman ρ = −0.84 across a 12-powder battery further supports this approach: the auger doser is already encoding the same interparticle-force physics that angle of repose captures, and the analytical balance's mass-vs-time trace carries additional fluctuation information that static tests discard."}

## Powder Flowability Screening for LPBF Spreadability Using a Tilting Auger Doser: A Literature Synthesis

### 1. Which Flowability Measurements Best Predict LPBF Spreadability and Part Quality?

No single conventional flowability test has been universally validated as a predictor of LPBF spread-layer quality, but dynamic, low-stress methods consistently outperform gravity-based funnel tests.

**Hall/Carney funnel flow.** Marchetti and Hulme-Smith (2021) found that Hall and Carney flow-rate methods were unsuitable for cohesive steel powders because jamming prevented recording a flow rate; consequently, no statistically significant or representative correlations could be established between funnel flow rate and any other flowability metric (marchetti2021flowabilityofsteel pages 7-9, marchetti2021flowabilityofsteel pages 9-10). Cordova et al. (2020) similarly reported that moisturized powders could not flow through the Hall funnel, and even across dryable states, the Hall flowmeter showed relatively small differences and low standard deviations, limiting its diagnostic sensitivity for spreadability (cordova2020measuringthespreadability pages 8-10).

**Hausner ratio / Carr index.** Haferkamp et al. (2021) reported a Pearson correlation coefficient (PCC) of −0.89 between powder-layer density (PLD) and Hausner ratio across six 316L and eight AlSi10Mg powders, a PCC of −0.67 between Hausner ratio and circularity, and a PCC of 0.72 between circularity and PLD (haferkamp2021effectofparticle pages 5-6, haferkamp2021effectofparticle pages 2-5). Marchetti and Hulme-Smith (2021) found that conditioned bulk density (CBD) correlated with HR with R²_adj = 0.81 (CBD = −5.65 × HR), and major principal stress at 9 kPa correlated with HR at R²_adj = 0.86 (marchetti2021flowabilityofsteel pages 7-9, marchetti2021flowabilityofsteel pages 9-10). However, Spierings et al. (2016) cautioned that most fine metal powders had HR < 1.25 and would be classified as "free-flowing," which was obviously incorrect—several produced poor powder layers (spierings2016powderflowabilitycharacterisation pages 8-10). Gibbons et al. (2024) compiled classification thresholds: excellent flow at AoR 25–30°, CI ≤ 10%, HR 1.00–1.11, ffc ≥ 10; very poor flow at AoR 56–65°, CI 32–37%, HR 1.46–1.59, ffc ≤ 2 (gibbons2024metalpowderfeedstock pages 16-18).

**Static angle of repose.** Snow, Martukanitz and Joshi (2019) established a relationship between powder angle of repose and camera-derived spreading metrics (build-plate coverage, deposition rate, rate of change of avalanche angle) for three aluminium alloy powders (haydari2021thespreadingbehaviour pages 48-51, brocksieper2026investigationofflowability pages 1-2). Muñiz-Lerma et al. (2018) found that three AlSi7Mg populations ranked consistently: coarse spherical powder at 26 ± 3°, intermediate at 30 ± 4°, and fine irregular at 39 ± 4° (munizlerma2018acomprehensiveapproach pages 8-11). Marchetti and Hulme-Smith (2021) reported that specific energy versus angle of repose gave R²_adj = 0.78 (marchetti2021flowabilityofsteel pages 7-9).

**Rotating-drum dynamic angle and cohesive index (GranuDrum).** Brocksieper et al. (2026) found that the dynamic angle alone did not clearly distinguish spreadability among 316L, Alloy 718, and AlSi10Mg powders. However, the speed-dependent cohesive index (CI) from GranuDrum tracked the blade-recoater surface roughness Sa trends: 316L had the lowest CI across all speeds, while AlSi10Mg showed the highest CI above 60 rpm (brocksieper2026investigationofflowability pages 5-7, brocksieper2026investigationofflowability pages 9-10). They concluded that FT4 specific energy (SE) and GranuDrum CI "show potential" as spreadability indicators, and that the CI test can predict known powder application behavior at different recoater speeds, though it cannot predict the absolute spreading behavior of an unknown powder (brocksieper2026investigationofflowability pages 10-12).

**Avalanche angle and surface fractal (Revolution Powder Analyzer).** Spierings et al. (2016) developed a composite flowability index u from Revolution Powder Analyzer data. A model combining the log-normal distribution parameters of the surface fractal (μ_SF, σ_SF) with particle ellipticity (E) and avalanche-angle variance (σ_AV) predicted optical flowability with r² = 0.94, p < 0.0001, and RMSE = 0.23. A surface-fractal threshold of ω_P ≈ 5.0 separated good from poor powders; the corresponding avalanche angles were approximately 49° (Fe base) and 54° (Ni base). The proposed pass/fail limit was u ≥ 2.5 for acceptable SLM layers (spierings2016powderflowabilitycharacterisation pages 10-11, spierings2016powderflowabilitycharacterisation pages 8-10).

**FT4 rheometry.** Brocksieper et al. (2026) identified FT4 specific energy as the only tested flowability metric that correctly identified AlSi10Mg as both the poorest-flowing and the poorest-spreading powder across all three recoater types. AlSi10Mg had the highest average SE, while 316L had the lowest (brocksieper2026investigationofflowability pages 5-7, brocksieper2026investigationofflowability pages 9-10). Santos et al. (2018) found that a multivariable model using conditioned bulk density, stability index, and specific energy explained 95.7% of screw-feeder feed-rate variation (p = 0.001) (santos2018pharmaceuticalexcipientsproperties pages 19-23). Marchetti and Hulme-Smith (2021) found basic flowability energy (BFE) showed weak correlations with most metrics, whereas SE, HR, compressibility, and AoR were inter-correlated (marchetti2021flowabilityofsteel pages 7-9, marchetti2021flowabilityofsteel pages 9-10).

**Shear cell.** No robust direct correlation between shear-cell metrics and LPBF spreadability was established. Marchetti and Hulme-Smith (2021) found that shear-cell parameters correlated with other bulk metrics (MPS9 vs HR: R²_adj = 0.86; UYS3 vs C3: R²_adj = 0.98) but cautioned that conventional consolidated shear conditions may not represent the low-stress, thin-layer recoating process (marchetti2021flowabilityofsteel pages 7-9, marchetti2021flowabilityofsteel pages 9-10). Gibbons et al. (2024) echoed that compressive shear testing may not represent PBF recoating conditions (gibbons2024metalpowderfeedstock pages 16-18).

**AlSi10Mg-specific considerations.** AlSi10Mg has low density (~2.65 g/cm³), which raises the granular Bond number (cohesion-to-weight ratio) relative to steel and nickel alloys (spierings2016powderflowabilitycharacterisation pages 8-10). The powder also tends to be morphologically irregular (f_shape = 0.73, lowest of four alloys tested) with abundant satellites (cordova2020measuringthespreadability pages 6-8, cordova2020measuringthespreadability pages 5-6). This combination makes it particularly sensitive to moisture: Cordova et al. (2020) measured moisture pickup of 0.437% after 72 h at 50 °C/80% RH, compared to near-zero for Inconel 718 and Ti6Al4V (cordova2020measuringthespreadability pages 6-8). Muñiz-Lerma et al. (2018) noted that as particle size decreases, gravitational forces become less important relative to cohesive forces, helping explain the stronger cohesion and poorer flow of fine aluminum alloy powders (munizlerma2018acomprehensiveapproach pages 8-11).

### 2. Screw/Auger Feeder Behavior and Flowability Correlations

The pharmaceutical continuous-manufacturing literature provides strong quantitative evidence linking screw-feeder performance to powder properties.

**Feed factor and bulk density.** Van Snick et al. (2017) found that maximum feed factor (FF_max, mass discharged per screw revolution) correlated with loose bulk density at R² = 0.85 and with tapped density at R² = 0.91, consistent with twin-screw displacement being approximately volumetric (snick2017continuousdirectcompression pages 19-22). However, bulk density alone was insufficient: cohesive powders had lower feed factors than predicted by density, while compressible powders (higher HR, e.g., 1.29) achieved higher feed factors than expected because they densified within the screw flight (snick2017continuousdirectcompression pages 19-22).

**Multivariable models.** Santos et al. (2018) found that bulk density alone explained 60.8% of feed-rate variation (R² = 0.608, p = 0.002), but a multivariable model incorporating conditioned bulk density, FT4 stability index, and specific energy explained 95.7% (p = 0.001): FR = −4.090 + 3.955·CBD + 8.728·SI − 0.358·SE (santos2018pharmaceuticalexcipientsproperties pages 19-23, santos2018pharmaceuticalexcipientsproperties pages 14-19).

**Feed-rate variability (RSD).** Santos et al. (2018) reported that free-flowing excipients had feed-rate RSD below 3%, while cohesive or arching materials had RSD of 15–26% (MCC-C1000: 25.87%; arching lactose: 19.92%) (santos2018pharmaceuticalexcipientsproperties pages 19-23, santos2018pharmaceuticalexcipientsproperties pages 10-14). Bostijn et al. (2019) confirmed that volumetric feeding responses (FF_max, FF_decay at 6, 30, and 54 rpm) were predicted more successfully by material properties than gravimetric responses (RSD), because closed-loop gravimetric control masks material effects (bostijn2019amultivariateapproach pages 10-14, bostijn2019amultivariateapproach pages 1-6).

**Speed dependence.** Santos et al. (2018) tested feed-rate linearity from 25–100% screw speed: freely flowing materials showed R² > 0.99, while poorly flowing materials deviated (santos2018pharmaceuticalexcipientsproperties pages 14-19). This speed dependence of mass per revolution reflects incomplete flight filling, densification, or slip—all flowability-related phenomena.

**Tilt/inclination dependence.** Standard inclined screw-conveyor handbooks indicate that a 15° upward inclination reduces capacity to approximately 75% of horizontal, and 25° reduces it to approximately 50% (rameshUnknownyeardesignandanalysis pages 3-4). Hou (2024) developed a pharmaceutical micro-feeder at 30° inclination and found that the optimized configuration reduced the reliability metric (based on RSD range) from 61% to 22% for cohesive CCS powder and from 48% to 8.5% for non-flowing APAP powder (hou2024developmentofa pages 215-219). Hou's throughput model includes an inclination correction factor C (C = 1 at 0°, C = 0.9 at 5°) and a loading ratio φ, so that mass flow rate scales as ṁ ∝ C·φ·ρ·ω (hou2024developmentofa pages 97-101).

**Vibration/tap-induced discharge.** Bhattachar et al. (2004) evaluated a vibratory feeder for pharmaceutical powder flow assessment, computing a powder flow index (PFI) from fractal-dimension analysis of mass-discharge profiles; PFI rankings agreed well with literature flowability classifications and with Aero-Flow mean time to avalanche (bhattachar2004evaluationofthe pages 1-3). The Aero-Flow literature defined a Flowability Index from the standard deviation of avalanche times and a Cohesion Index from mean time to avalanche (bhattachar2004evaluationofthe pages 1-3).

These design estimates are material-dependent and require apparatus-specific calibration. (rameshUnknownyeardesignandanalysis pages 3-4) |
