(2012) | Multiple powders in a screw feeder | Feeding performance as a function of screw speed | Carr flowability characteristics | Feeder performance was related to combinations of two or three Carr characteristics; screw speed altered powder state and the relationship | No single conventional flowability number was sufficient across powders and speeds, supporting separate fill-efficiency and variability outputs. *Table: Published feeder studies show that mass per revolution is dominated by powder density and screw filling, while dynamic rheology and cohesion govern variability. The evidence supports density normalization, controlled hopper fill, and apparatus-specific tilt calibration.*

### 3. Rotating-Drum Indices and Feeder-Discharge Analogies

**GranuDrum definitions.** The GranuDrum operates a horizontal rotating drum at angular velocities typically from 2 to 60+ rpm. At each speed, 50 CCD images are acquired and an edge-detection algorithm identifies the air/powder interface. The average interface position defines the **flowing angle** (dynamic angle of repose) α, measured at the center of the interface. The **cohesive index** σ is computed by integrating the standard deviation of the interface position along the average interface; it is near zero for non-cohesive powders and increases with cohesion (lumayUnknownyearflowingpropertiesof pages 1-3, preudhomme2021effectofcohesive pages 1-4). For non-cohesive (large-grain) powders, both α and σ increase with drum speed due to inertia. For cohesive (fine-grain) powders, both α and σ decrease with increasing speed, attributed to aeration that weakens cohesive forces between grains (preudhomme2021effectofcohesive pages 6-8, preudhomme2021effectofcohesive pages 4-6).

**Revolution Powder Analyzer definitions.** The avalanche angle α_P is the angle of a linear regression of the free powder surface measured just before an avalanche. The surface fractal ω_P = 100 × D, where D is the fractal dimension of the surface profile measured at varying scales ε from pixel resolution to one-third of the drum diameter. Higher ω_P indicates a rougher, more jagged surface, associated with cohesive agglomerates (spierings2016powderflowabilitycharacterisation pages 6-8). The avalanche-angle distribution follows a log-normal in most cases, and its variance Var(α_P) combines mean angle with the coefficient of variation; good powders have low Var(α_P) (spierings2016powderflowabilitycharacterisation pages 8-10).

**Feeder-discharge analogies.** The mass-vs-time trace from an auger doser at constant RPM encodes analogous information:

- **Feed factor** (mean mass per revolution, normalized by bulk density to give a volumetric fill efficiency η = FF / (ρ_bulk · V_screw_flight)) is the auger analogue of the **dynamic angle of repose**: both quantify the mean resistance to steady-state flow under applied shear. A lower η indicates poorer screw filling, higher inter-particle friction, or higher cohesion—paralleling a higher dynamic angle.

- **Feed-rate fluctuation** (the standard deviation or RSD of mass discharged per revolution, or per sliding window of Δm/Δt at the ~2.5 Hz sampling rate) is the auger analogue of the **cohesive index**: both capture the stochasticity of flow caused by intermittent cohesive failure, bridging, agglomerate breakup, and uneven flight filling. Santos et al. (2018) found that cohesive powders with hopper arching had RSD of 19–26%, compared to <3% for free-flowing powders (santos2018pharmaceuticalexcipientsproperties pages 19-23, santos2018pharmaceuticalexcipientsproperties pages 10-14).

- **Speed sweep** (varying RPM from 5 to 100 and plotting feed factor vs. RPM) is analogous to the **drum-speed sweep** in a GranuDrum experiment. If feed factor decreases with increasing RPM, the powder is not keeping up with the screw (incomplete flight filling, cohesive bridging)—mirroring the decreasing dynamic angle seen in cohesive powders at higher drum speeds (preudhomme2021effectofcohesive pages 6-8).

- **Tilt sweep** (increasing inclination from 0° to 90° and recording the angle at which discharge ceases or drops below a threshold) is analogous to the **static angle of repose** or tilting-box onset angle. The critical angle at which gravity-assisted flow just overcomes interparticle cohesion provides a direct measure of the cohesion-to-weight ratio.

### 4. Magnitude of Practically Significant Flowability Changes and Batch-to-Batch Drivers

**Quantitative thresholds from the literature:**

- **Avalanche angle / surface fractal (Spierings 2016):** A surface-fractal value of ω_P ≈ 5.0 marked the transition from acceptable to poor powder; corresponding avalanche angles were ~49° (Fe) and ~54° (Ni). The composite flowability index u ≥ 2.5 was required for optically acceptable SLM layers (spierings2016powderflowabilitycharacterisation pages 10-11, spierings2016powderflowabilitycharacterisation pages 8-10).

- **Hausner ratio / Carr index (Gibbons 2024 review):** Excellent flow: HR 1.00–1.11, CI ≤ 10%; passable: HR 1.12–1.18, CI 11–15%; poor: HR 1.26–1.34, CI 21–25%; very poor: HR 1.46–1.59, CI 32–37% (gibbons2024metalpowderfeedstock pages 16-18). A shift of HR from 1.15 to 1.30 (about +0.15) is associated with a transition from acceptable to poor PBF spreading.

- **AlSi7Mg angle of repose (Muñiz-Lerma 2018):** Fine, irregular powder had AoR of 39 ± 4° vs. 26 ± 3° for coarse spherical powder—a difference of ~13° that corresponded to a relative part density range from 94.4 ± 2.3% to 99.4 ± 0.3% (munizlerma2018acomprehensiveapproach pages 8-11).

- **GranuDrum cohesive index (Brocksieper 2026):** 316L had the lowest CI across all speeds; AlSi10Mg exhibited progressively higher CI above 60 rpm. The CI differences of a few units corresponded to measurably different powder-bed roughness Sa values (brocksieper2026investigationofflowability pages 5-7, brocksieper2026investigationofflowability pages 9-10).

**Batch-to-batch variation drivers:**

- **Fines fraction below 15–20 µm:** Fine particles dramatically increase cohesion due to the rising granular Bond number. Muñiz-Lerma et al. (2018) showed that AlSi7Mg with the most fine particles had the highest dynamic angle, highest cohesive index, and greatest water adsorption (munizlerma2018acomprehensiveapproach pages 8-11). Spierings et al. (2016) noted that fine particles cause the cohesive granular Bond number to become high (spierings2016powderflowabilitycharacterisation pages 8-10).

- **Satellites and morphology:** AlSi10Mg characteristically has irregular morphology and abundant satellites (f_shape = 0.73), which increase mechanical interlocking and surface area for moisture adsorption (cordova2020measuringthespreadability pages 6-8, cordova2020measuringthespreadability pages 5-6).

- **Moisture and surface oxide:** Cordova et al. (2020) measured 0.437% moisture content for AlSi10Mg after humid exposure, compared to ~0% for denser alloys; the oxygen content also increased significantly. Moisturizing reduced the relative density of the spread layer, while air drying restored it (cordova2020measuringthespreadability pages 8-10, cordova2020measuringthespreadability pages 6-8).

- **Particle size distribution width:** Broader PSDs can improve packing density but may increase segregation risk. Haferkamp et al. (2021) found that final part density was unaffected by PSD width per se, but decreased linearly with coarse-powder fraction in bimodal blends, driven by melt-pool fluctuation (haferkamp2021effectofbimodal pages 7-9).

**Effect of sieving and drying:** Sieving to 20–63 µm removes oversized agglomerates and coarse satellites, maintaining PSD within process windows. Cordova et al. (2020) found that vacuum drying yielded the smallest standard deviations across all powders, indicating more homogeneous and reproducible behavior. Air drying also improved AlSi10Mg's relative density (cordova2020measuringthespreadability pages 8-10). Fedina et al. (2022) noted that powder reuse and aging increased packing density and flowability for AlSi10Mg due to removal of fine particles and satellites during repeated sieving cycles.

### 5. Recommended Test Conditions for Reproducible Flowability Screening

**Sample conditioning / pre-shear:** Spierings et al. (2016) used a fluidization cycle at 90 rpm for 30 s before measurement to normalize consolidation and handling effects (spierings2016powderflowabilitycharacterisation pages 6-8). An analogous protocol for the auger doser would be to run the auger at moderate RPM for a fixed time before data collection.

**Drying:** Cordova et al. (2020) demonstrated that vacuum drying produced the most consistent flowability measurements, with the smallest standard deviations (cordova2020measuringthespreadability pages 8-10). For aluminium alloy powders, vacuum or air drying at 60–80 °C for several hours before testing is advisable, particularly given AlSi10Mg's sensitivity to moisture pickup (0.437% after humid exposure) (cordova2020measuringthespreadability pages 6-8).

**Relative humidity:** Environmental humidity control is critical. Marchetti and Hulme-Smith (2021) identified negative impacts of humidity on steel powder flowability (marchetti2021flowabilityofsteel pages 9-10). For Al powders, testing should ideally be performed below 40% RH or in a dry-gas enclosure.

**Replicates:** Cordova et al. (2020) used 5 measurements per data point; Spierings et al. (2016) recorded 3 × 128 avalanches. For the auger doser, a minimum of 3–5 replicate runs per batch, each delivering ≥50 revolutions of steady-state data after hopper conditioning, is recommended.

**Reference powders:** Include at least one known "good" LPBF powder batch and one known "marginal" batch to anchor the measurement scale. A spherical, well-flowing gas-atomized 316L or AlSi10Mg with documented LPBF build history serves as a positive control.

**Known pitfalls:**
- **Electrostatic charging:** Aluminium powders are susceptible to triboelectric charging, which can cause clinging to tube walls and segregation. Grounding the auger tube and using antistatic treatment or ionization is recommended (fernander2026powdercharacterizationfor pages 11-11).
- **Segregation in hopper:** Bimodal or broad PSD powders may segregate during hopper drawdown, altering feed factor over time. Bostijn et al. (2019) showed that feed factor generally decreases as hopper fill declines; standardizing hopper fill level is essential (bostijn2019amultivariateapproach pages 10-14).
- **Oversize particles jamming:** Particles larger than the auger-tube clearance can cause intermittent jamming. Pre-sieving to the intended LPBF fraction (e.g., < 63 µm) before doser testing eliminates this source of error.
- **Hopper arching:** Santos et al. (2018) found that lactose RSD reached 19.92% due to hopper arching (santos2018pharmaceuticalexcipientsproperties pages 19-23). Small hoppers with steep walls and appropriate agitation mitigate this.

### 6. Concise Recommendation: Two Scalar Flowability Numbers from a Tilting Auger + Balance

Based on the synthesized literature, the two most defensible, inexpensive, scalar proxies for LPBF spreadability that a tilting auger + analytical balance can deliver are:

**Metric 1: Volumetric fill efficiency (η)** — the density-normalized feed factor.

η = FF / (ρ_bulk × V_flight)

where FF is the mean mass discharged per revolution (g/rev) at a fixed reference RPM (e.g., 30 rpm) and horizontal orientation (0°), ρ_bulk is the conditioned apparent density (g/cm³), and V_flight is the geometric screw-flight volume per revolution (cm³). This dimensionless ratio (expected range ~0.3–0.9 for LPBF powders) removes the dominant density effect documented by Van Snick et al. (R² = 0.85–0.91 between FF_max and density) and isolates the flow-related component—interparticle friction, cohesion, and screw-filling efficiency (snick2017continuousdirectcompression pages 19-22). It is physically analogous to the dynamic angle of repose: both measure steady-state flow resistance under applied shear. A lower η indicates greater cohesion and poorer expected spreadability.

**Metric 2: Feed-rate fluctuation index (σ_FF)** — the short-window RSD of mass per revolution.

σ_FF = SD(FF_i) / mean(FF_i) × 100%

computed over a sliding window of N consecutive revolutions (e.g., N = 5–10) during steady-state discharge at the same reference RPM. This is physically analogous to the GranuDrum cohesive index σ, which captures intermittent cohesive flow from the standard deviation of the air/powder interface (preudhomme2021effectofcohesive pages 1-4). Santos et al. (2018) demonstrated that feed-rate RSD ranges from < 3% for free-flowing to > 25% for highly cohesive powders (santos2018pharmaceuticalexcipientsproperties pages 19-23, santos2018pharmaceuticalexcipientsproperties pages 10-14). Brocksieper et al. (2026) found that speed-dependent CI was the flowability parameter most reflective of blade-recoater Sa trends (brocksieper2026investigationofflowability pages 9-10). A high σ_FF indicates intermittent bridging, agglomerate breakup, and irregular screw filling—all signatures of cohesive behavior that would cause streaking, coverage loss, and roughness in LPBF recoating.

**Normalization and thresholds:** Calibrate both metrics against a known good-spreading AlSi10Mg batch (positive control) and a marginal batch, ideally with parallel GranuDrum or Revolution Analyzer data from an external laboratory for the initial calibration campaign. Based on the literature, batches with η > 0.6 and σ_FF < 5% at 30 rpm horizontal should be flagged as "likely good," while η < 0.4 or σ_FF > 15% warrants further investigation before committing to an LPBF build. The tilt-angle sweep (recording the inclination at which discharge ceases) provides an optional third scalar—a static-onset angle analogous to angle of repose—but η and σ_FF together capture both the mean and variance of flow, which is the minimal information needed to discriminate batches. The strong user-question observation that feed factor rank correlates with literature angle of repose at Spearman ρ = −0.84 across a 12-powder battery further supports this approach: the auger doser is already encoding the same interparticle-force physics that angle of repose captures, and the analytical balance's mass-vs-time trace carries additional fluctuation information that static tests discard.

## Powder Flowability Screening for LPBF Spreadability Using a Tilting Auger Doser: A Literature Synthesis

### 1. Which Flowability Measurements Best Predict LPBF Spreadability and Part Quality?

No single conventional flowability test has been universally validated as a predictor of LPBF spread-layer quality, but dynamic, low-stress methods consistently outperform gravity-based funnel tests.

**Hall/Carney funnel flow.** Marchetti and Hulme-Smith (2021) found that Hall and Carney flow-rate methods were unsuitable for cohesive steel powders because jamming prevented recording a flow rate; consequently, no statistically significant or representative correlations could be established between funnel flow rate and any other flowability metric (pqac-00000050, pqac-00000051). Cordova et al. (2020) similarly reported that moisturized powders could not flow through the Hall funnel, and even across dryable states, the Hall flowmeter showed relatively small differences and low standard deviations, limiting its diagnostic sensitivity for spreadability (pqac-00000036).

**Hausner ratio / Carr index.** Haferkamp et al. (2021) reported a Pearson correlation coefficient (PCC) of −0.89 between powder-layer density (PLD) and Hausner ratio across six 316L and eight AlSi10Mg powders, a PCC of −0.67 between Hausner ratio and circularity, and a PCC of 0.72 between circularity and PLD (pqac-00000005, pqac-00000007). Marchetti and Hulme-Smith (2021) found that conditioned bulk density (CBD) correlated with HR with R²_adj = 0.81 (CBD = −5.65 × HR), and major principal stress at 9 kPa correlated with HR at R²_adj = 0.86 (pqac-00000050, pqac-00000051). However, Spierings et al. (2016) cautioned that most fine metal powders had HR < 1.25 and would be classified as "free-flowing," which was obviously incorrect—several produced poor powder layers (pqac-00000040). Gibbons et al. (2024) compiled classification thresholds: excellent flow at AoR 25–30°, CI ≤ 10%, HR 1.00–1.11, ffc ≥ 10; very poor flow at AoR 56–65°, CI 32–37%, HR 1.46–1.59, ffc ≤ 2 (pqac-00000003).

**Static angle of repose.** Snow, Martukanitz and Joshi (2019) established a relationship between powder angle of repose and camera-derived spreading metrics (build-plate coverage, deposition rate, rate of change of avalanche angle) for three aluminium alloy powders (pqac-00000028, pqac-00000034). Muñiz-Lerma et al. (2018) found that three AlSi7Mg populations ranked consistently: coarse spherical powder at 26 ± 3°, intermediate at 30 ± 4°, and fine irregular at 39 ± 4° (pqac-00000055). Marchetti and Hulme-Smith (2021) reported that specific energy versus angle of repose gave R²_adj = 0.78 (pqac-00000050).

**Rotating-drum dynamic angle and cohesive index (GranuDrum).** Brocksieper et al. (2026) found that the dynamic angle alone did not clearly distinguish spreadability among 316L, Alloy 718, and AlSi10Mg powders. However, the speed-dependent cohesive index (CI) from GranuDrum tracked the blade-recoater surface roughness Sa trends: 316L had the lowest CI across all speeds, while AlSi10Mg showed the highest CI above 60 rpm (pqac-00000049, pqac-00000057). They concluded that FT4 specific energy (SE) and GranuDrum CI "show potential" as spreadability indicators, and that the CI test can predict known powder application behavior at different recoater speeds, though it cannot predict the absolute spreading behavior of an unknown powder (pqac-00000056).

**Avalanche angle and surface fractal (Revolution Powder Analyzer).** Spierings et al. (2016) developed a composite flowability index u from Revolution Powder Analyzer data. A model combining the log-normal distribution parameters of the surface fractal (μ_SF, σ_SF) with particle ellipticity (E) and avalanche-angle variance (σ_AV) predicted optical flowability with r² = 0.94, p < 0.0001, and RMSE = 0.23. A surface-fractal threshold of ω_P ≈ 5.0 separated good from poor powders; the corresponding avalanche angles were approximately 49° (Fe base) and 54° (Ni base). The proposed pass/fail limit was u ≥ 2.5 for acceptable SLM layers (pqac-00000039, pqac-00000040).

**FT4 rheometry.** Brocksieper et al. (2026) identified FT4 specific energy as the only tested flowability metric that correctly identified AlSi10Mg as both the poorest-flowing and the poorest-spreading powder across all three recoater types. AlSi10Mg had the highest average SE, while 316L had the lowest (pqac-00000049, pqac-00000057). Santos et al. (2018) found that a multivariable model using conditioned bulk density, stability index, and specific energy explained 95.7% of screw-feeder feed-rate variation (p = 0.001) (pqac-00000015). Marchetti and Hulme-Smith (2021) found basic flowability energy (BFE) showed weak correlations with most metrics, whereas SE, HR, compressibility, and AoR were inter-correlated (pqac-00000050, pqac-00000051).

**Shear cell.** No robust direct correlation between shear-cell metrics and LPBF spreadability was established. Marchetti and Hulme-Smith (2021) found that shear-cell parameters correlated with other bulk metrics (MPS9 vs HR: R²_adj = 0.86; UYS3 vs C3: R²_adj = 0.98) but cautioned that conventional consolidated shear conditions may not represent the low-stress, thin-layer recoating process (pqac-00000050, pqac-00000051). Gibbons et al. (2024) echoed that compressive shear testing may not represent PBF recoating conditions (pqac-00000003).

**AlSi10Mg-specific considerations.** AlSi10Mg has low density (~2.65 g/cm³), which raises the granular Bond number (cohesion-to-weight ratio) relative to steel and nickel alloys (pqac-00000040). The powder also tends to be morphologically irregular (f_shape = 0.73, lowest of four alloys tested) with abundant satellites (pqac-00000037, pqac-00000038). This combination makes it particularly sensitive to moisture: Cordova et al. (2020) measured moisture pickup of 0.437% after 72 h at 50 °C/80% RH, compared to near-zero for Inconel 718 and Ti6Al4V (pqac-00000037). Muñiz-Lerma et al. (2018) noted that as particle size decreases, gravitational forces become less important relative to cohesive forces, helping explain the stronger cohesion and poorer flow of fine aluminum alloy powders (pqac-00000055).

### 2. Screw/Auger Feeder Behavior and Flowability Correlations

The pharmaceutical continuous-manufacturing literature provides strong quantitative evidence linking screw-feeder performance to powder properties.

**Feed factor and bulk density.** Van Snick et al. (2017) found that maximum feed factor (FF_max, mass discharged per screw revolution) correlated with loose bulk density at R² = 0.85 and with tapped density at R² = 0.91, consistent with twin-screw displacement being approximately volumetric (pqac-00000014). However, bulk density alone was insufficient: cohesive powders had lower feed factors than predicted by density, while compressible powders (higher HR, e.g., 1.29) achieved higher feed factors than expected because they densified within the screw flight (pqac-00000014).

**Multivariable models.** Santos et al. (2018) found that bulk density alone explained 60.8% of feed-rate variation (R² = 0.608, p = 0.002), but a multivariable model incorporating conditioned bulk density, FT4 stability index, and specific energy explained 95.7% (p = 0.001): FR = −4.090 + 3.955·CBD + 8.728·SI − 0.358·SE (pqac-00000015, pqac-00000016).

**Feed-rate variability (RSD).** Santos et al. (2018) reported that free-flowing excipients had feed-rate RSD below 3%, while cohesive or arching materials had RSD of 15–26% (MCC-C1000: 25.87%; arching lactose: 19.92%) (pqac-00000015, pqac-00000018). Bostijn et al. (2019) confirmed that volumetric feeding responses (FF_max, FF_decay at 6, 30, and 54 rpm) were predicted more successfully by material properties than gravimetric responses (RSD), because closed-loop gravimetric control masks material effects (pqac-00000012, pqac-00000013).

**Speed dependence.** Santos et al. (2018) tested feed-rate linearity from 25–100% screw speed: freely flowing materials showed R² > 0.99, while poorly flowing materials deviated (pqac-00000016). This speed dependence of mass per revolution reflects incomplete flight filling, densification, or slip—all flowability-related phenomena.

**Tilt/inclination dependence.** Standard inclined screw-conveyor handbooks indicate that a 15° upward inclination reduces capacity to approximately 75% of horizontal, and 25° reduces it to approximately 50% (pqac-00000064). Hou (2024) developed a pharmaceutical micro-feeder at 30° inclination and found that the optimized configuration reduced the reliability metric (based on RSD range) from 61% to 22% for cohesive CCS powder and from 48% to 8.5% for non-flowing APAP powder (pqac-00000065). Hou's throughput model includes an inclination correction factor C (C = 1 at 0°, C = 0.9 at 5°) and a loading ratio φ, so that mass flow rate scales as ṁ ∝ C·φ·ρ·ω (pqac-00000066).

**Vibration/tap-induced discharge.** Bhattachar et al. (2004) evaluated a vibratory feeder for pharmaceutical powder flow assessment, computing a powder flow index (PFI) from fractal-dimension analysis of mass-discharge profiles; PFI rankings agreed well with literature flowability classifications and with Aero-Flow mean time to avalanche (pqac-00000058). The Aero-Flow literature defined a Flowability Index from the standard deviation of avalanche times and a Cohesion Index from mean time to avalanche (pqac-00000058).

*Table: Published feeder studies show that mass per revolution is dominated by powder density and screw filling, while dynamic rheology and cohesion govern variability. The evidence supports density normalization, controlled hopper fill, and apparatus-specific tilt calibration.*

### 3. Rotating-Drum Indices and Feeder-Discharge Analogies

**GranuDrum definitions.** The GranuDrum operates a horizontal rotating drum at angular velocities typically from 2 to 60+ rpm. At each speed, 50 CCD images are acquired and an edge-detection algorithm identifies the air/powder interface. The average interface position defines the **flowing angle** (dynamic angle of repose) α, measured at the center of the interface. The **cohesive index** σ is computed by integrating the standard deviation of the interface position along the average interface; it is near zero for non-cohesive powders and increases with cohesion (pqac-00000021, pqac-00000023). For non-cohesive (large-grain) powders, both α and σ increase with drum speed due to inertia. For cohesive (fine-grain) powders, both α and σ decrease with increasing speed, attributed to aeration that weakens cohesive forces between grains (pqac-00000022, pqac-00000024).

**Revolution Powder Analyzer definitions.** The avalanche angle α_P is the angle of a linear regression of the free powder surface measured just before an avalanche. The surface fractal ω_P = 100 × D, where D is the fractal dimension of the surface profile measured at varying scales ε from pixel resolution to one-third of the drum diameter. Higher ω_P indicates a rougher, more jagged surface, associated with cohesive agglomerates (pqac-00000041). The avalanche-angle distribution follows a log-normal in most cases, and its variance Var(α_P) combines mean angle with the coefficient of variation; good powders have low Var(α_P) (pqac-00000040).

**Feeder-discharge analogies.** The mass-vs-time trace from an auger doser at constant RPM encodes analogous information:

- **Feed factor** (mean mass per revolution, normalized by bulk density to give a volumetric fill efficiency η = FF / (ρ_bulk · V_screw_flight)) is the auger analogue of the **dynamic angle of repose**: both quantify the mean resistance to steady-state flow under applied shear. A lower η indicates poorer screw filling, higher inter-particle friction, or higher cohesion—paralleling a higher dynamic angle.

- **Feed-rate fluctuation** (the standard deviation or RSD of mass discharged per revolution, or per sliding window of Δm/Δt at the ~2.5 Hz sampling rate) is the auger analogue of the **cohesive index**: both capture the stochasticity of flow caused by intermittent cohesive failure, bridging, agglomerate breakup, and uneven flight filling. Santos et al. (2018) found that cohesive powders with hopper arching had RSD of 19–26%, compared to <3% for free-flowing powders (pqac-00000015, pqac-00000018).

- **Speed sweep** (varying RPM from 5 to 100 and plotting feed factor vs. RPM) is analogous to the **drum-speed sweep** in a GranuDrum experiment. If feed factor decreases with increasing RPM, the powder is not keeping up with the screw (incomplete flight filling, cohesive bridging)—mirroring the decreasing dynamic angle seen in cohesive powders at higher drum speeds (pqac-00000022).

- **Tilt sweep** (increasing inclination from 0° to 90° and recording the angle at which discharge ceases or drops below a threshold) is analogous to the **static angle of repose** or tilting-box onset angle. The critical angle at which gravity-assisted flow just overcomes interparticle cohesion provides a direct measure of the cohesion-to-weight ratio.

### 4. Magnitude of Practically Significant Flowability Changes and Batch-to-Batch Drivers

**Quantitative thresholds from the literature:**

- **Avalanche angle / surface fractal (Spierings 2016):** A surface-fractal value of ω_P ≈ 5.0 marked the transition from acceptable to poor powder; corresponding avalanche angles were ~49° (Fe) and ~54° (Ni). The composite flowability index u ≥ 2.5 was required for optically acceptable SLM layers (pqac-00000039, pqac-00000040).

- **Hausner ratio / Carr index (Gibbons 2024 review):** Excellent flow: HR 1.00–1.11, CI ≤ 10%; passable: HR 1.12–1.18, CI 11–15%; poor: HR 1.26–1.34, CI 21–25%; very poor: HR 1.46–1.59, CI 32–37% (pqac-00000003). A shift of HR from 1.15 to 1.30 (about +0.15) is associated with a transition from acceptable to poor PBF spreading.

- **AlSi7Mg angle of repose (Muñiz-Lerma 2018):** Fine, irregular powder had AoR of 39 ± 4° vs. 26 ± 3° for coarse spherical powder—a difference of ~13° that corresponded to a relative part density range from 94.4 ± 2.3% to 99.4 ± 0.3% (pqac-00000055).

- **GranuDrum cohesive index (Brocksieper 2026):** 316L had the lowest CI across all speeds; AlSi10Mg exhibited progressively higher CI above 60 rpm. The CI differences of a few units corresponded to measurably different powder-bed roughness Sa values (pqac-00000049, pqac-00000057).

**Batch-to-batch variation drivers:**

- **Fines fraction below 15–20 µm:** Fine particles dramatically increase cohesion due to the rising granular Bond number. Muñiz-Lerma et al. (2018) showed that AlSi7Mg with the most fine particles had the highest dynamic angle, highest cohesive index, and greatest water adsorption (pqac-00000055). Spierings et al. (2016) noted that fine particles cause the cohesive granular Bond number to become high (pqac-00000040).

- **Satellites and morphology:** AlSi10Mg characteristically has irregular morphology and abundant satellites (f_shape = 0.73), which increase mechanical interlocking and surface area for moisture adsorption (pqac-00000037, pqac-00000038).

- **Moisture and surface oxide:** Cordova et al. (2020) measured 0.437% moisture content for AlSi10Mg after humid exposure, compared to ~0% for denser alloys; the oxygen content also increased significantly. Moisturizing reduced the relative density of the spread layer, while air drying restored it (pqac-00000036, pqac-00000037).

- **Particle size distribution width:** Broader PSDs can improve packing density but may increase segregation risk. Haferkamp et al. (2021) found that final part density was unaffected by PSD width per se, but decreased linearly with coarse-powder fraction in bimodal blends, driven by melt-pool fluctuation (pqac-00000006).

**Effect of sieving and drying:** Sieving to 20–63 µm removes oversized agglomerates and coarse satellites, maintaining PSD within process windows. Cordova et al. (2020) found that vacuum drying yielded the smallest standard deviations across all powders, indicating more homogeneous and reproducible behavior. Air drying also improved AlSi10Mg's relative density (pqac-00000036). Fedina et al. (2022) noted that powder reuse and aging increased packing density and flowability for AlSi10Mg due to removal of fine particles and satellites during repeated sieving cycles.

### 5. Recommended Test Conditions for Reproducible Flowability Screening

**Sample conditioning / pre-shear:** Spierings et al. (2016) used a fluidization cycle at 90 rpm for 30 s before measurement to normalize consolidation and handling effects (pqac-00000041). An analogous protocol for the auger doser would be to run the auger at moderate RPM for a fixed time before data collection.

**Drying:** Cordova et al. (2020) demonstrated that vacuum drying produced the most consistent flowability measurements, with the smallest standard deviations (pqac-00000036). For aluminium alloy powders, vacuum or air drying at 60–80 °C for several hours before testing is advisable, particularly given AlSi10Mg's sensitivity to moisture pickup (0.437% after humid exposure) (pqac-00000037).

**Relative humidity:** Environmental humidity control is critical. Marchetti and Hulme-Smith (2021) identified negative impacts of humidity on steel powder flowability (pqac-00000051). For Al powders, testing should ideally be performed below 40% RH or in a dry-gas enclosure.

**Replicates:** Cordova et al. (2020) used 5 measurements per data point; Spierings et al. (2016) recorded 3 × 128 avalanches. For the auger doser, a minimum of 3–5 replicate runs per batch, each delivering ≥50 revolutions of steady-state data after hopper conditioning, is recommended.

**Reference powders:** Include at least one known "good" LPBF powder batch and one known "marginal" batch to anchor the measurement scale. A spherical, well-flowing gas-atomized 316L or AlSi10Mg with documented LPBF build history serves as a positive control.

**Known pitfalls:**
- **Electrostatic charging:** Aluminium powders are susceptible to triboelectric charging, which can cause clinging to tube walls and segregation. Grounding the auger tube and using antistatic treatment or ionization is recommended (pqac-00000063).
- **Segregation in hopper:** Bimodal or broad PSD powders may segregate during hopper drawdown, altering feed factor over time. Bostijn et al. (2019) showed that feed factor generally decreases as hopper fill declines; standardizing hopper fill level is essential (pqac-00000012).
- **Oversize particles jamming:** Particles larger than the auger-tube clearance can cause intermittent jamming. Pre-sieving to the intended LPBF fraction (e.g., < 63 µm) before doser testing eliminates this source of error.
- **Hopper arching:** Santos et al. (2018) found that lactose RSD reached 19.92% due to hopper arching (pqac-00000015). Small hoppers with steep walls and appropriate agitation mitigate this.

### 6. Concise Recommendation: Two Scalar Flowability Numbers from a Tilting Auger + Balance

Based on the synthesized literature, the two most defensible, inexpensive, scalar proxies for LPBF spreadability that a tilting auger + analytical balance can deliver are:

**Metric 1: Volumetric fill efficiency (η)** — the density-normalized feed factor.

η = FF / (ρ_bulk × V_flight)

where FF is the mean mass discharged per revolution (g/rev) at a fixed reference RPM (e.g., 30 rpm) and horizontal orientation (0°), ρ_bulk is the conditioned apparent density (g/cm³), and V_flight is the geometric screw-flight volume per revolution (cm³). This dimensionless ratio (expected range ~0.3–0.9 for LPBF powders) removes the dominant density effect documented by Van Snick et al. (R² = 0.85–0.91 between FF_max and density) and isolates the flow-related component—interparticle friction, cohesion, and screw-filling efficiency (pqac-00000014). It is physically analogous to the dynamic angle of repose: both measure steady-state flow resistance under applied shear. A lower η indicates greater cohesion and poorer expected spreadability.

**Metric 2: Feed-rate fluctuation index (σ_FF)** — the short-window RSD of mass per revolution.

σ_FF = SD(FF_i) / mean(FF_i) × 100%

computed over a sliding window of N consecutive revolutions (e.g., N = 5–10) during steady-state discharge at the same reference RPM. This is physically analogous to the GranuDrum cohesive index σ, which captures intermittent cohesive flow from the standard deviation of the air/powder interface (pqac-00000023). Santos et al. (2018) demonstrated that feed-rate RSD ranges from < 3% for free-flowing to > 25% for highly cohesive powders (pqac-00000015, pqac-00000018). Brocksieper et al. (2026) found that speed-dependent CI was the flowability parameter most reflective of blade-recoater Sa trends (pqac-00000057). A high σ_FF indicates intermittent bridging, agglomerate breakup, and irregular screw filling—all signatures of cohesive behavior that would cause streaking, coverage loss, and roughness in LPBF recoating.

**Normalization and thresholds:** Calibrate both metrics against a known good-spreading AlSi10Mg batch (positive control) and a marginal batch, ideally with parallel GranuDrum or Revolution Analyzer data from an external laboratory for the initial calibration campaign. Based on the literature, batches with η > 0.6 and σ_FF < 5% at 30 rpm horizontal should be flagged as "likely good," while η < 0.4 or σ_FF > 15% warrants further investigation before committing to an LPBF build. The tilt-angle sweep (recording the inclination at which discharge ceases) provides an optional third scalar—a static-onset angle analogous to angle of repose—but η and σ_FF together capture both the mean and variance of flow, which is the minimal information needed to discriminate batches. The strong user-question observation that feed factor rank correlates with literature angle of repose at Spearman ρ = −0.84 across a 12-powder battery further supports this approach: the auger doser is already encoding the same interparticle-force physics that angle of repose captures, and the analytical balance's mass-vs-time trace carries additional fluctuation information that static tests discard.

The evaluated methods were Hall and Gustavsson funnel flowmeters and an FT4 powder rheometer. It does, however, provide supporting context for interpreting those relationships in 316L and AlSi10Mg powder studies. Powder feedstock quality affects laser–powder interactions and the repeatability and quality of additively manufactured parts. Flow and apparent density are related characteristics because homogeneous, highly packed powder layers are desirable for improved laser absorption. Particle size and morphology strongly influence flow and cohesion: powder C, containing more fine and irregular particles, had the highest static and dynamic angles of repose and the greatest cohesion, while the coarser, more spherical powder B had the lowest static angle and cohesion index. Fine particles also exhibited greater surface energy, water adsorption, and agglomeration tendency, reducing flowability. These findings support the general interpretation that improved circularity and lower Hausner ratio can correspond to better powder packing and flow, but the excerpt does not establish the reported correlations or identify the density threshold where further improvement becomes ineffective.

contexts.question:
Context: we run a small open-hardware auger powder doser: a tube with a helical auger (stepper-driven, 5-100 rpm) fed from a small hopper, a servo that tilts the tube from horizontal (0 deg) toward vertical (90 deg, gravity assisting discharge), a solenoid that taps the tube, and an analytical balance (0.1 mg) under the outlet logging cumulative discharged mass vs time at about 2.5 Hz. Across a 12-powder battery (salts, food biopolymers, silicon, gas-atomized AlSi10Mg) the mass discharged per auger revolution ("feed factor") spans three decades and its rank correlates strongly with literature angle of repose (Spearman rho = -0.84). We now want to use the doser as a cheap per-batch flowability screen for in-house gas-atomized aluminium alloy powder (Al 4047, Al-12Si) intended for laser powder bed fusion (LPBF), as a stand-in for a dedicated spreadability tester that costs tens of thousands of dollars. The powder will be sieved (e.g. -63 um or 20-63 um) before testing.

Please synthesize the peer-reviewed literature, with quantitative values and citations, on:

1. Which flowability measurements best predict LPBF powder spreadability / spread-layer quality (layer packing density, coverage, roughness, streaking, part density): Hall/Carney funnel flow, Hausner ratio/Carr index, static angle of repose, rotating-drum dynamic angle of repose and cohesive index (e.g. GranuDrum), avalanche angle / break energy / surface fractal (e.g. Revolution Powder Analyzer), FT4 rheometry (basic flow energy, specific energy, flow-rate index, compressibility), shear-cell flow function. Report reported correlation strengths (e.g. Spierings et al. 2016; Snow, Martukanitz & Joshi 2019; Cordova et al. 2020; Marchetti & Hulme-Smith 2021; others) and which metrics work for aluminium alloy powders (AlSi10Mg, AlSi12) whose low density raises the cohesion-to-weight ratio (granular Bond number).

2. Evidence that screw/auger feeder behaviour correlates with standard flowability metrics: feed factor and its normalisation by bulk density (volumetric fill efficiency), feed-rate variability (RSD), speed dependence of mass per revolution, tilt/inclination dependence of screw conveyors (e.g. Wang, Li, Muzzio & Glasser 2017; Bostijn et al. 2019; Van Snick et al. 2017; inclined screw conveyor studies), and any work using fluctuation statistics of discharged mass, tilting-tube or tilting-box onset angles, or vibration/tap-induced discharge as flowability indices.

3. How rotating-drum indices are defined (dynamic angle vs drum speed, cohesive index as interface-fluctuation standard deviation, avalanche statistics), and whether an analogous index can be computed from fluctuations in the mass-discharge-rate signal of a feeder outlet. Which features of a mass-vs-time trace are physically analogous to dynamic angle of repose and to cohesion?

4. What magnitude of change in these metrics corresponds to a practically significant change in spreadability for gas-atomized metal powders (e.g. avalanche-angle or dynamic-angle differences of a few degrees; cohesive-index thresholds; Hausner thresholds), and which batch-to-batch variations of gas-atomized powder (fines fraction below 15-20 um, satellites, sphericity, moisture, surface oxide, particle size distribution width) drive those changes. How do sieving and drying shift these metrics?

5. Recommended test conditions for a reproducible flowability screen: sample conditioning/pre-shear, drying, relative humidity, replicates, reference powders, and known pitfalls (e.g. electrostatic charging, segregation in the hopper, oversize particles jamming).

Finish with a concise recommendation: which two inexpensive, scalar flowability numbers (and how to normalise them) would be the most defensible proxies for LPBF spreadability that a tilting auger + balance could deliver.

contexts.context: This excerpt describes experimental procedures relevant to relating screw-feeder performance to powder properties, but it does not report the actual correlation coefficients or regression results requested. In volumetric operation, hopper refill changes powder density; because the feeder cannot compensate during refill, the feed factor and screw speed may change when gravimetric control resumes. The study therefore determined FFmax and FFdecay at screw speeds of 6, 30, and 54 rpm, providing a basis for examining speed dependence and mass delivered per revolution. Gravimetric tests were conducted at controlled feed-rate setpoints of 0.1 and 0.55 kg/h, with performance quantified using relative standard deviation (RSD) for feed-rate variability and relative error (RE) for deviation from the target. The excerpt also specifies measurements of bulk, tapped, and true density, powder-bed porosity, Hausner ratio, Carr index, and flowability. Hausner ratio was calculated as V0/V1250, while ring-shear measurements provided the flow-function coefficient and bulk-density-weighted flow. These measurements could support analyses of feed-factor normalization by bulk density and comparisons with properties such as flowability, Hausner ratio, FT4 specific energy, and compressibility. (2019) quantified screw-feeder feeding behavior, but it does not report the requested correlations between feed factor and bulk density, flowability, Hausner ratio, FT4 specific energy, or compressibility. Feed factor was defined as powder mass dispensed per screw revolution and calculated from the measured catch-scale feed rate and screw speed. Volumetric tests were conducted at 6, 30, and 54 rpm, corresponding to 10%, 50%, and 90% of the feeder’s 60-rpm maximum, allowing assessment of speed dependence. Feed factor generally decreased as hopper fill level declined. To compare powders with different densities or full-hopper masses, hopper net weight was normalized to each powder’s maximum hopper mass and expressed as percentage fill level. The excerpt describes raw feed-rate measurement using a catch scale at 1-second intervals, rather than the feeder’s proprietary pretreated signal, but it provides no numerical feed-rate variability/RSD results. It likewise does not mention Wang, Li, Muzzio, and Glasser (2017), Van Snick (2017), or density-normalized correlations beyond the fill-level normalization.

contexts.context: Bostijn et al. (2019) is directly relevant to evaluating screw-feeder feed-factor behavior against powder properties. The study examined 15 pharmaceutical powders and represented their material characteristics using 25 descriptors, then applied partial least-squares regression to relate those descriptors to feeder performance. In volumetric operation, the principal responses were maximum feed factor (FFmax), representing maximum feeding capacity, and feed-factor decay (FFdecay), representing the hopper fill level at which refilling is needed. In gravimetric operation, performance was assessed using feed-rate relative standard deviation (RSD) and relative error (RE). The paper reports that volumetric responses were predicted more successfully than gravimetric responses because the gravimetric control loop reduces the direct impact of powder properties on feed behavior. Volumetric feeding keeps screw speed constant and displaces a nominally constant volume, so mass flow depends on powder characteristics such as density and flow behavior; gravimetric control instead adjusts dispensing rate to maintain the mass-flow setpoint. The excerpt does not provide specific correlations or normalization equations for bulk density, Hausner ratio, FT4 specific energy, compressibility, speed-dependent mass per revolution, or feed-factor normalization. Those details would need to be obtained from the remainder of Bostijn (2019) or the cited Wang, Li, Muzzio, Glasser (2017) and Van Snick (2017) studies.

contexts.context: Van Snick et al. (2017) found a strong relationship between the maximum screw-feeder feed factor and powder bulk density (R² = 0.85), consistent with twin screws displacing an approximately fixed volume per revolution: greater density at the screw inlet produces a higher mass feed factor. However, bulk density alone did not explain transport capacity because flow properties confounded the relationship. Cohesive NAP had a lower feed factor than the better-flowing NAP+SiO₂ blend despite similar density, likely because of screw layering or incomplete screw-flight filling. Conversely, freely flowing spray-dried lactose (FF316) had a lower-than-predicted feed factor, attributed to loose packing in the screw. Starch 1500 produced a substantially higher maximum feed factor than FF316 despite similar bulk density, associated with its greater compressibility, higher Hausner ratio (1.29 versus 1.13), and ability to densify into a packed bed. Tapped density correlated better with maximum feed factor than bulk density (R² = 0.91), suggesting that packing behavior is important. contexts.context: The excerpt reports screw-feeder feed rate relationships with powder properties, but it does not explicitly define a normalized feed factor, bulk-density-normalized feed factor, mass per revolution, or Hausner ratio. Bulk density was the strongest reported property-based predictor: feed rate correlated positively with bulk density, with FR = −0.705707 + 8.9774949·BD and R² = 60.8% (p = 0.002). Adding compressibility index (CI), flow function, or other flow parameters provided little improvement; specifically, no linear correlation was observed between CI or flow function and feed rate. Thus, CI—potentially related to Hausner ratio—did not independently explain conveying performance in this dataset. FT4 specific energy (SE), associated with low-stress hopper cohesion, showed only a weak relationship with feed rate (R² = 0.265, p < 0.07). Feed-rate linearity was tested at 25–100% screw speed: several materials showed excellent linearity (R² > 0.99), while poorly flowing materials had poorer linearity. Variability was reported using RSD; MCC-C1000 was notably inconsistent (0.76 g/10 sec, RSD 25.87%), whereas other MCC grades had approximately 3–5% RSD. contexts.context:
The excerpt reports that Cordova et al. evaluated the effect of moisture on the spreadability of several metal powders, including AlSi10Mg, using open and funnel tools intended to approximate powder-layer spreading in powder-bed fusion. Moisture reduced flowability and the relative density of the spread layer for all tested powders. AlSi10Mg was particularly sensitive because its greater surface roughness and more irregular particle shape promoted moisture adsorption; air drying improved the relative density of AlSi10Mg layers. The excerpt also notes that surface satellites and roughness can increase water adsorption, while humidity harms spreading repeatability. These findings support measuring both powder flowability and deposited-layer density when assessing pre-treatment and drying.

For Snow et al., spreadability is characterized through measurable relationships between powder properties and spreading performance. The proposed metrics include build-plate coverage percentage, powder deposition rate, and the rate of change of the avalanche angle. Input variables include layer thickness, recoating speed, spreader material, and powder quality, while angle of repose is treated as an indicator of spreadability. Increasing recoating speed increased deposition rate and the rate of change of avalanche angle, but did not directly affect build-plate coverage. Blade material had a notable effect on coverage. The work did not provide in-depth quantification of packing fraction or a direct spread-layer-density correlation.

contexts.context: Cordova et al. (2020) investigates powder spreadability in laser powder bed fusion using two applicator tools designed specifically for thin-layer application. The study examines four metal powders—Inconel 718, Ti6Al4V, AlSi10Mg, and Scalmalloy—in four humidity-related conditions, including as-received, vacuum-dried, air-dried, and moisturized states. Standard characterization includes powder morphology, moisture content, chemical composition, and Hall-flowmeter flowability. The excerpt identifies AlSi10Mg as particularly sensitive to moisture and oxygen uptake; these contaminants substantially reduce spreadability and the relative density of the deposited layer. It also emphasizes that successful L-PBF requires both high powder flowability and high apparent density, because continuous and uniform layers generally support higher final-part density. Flow behavior is affected by friction, mechanical interlocking, van der Waals forces, liquid bridging, particle morphology, particle-size distribution, and surface topology. Moisture adsorption can additionally promote a thicker oxide layer, especially for aluminum powders exposed to air. The excerpt does not provide Snow, Martukanitz, and Joshi’s 2019 avalanche-angle or cohesive-index metrics, nor does it report their correlations with spread-layer density or coverage; those comparisons would require the corresponding study.

snippets: To achieve high product quality, the powder is best spread as a uniform, dense layer.
The challenge for LPBF manufacturers is to develop a spreading process that can produce a consistent layer quality for the many powders used, which show considerable differences in spreadability.

particle shape and surface roughness in terms of rolling resistance and interparticle sliding friction as well as particle cohesion all have a major (sometimes surprising) influence on the powder layer quality
The “spreadability” of a powder can be defined as the powder ability to spread under certain conditions to form a uniform and highly packed powder layer.
Bad spreadability can lead to powder bed defects, segregation, non-uniform density and/or a loose particle packing

contexts.context: The excerpt reports that for fine AM metal powders, Hausner ratio (HR) is inadequate: most were classified “freely flowing” (HR < 1.25) despite poor optical flowability (uopt > 2.5). Avalanche angle (aP) and surface fractal (wP) correlated more clearly with uopt, though alloy, particle-size distribution, shape, and interparticle forces contributed scatter. Good powders had low mean and narrow avalanche distributions; low aP corresponded to low coefficient of variation. A surface-fractal threshold near wP = 5.0 indicated good flow, associated with aP ≈49° (Fe)–54° (Ni). A combined model predicted uopt with r² = 0.94 (RMSE 0.23).
contexts.question:
Context: we run a small open-hardware auger powder doser: a tube with a helical auger (stepper-driven, 5-100 rpm) fed from a small hopper, a servo that tilts the tube from horizontal (0 deg) toward vertical (90 deg, gravity assisting discharge), a solenoid that taps the tube, and an analytical balance (0.1 mg) under the outlet logging cumulative discharged mass vs time at about 2.5 Hz. Across a 12-powder battery (salts, food biopolymers, silicon, gas-atomized AlSi10Mg) the mass discharged per auger revolution ("feed factor") spans three decades and its rank correlates strongly with literature angle of repose (Spearman rho = -0.84). We now want to use the doser as a cheap per-batch flowability screen for in-house gas-atomized aluminium alloy powder (Al 4047, Al-12Si) intended for laser powder bed fusion (LPBF), as a stand-in for a dedicated spreadability tester that costs tens of thousands of dollars. The powder will be sieved (e.g. -63 um or 20-63 um) before testing.

Please synthesize the peer-reviewed literature, with quantitative values and citations, on:

1. Which flowability measurements best predict LPBF powder spreadability / spread-layer quality (layer packing density, coverage, roughness, streaking, part density): Hall/Carney funnel flow, Hausner ratio/Carr index, static angle of repose, rotating-drum dynamic angle of repose and cohesive index (e.g. GranuDrum), avalanche angle / break energy / surface fractal (e.g. Revolution Powder Analyzer), FT4 rheometry (basic flow energy, specific energy, flow-rate index, compressibility), shear-cell flow function. Report reported correlation strengths (e.g. Spierings et al. 2016; Snow, Martukanitz & Joshi 2019; Cordova et al. 2020; Marchetti & Hulme-Smith 2021; others) and which metrics work for aluminium alloy powders (AlSi10Mg, AlSi12) whose low density raises the cohesion-to-weight ratio (granular Bond number).

2. Evidence that screw/auger feeder behaviour correlates with standard flowability metrics: feed factor and its normalisation by bulk density (volumetric fill efficiency), feed-rate variability (RSD), speed dependence of mass per revolution, tilt/inclination dependence of screw conveyors (e.g. Wang, Li, Muzzio & Glasser 2017; Bostijn et al. 2019; Van Snick et al. 2017; inclined screw conveyor studies), and any work using fluctuation statistics of discharged mass, tilting-tube or tilting-box onset angles, or vibration/tap-induced discharge as flowability indices.

3. How rotating-drum indices are defined (dynamic angle vs drum speed, cohesive index as interface-fluctuation standard deviation, avalanche statistics), and whether an analogous index can be computed from fluctuations in the mass-discharge-rate signal of a feeder outlet. Which features of a mass-vs-time trace are physically analogous to dynamic angle of repose and to cohesion?

4. What magnitude of change in these metrics corresponds to a practically significant change in spreadability for gas-atomized metal powders (e.g. avalanche-angle or dynamic-angle differences of a few degrees; cohesive-index thresholds; Hausner thresholds), and which batch-to-batch variations of gas-atomized powder (fines fraction below 15-20 um, satellites, sphericity, moisture, surface oxide, particle size distribution width) drive those changes. How do sieving and drying shift these metrics?

5. Recommended test conditions for a reproducible flowability screen: sample conditioning/pre-shear, drying, relative humidity, replicates, reference powders, and known pitfalls (e.g. electrostatic charging, segregation in the hopper, oversize particles jamming).

Finish with a concise recommendation: which two inexpensive, scalar flowability numbers (and how to normalise them) would be the most defensible proxies for LPBF spreadability that a tilting auger + balance could deliver.

contexts.context: Cordova et al. (2020) studied LPBF powders including AlSi10Mg. AlSi10Mg’s true density was \(2.65 \pm 0.01\) g/cm³. After humid exposure (50 °C, 80% RH, 72 h), it formed agglomerates; moisture increased from \(0.057 \pm 0.020\%\) as-received to \(0.437 \pm 0.140\%\), and oxygen increased, consistent with additional surface oxidation. contexts.context: Cordova et al. examined four LPBF powders under drying/moisture conditions. AlSi10Mg had irregular particles, many satellites, the lowest shape index (fshape = 0.73 versus 0.84 Inconel 718, 0.90 Ti6Al4V, 0.79 Scalmalloy), and a broader PSD than the other alloys. After 72 h at 50 °C/80% RH, AlSi10Mg showed the strongest moisture response: approximately 0.437% moisture, visible compaction and layered discoloration. Other powders formed agglomerates that were easily separated by shaking. SEM found no significant morphology or surface changes; moisture primarily affected powders physically, not chemically.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes the Revolution Powder Analyzer: a 100-mm-diameter, 35-mm-wide transparent rotating drum with camera imaging. Powder is fluidized at 90 rpm for 30 s, then measured at 0.6 rpm (15 fps), using 99.4 cm³ tap-density samples; typically 3–128 avalanches are recorded. Avalanche angle \(a_P\) is the free-surface angle immediately before an avalanche. Surface fractal \(w_P\), scaled as software value \(100D\), indirectly reflects interparticle forces and agglomeration. Volume expansion ratio compares drum powder volume with the tapped reference volume and is related to Hausner ratio, with reduced operator sensitivity.

contexts.context: Cordova et al. (Additive Manufacturing 32, 2020, 101082) found Hall-flow behavior fastest for dense, regular Inconel 718, then Ti6Al4V; lightweight AlSi10Mg and Scalmalloy flowed more slowly. Moisturized powders sometimes did not flow; vacuum drying slightly improved flow and reduced variability, while humidity effects were substantial. AlSi10Mg’s spreadability was especially affected by particle–wall interactions, low density, and irregular morphology (shape index 0.73). Funnel/open-tool relative-density measurements had high standard deviations; Hall flow was more repeatable. Flow depends on friction, interlocking, van der Waals/electrostatic forces, liquid bridges, morphology, and PSD.
contexts.question:
Context: we run a small open-hardware auger powder doser: a tube with a helical auger (stepper-driven, 5-100 rpm) fed from a small hopper, a servo that tilts the tube from horizontal (0 deg) toward vertical (90 deg, gravity assisting discharge), a solenoid that taps the tube, and an analytical balance (0.1 mg) under the outlet logging cumulative discharged mass vs time at about 2.5 Hz. Across a 12-powder battery (salts, food biopolymers, silicon, gas-atomized AlSi10Mg) the mass discharged per auger revolution ("feed factor") spans three decades and its rank correlates strongly with literature angle of repose (Spearman rho = -0.84). We now want to use the doser as a cheap per-batch flowability screen for in-house gas-atomized aluminium alloy powder (Al 4047, Al-12Si) intended for laser powder bed fusion (LPBF), as a stand-in for a dedicated spreadability tester that costs tens of thousands of dollars. The powder will be sieved (e.g. -63 um or 20-63 um) before testing.

Please synthesize the peer-reviewed literature, with quantitative values and citations, on:

1. Which flowability measurements best predict LPBF powder spreadability / spread-layer quality (layer packing density, coverage, roughness, streaking, part density): Hall/Carney funnel flow, Hausner ratio/Carr index, static angle of repose, rotating-drum dynamic angle of repose and cohesive index (e.g. GranuDrum), avalanche angle / break energy / surface fractal (e.g. Revolution Powder Analyzer), FT4 rheometry (basic flow energy, specific energy, flow-rate index, compressibility), shear-cell flow function. Report reported correlation strengths (e.g. Spierings et al. 2016; Snow, Martukanitz & Joshi 2019; Cordova et al. 2020; Marchetti & Hulme-Smith 2021; others) and which metrics work for aluminium alloy powders (AlSi10Mg, AlSi12) whose low density raises the cohesion-to-weight ratio (granular Bond number).

2. Evidence that screw/auger feeder behaviour correlates with standard flowability metrics: feed factor and its normalisation by bulk density (volumetric fill efficiency), feed-rate variability (RSD), speed dependence of mass per revolution, tilt/inclination dependence of screw conveyors (e.g. Wang, Li, Muzzio & Glasser 2017; Bostijn et al. 2019; Van Snick et al. 2017; inclined screw conveyor studies), and any work using fluctuation statistics of discharged mass, tilting-tube or tilting-box onset angles, or vibration/tap-induced discharge as flowability indices.

3. How rotating-drum indices are defined (dynamic angle vs drum speed, cohesive index as interface-fluctuation standard deviation, avalanche statistics), and whether an analogous index can be computed from fluctuations in the mass-discharge-rate signal of a feeder outlet. Which features of a mass-vs-time trace are physically analogous to dynamic angle of repose and to cohesion?

4. What magnitude of change in these metrics corresponds to a practically significant change in spreadability for gas-atomized metal powders (e.g. avalanche-angle or dynamic-angle differences of a few degrees; cohesive-index thresholds; Hausner thresholds), and which batch-to-batch variations of gas-atomized powder (fines fraction below 15-20 um, satellites, sphericity, moisture, surface oxide, particle size distribution width) drive those changes. How do sieving and drying shift these metrics?

5. Recommended test conditions for a reproducible flowability screen: sample conditioning/pre-shear, drying, relative humidity, replicates, reference powders, and known pitfalls (e.g. electrostatic charging, segregation in the hopper, oversize particles jamming).

Finish with a concise recommendation: which two inexpensive, scalar flowability numbers (and how to normalise them) would be the most defensible proxies for LPBF spreadability that a tilting auger + balance could deliver.

contexts.context: The excerpt reports that the Revolution Powder Analyzer quantitatively distinguishes AM powders with adequate versus inadequate flowability, correlating with optical layer-flow assessments. A proposed composite flowability \(u\) uses avalanche-angle distribution (\(r_{aP}\)), avalanche-surface fractal (\(w_P\)), its distribution (\(r_{wP}\)), and particle ellipticity \(E\). For the tested machine, \(u<2.5\) guaranteed optically high-quality SLM layers, though limits are machine-specific. \(w_P=5.0\) corresponded to avalanche angles of approximately \(49^\circ\) (Fe)–\(54^\circ\) (Ni), with substantial scatter. Lightweight Al/Ti powders may behave differently because material density affects interparticle-force-to-weight ratios.

contexts.context: The excerpt emphasizes that AM powder qualification lacks standardized, practical methods, and that different batches can have markedly different flow despite similar particle-size distributions (Lyckfeldt). Gas-atomized powders are typically tens of micrometers, mostly spherical but containing nonspherical particles; size distributions support powder-bed packing. Hall flowmeters/funnel methods have limited sensitivity to fine friction differences. Bulk and tap density do not represent actual spread-layer packing. Particle morphology, surface roughness/chemistry, size distribution, and environmental conditions affect measurements; advanced rheometry may better distinguish AM powders.

contexts.context: Slotwinski and Garboczi (2015, JOM 67, DOI 10.1007/s11837-014-1290-7) review metrology needs for metal-AM powders and ASTM F3049 standardization. They emphasize that powder size distribution and its interaction with a specific AM process remain insufficiently quantified. Clayton showed that powders with identical shear-cell behavior can have “markedly different dynamic behavior,” potentially more representative of AM flow. The authors caution against relying on a single powder characteristic and recommend combining “shear, dynamic, and bulk property measurements.” They identify powder size, shape, chemistry, and day-to-day/machine variability as unresolved challenges.

contexts.context: The excerpt provides background for comparing powder-flowability tests, but it does not report the Marchetti and Hulme-Smith (2021) regression analysis or identify which metric best correlated with spreadability. It emphasizes that flowability is multidimensional and depends on powder properties as well as handling, storage, measurement conditions, and equipment. The described metrics include Jenike flow function, internal and wall friction from shear testing, angle of repose, Hall flow time, density measurements, and FT4 powder rheometry. Flow function is classified using the ratio of major consolidation stress to unconfined yield strength, with higher values indicating easier flow. Angle of repose is interpreted such that steeper heaps indicate greater cohesiveness. Hall flow is a comparative gravity-flow test mainly appropriate for free-flowing powders and may not represent additive-manufacturing conditions because the laboratory stress state differs from real processing; it is also affected by arching, bridging, clinging, and other effects. FT4 rheometry measures dynamic flow resistance and shear-related properties, making it particularly relevant to powder-bed spreading because shear is an important force in that process. Thus, the excerpt supports methodological distinctions and limitations but contains no comparative regression outcomes for Hall flow, Hausner ratio, FT4, shear cell, or angle of repose.

contexts.context: The excerpt does not report Marchetti and Hulme’s 2021 regression analysis or identify which flowability metric best correlated with spreadability. It provides relevant background by emphasizing that metal-powder flowability depends on particle properties, stress state, equipment, and handling method, so results from different tests may not be directly interchangeable. The methods mentioned include Hall-type flow testing in the broader context of flow-rate measurements, Hausner ratio and Carr index derived from bulk and tapped density, static and dynamic angle of repose (AOR), and shear-cell testing. The article specifically notes that AOR is affected by particle shape and size, moisture, bulk density, and gravity. Shear cells measure flowability through the Jenike flow index and can also determine bulk density under applied normal stress. Comparisons among RST, Brookfield PFT, and FT4 testers showed that agreement depends strongly on the powder and flowability class, with larger discrepancies for very cohesive powders. Thus, this excerpt supports the need for cross-method comparison but contains no steel-powder spreadability data, regression coefficients, or ranking of Hall flow, Hausner ratio, FT4 rheometry, shear cell, and angle of repose.

It emphasizes that powder flowability is multidimensional and depends not only on powder properties but also on handling, storage, measurement conditions, and equipment. The relevant methods include Hall flowmeter testing, Hausner ratio or density-based measures (although the Hausner ratio itself is not discussed in this excerpt), FT4 powder rheometry, shear-cell measurements, and angle of repose. Shear-cell characterization measures flow function, internal friction, and wall friction; flow function is calculated from consolidation stress and unconfined yield strength, while particle angularity, size distribution, voids, loading, and surface properties affect internal friction. Angle of repose is a gravity-based indicator in which steeper heaps generally indicate greater cohesion. Hall flow measures the time required for powder to pass through an orifice, but is primarily suitable for free-flowing powders and may not represent additive-manufacturing stress states. In contrast, FT4 rheometry measures dynamic shear resistance, and the excerpt specifically notes that shear is indicative of powder-bed-fusion spreading. Thus, the passage supports interpreting FT4 and shear-related metrics as physically relevant to spreadability, while warning that conventional tests may have limited applicability or comparability.

It emphasizes that no single flow index is necessarily sufficient for classifying flow regimes. Particle size strongly affects flowability because smaller particles have greater surface area and stronger cohesive interactions, but powders with similar particle sizes can behave differently because of particle morphology and surface roughness. contexts.context: A 2026 PBF-LB/M study tested 316L, Alloy 718, and AlSi10Mg with blade, roller, and hopper recoaters at 50, 150, and 250 mm/s. Across 27 trials and 405 layers, powder-layer arithmetic roughness (Sa) depended significantly on powder, recoater, speed, and interactions; the regression model achieved R² = 90.64% (adjusted 89.99%). AlSi10Mg generally produced the highest Sa, partly attributed to larger particles and lower density. Roller recoating yielded smoother, more uniform layers; hopper recoating produced grooves, and blade layers were rougher. AlSi10Mg roughness increased notably at higher recoater speeds.
contexts.question:
Context: we run a small open-hardware auger powder doser: a tube with a helical auger (stepper-driven, 5-100 rpm) fed from a small hopper, a servo that tilts the tube from horizontal (0 deg) toward vertical (90 deg, gravity assisting discharge), a solenoid that taps the tube, and an analytical balance (0.1 mg) under the outlet logging cumulative discharged mass vs time at about 2.5 Hz. Across a 12-powder battery (salts, food biopolymers, silicon, gas-atomized AlSi10Mg) the mass discharged per auger revolution ("feed factor") spans three decades and its rank correlates strongly with literature angle of repose (Spearman rho = -0.84). We now want to use the doser as a cheap per-batch flowability screen for in-house gas-atomized aluminium alloy powder (Al 4047, Al-12Si) intended for laser powder bed fusion (LPBF), as a stand-in for a dedicated spreadability tester that costs tens of thousands of dollars. The powder will be sieved (e.g. -63 um or 20-63 um) before testing.

Please synthesize the peer-reviewed literature, with quantitative values and citations, on:

1. Which flowability measurements best predict LPBF powder spreadability / spread-layer quality (layer packing density, coverage, roughness, streaking, part density): Hall/Carney funnel flow, Hausner ratio/Carr index, static angle of repose, rotating-drum dynamic angle of repose and cohesive index (e.g. GranuDrum), avalanche angle / break energy / surface fractal (e.g. Revolution Powder Analyzer), FT4 rheometry (basic flow energy, specific energy, flow-rate index, compressibility), shear-cell flow function. Report reported correlation strengths (e.g. Spierings et al. 2016; Snow, Martukanitz & Joshi 2019; Cordova et al. 2020; Marchetti & Hulme-Smith 2021; others) and which metrics work for aluminium alloy powders (AlSi10Mg, AlSi12) whose low density raises the cohesion-to-weight ratio (granular Bond number).

2. Evidence that screw/auger feeder behaviour correlates with standard flowability metrics: feed factor and its normalisation by bulk density (volumetric fill efficiency), feed-rate variability (RSD), speed dependence of mass per revolution, tilt/inclination dependence of screw conveyors (e.g. Wang, Li, Muzzio & Glasser 2017; Bostijn et al. 2019; Van Snick et al. 2017; inclined screw conveyor studies), and any work using fluctuation statistics of discharged mass, tilting-tube or tilting-box onset angles, or vibration/tap-induced discharge as flowability indices.

3. How rotating-drum indices are defined (dynamic angle vs drum speed, cohesive index as interface-fluctuation standard deviation, avalanche statistics), and whether an analogous index can be computed from fluctuations in the mass-discharge-rate signal of a feeder outlet. Which features of a mass-vs-time trace are physically analogous to dynamic angle of repose and to cohesion?

4. What magnitude of change in these metrics corresponds to a practically significant change in spreadability for gas-atomized metal powders (e.g. avalanche-angle or dynamic-angle differences of a few degrees; cohesive-index thresholds; Hausner thresholds), and which batch-to-batch variations of gas-atomized powder (fines fraction below 15-20 um, satellites, sphericity, moisture, surface oxide, particle size distribution width) drive those changes. How do sieving and drying shift these metrics?

5. Recommended test conditions for a reproducible flowability screen: sample conditioning/pre-shear, drying, relative humidity, replicates, reference powders, and known pitfalls (e.g. electrostatic charging, segregation in the hopper, oversize particles jamming).

Finish with a concise recommendation: which two inexpensive, scalar flowability numbers (and how to normalise them) would be the most defensible proxies for LPBF spreadability that a tilting auger + balance could deliver.

contexts.context: Marchetti and Hulme (2021) found angle of repose, specific energy, compressibility, and Hausner ratio mutually correlated, but warned that statistical significance does not ensure explanatory power. Of 59 significant relationships, only 15 achieved adjusted \(R^2>0.7\). Representative fits included MPS9–Hausner \(R^2=0.86\), conditioned bulk density–Hausner \(0.81\), specific energy–angle of repose \(0.78\), and several shear-cell relationships up to \(0.98\). Fine powders more often jammed Hall/Carney funnels: many samples with \(D_{50}/D_{\text{outlet}}\approx4\!-\!15\) jammed, whereas coarser sample 5 flowed (Hall 21 s; Carney 4.7 s).

contexts.context: Marchetti & Hulme (Powder Technology 384, 2021) found no representative Hall/Carney correlations for cohesive steel powders because funnel jamming prevents measurable flow rates. Conditioned bulk density (CBD) strongly correlated with most metrics; CBD–Hausner ratio followed “CBD = −5.65(±0.9)·HR,” adjusted R²=0.81, and CBD–MPS9 had R²=0.72. The authors recommend multiple tests because metrics probe different powder properties and are preparation-sensitive.

contexts.context: The study compared 316L, Alloy 718, and AlSi10Mg. AlSi10Mg had ~3.5% compressibility, highest FT4 specific energy, and intermediate Granudrum avalanche angle (AA 39° versus 316L 36° and Alloy 718 46°). Higher AA/DA generally indicates poorer flow. Granudrum cohesive index (CI) clearly differentiated powders: 316L was lowest from 2–70 rpm; above 60 rpm AlSi10Mg was highest. Spreadability testing used 50–250 mm/s recoating, 50-µm layers, and blade, roller, or hopper recoaters. Digital-microscope and laser-scanner roughness correlated significantly (r = 0.794).
contexts.question:
Context: we run a small open-hardware auger powder doser: a tube with a helical auger (stepper-driven, 5-100 rpm) fed from a small hopper, a servo that tilts the tube from horizontal (0 deg) toward vertical (90 deg, gravity assisting discharge), a solenoid that taps the tube, and an analytical balance (0.1 mg) under the outlet logging cumulative discharged mass vs time at about 2.5 Hz. Across a 12-powder battery (salts, food biopolymers, silicon, gas-atomized AlSi10Mg) the mass discharged per auger revolution ("feed factor") spans three decades and its rank correlates strongly with literature angle of repose (Spearman rho = -0.84). We now want to use the doser as a cheap per-batch flowability screen for in-house gas-atomized aluminium alloy powder (Al 4047, Al-12Si) intended for laser powder bed fusion (LPBF), as a stand-in for a dedicated spreadability tester that costs tens of thousands of dollars. The powder will be sieved (e.g. -63 um or 20-63 um) before testing.

Please synthesize the peer-reviewed literature, with quantitative values and citations, on:

1. Which flowability measurements best predict LPBF powder spreadability / spread-layer quality (layer packing density, coverage, roughness, streaking, part density): Hall/Carney funnel flow, Hausner ratio/Carr index, static angle of repose, rotating-drum dynamic angle of repose and cohesive index (e.g. GranuDrum), avalanche angle / break energy / surface fractal (e.g. Revolution Powder Analyzer), FT4 rheometry (basic flow energy, specific energy, flow-rate index, compressibility), shear-cell flow function. Report reported correlation strengths (e.g. Spierings et al. 2016; Snow, Martukanitz & Joshi 2019; Cordova et al. 2020; Marchetti & Hulme-Smith 2021; others) and which metrics work for aluminium alloy powders (AlSi10Mg, AlSi12) whose low density raises the cohesion-to-weight ratio (granular Bond number).

2. Evidence that screw/auger feeder behaviour correlates with standard flowability metrics: feed factor and its normalisation by bulk density (volumetric fill efficiency), feed-rate variability (RSD), speed dependence of mass per revolution, tilt/inclination dependence of screw conveyors (e.g. Wang, Li, Muzzio & Glasser 2017; Bostijn et al. 2019; Van Snick et al. 2017; inclined screw conveyor studies), and any work using fluctuation statistics of discharged mass, tilting-tube or tilting-box onset angles, or vibration/tap-induced discharge as flowability indices.

3. How rotating-drum indices are defined (dynamic angle vs drum speed, cohesive index as interface-fluctuation standard deviation, avalanche statistics), and whether an analogous index can be computed from fluctuations in the mass-discharge-rate signal of a feeder outlet. Which features of a mass-vs-time trace are physically analogous to dynamic angle of repose and to cohesion?

4. What magnitude of change in these metrics corresponds to a practically significant change in spreadability for gas-atomized metal powders (e.g. avalanche-angle or dynamic-angle differences of a few degrees; cohesive-index thresholds; Hausner thresholds), and which batch-to-batch variations of gas-atomized powder (fines fraction below 15-20 um, satellites, sphericity, moisture, surface oxide, particle size distribution width) drive those changes. How do sieving and drying shift these metrics?

5. Recommended test conditions for a reproducible flowability screen: sample conditioning/pre-shear, drying, relative humidity, replicates, reference powders, and known pitfalls (e.g. electrostatic charging, segregation in the hopper, oversize particles jamming).

Finish with a concise recommendation: which two inexpensive, scalar flowability numbers (and how to normalise them) would be the most defensible proxies for LPBF spreadability that a tilting auger + balance could deliver.
